name: The Christian walk
about: Separation, service, and walking with God.

teachings.title: Blessed is he that considereth the poor
teachings.summary: God blesses those who help the poor out of unfeigned charity rather than to be seen, because the heart behind the giving is what He rewards.
teachings.text:
**Psalm 41** is brief and to the point. David opens with the doctrine of the Lord's promise to preserve and give long life on the earth to those of His people who consider the poor. Who show mercy to the widows and take up the cause of the fatherless.

Just as the commandment to honor your parents comes with a promise, that it be well with you and lengthen your days, this practice of pure religion, to consider the poor, comes with a similar blessing.

Basic stuff, which we are told over and over again in scripture, because it often is the hardest thing for man to do; love the unlovable the way God loves us.

**Luke 14:13–14**
*But when thou makest a feast, call the poor, the maimed, the lame, the blind: And thou shalt be blessed; for they cannot recompense thee: for thou shalt be recompensed at the resurrection of the just*.

The act of giving alms or feeding the poor is not itself what gives us blessings. Many may be generous in their actions, to be seen of men or to make themselves self-righteous.

Helping people who cannot help you back out of love, is love unfeigned. It is the charity Paul calls us to. The selfless, sacrificial love for God and others, in your heart. More so than the actual alms or donation of goods. The spirit behind it is everything.

**1 Corinthians 13:3**
*And though I bestow all my goods to feed the poor, and though I give my body to be burned, and have not charity, it profiteth me nothing.*

So we see that the love behind the care given to the poor, is rewarded with strengthening us in our sickness, delivering us from our enemies, God showing to us the mercy we showed those who could never repay us for the kindness.

Those that do it for their own reasons, have their reward. But the heart behind it is what God wants from us.

**Matthew 25:40**
*And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me*.

**Proverbs 19:17**
*He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the Lord; and that which he hath given will he pay him again.*

God loves a cheerful giver, one who isn't seeking anything for himself.

**Proverbs 22:9**
*He that hath a bountiful eye shall be blessed; for he giveth of his bread to the poor.*

But those that oppress the poor, God hates.

**Proverbs 14:31**
*He that oppresseth the poor reproacheth his Maker: but he that honoureth him hath mercy on the needy*

teachings.title: The desires of thine heart
teachings.summary: When we trust the Lord and do good, our heart's desires become His, turning from our own lusts to pure religion and good works done for others so they glorify God.
teachings.text:
God promises those that trust in Him and do good will be given the desires of our hearts.

**Jeremiah 17:9–10**
*The heart is deceitful above all things, and desperately wicked: who can know it? I the LORD search the heart, I try the reins, even to give every man according to his ways, and according to the fruit of his doings.*

When we are right with God, and do according to His ways, our heart's desires are His. They are upright and good, because our will becomes His when in all our ways we acknowledge Him, and allow the Lord to direct our paths.

He tries the reins, and sees our good works and rewards us openly. We consider the poor and broken-hearted. We take up the cause of the fatherless and widows. We spread the good news of eternal life in Christ Jesus. We live lives separated unto the gospel, and consider the profit of others above our own. Our desires become for the good of others.

*Lord help me to live from day to day*
*In such a self-forgetful way,*
*That even when I kneel to pray*
*My prayer shall be for others*.

This hymn encapsulates the concept.

**James 1:27**
*Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.*

When we consider others, when we love our neighbors and even our enemies, when we practice pure religion, the outward works of our faith, it should be for others.

And our keeping ourselves from the filth of the world is part of that, that God will see our good works, and give us our desires, and make all things come to pass.

*He shall bring forth thy righteousness as the light, and thy judgment as the noonday.*

We are the light of the world. Our purpose is to magnify the light within us that others, yes others, see it and glorify God.

**Matthew 5:16**
*Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.*

By trusting the Lord and doing good, we preserve our nation, we get to dwell in the land, we are fed, and we see our hearts turn from desiring our own wicked lusts, to seeking good for others.

teachings.title: Delight in the saints, not Lordship salvation
teachings.summary: Calling Jesus Lord is a saved believer's statement of fact, not the false gospel of Lordship salvation; our good works add nothing to God but are poured out in love and service to the saints.
teachings.text:
**Psalm 16** presents another sacred hymn celebrating the Lord's salvation, the eternal security of the believer, and the promise of the risen Christ.

The preservation of the saints is the hope of all who place their trust in God. Our very being cries out to Him for salvation, recognizing He is Lord.

Note here that this isn't "Lordship salvation," a false gospel that says you must "make Jesus the Lord of your life" to be saved. It is saved believers, already trusting Him to save us, recognizing that He IS the Lord, as a statement of fact.

David writes, *Thou art my Lord: my goodness extendeth not to thee; But to the saints that are in the earth, and to the excellent, in whom is all my delight.* The good that we do isn't for Him, it adds nothing to the holy and perfect God.

The idea that Jesus needs us to make Him Lord, that by our "turning from sin," we justify ourselves before God, is hubris. It's a false gospel.

The good we do comes from Him, and is poured out to the brothers and sisters, the saints. We benefit others, and they glorify God. We obey His judgements, to one another's profit.

**Matthew 5:16**
*Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.*

We submit ourselves to the righteousness of God. We do not seek to establish our own righteousness, but to magnify His.

**Romans 10:3–4**
*For they being ignorant of God’s righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth.*

David's burden is for the saints in the earth, his delight is to the excellent of God. Just as we are commanded to.

**John 13:34–35**
*A new commandment I give unto you, That ye love one another; as I have loved you, that ye also love one another. By this shall all men know that ye are my disciples, if ye have love one to another.*

While we should seek to live peaceably with all men, we should especially look with love upon our fellow believers.

**Galatians 6:9–10**
*And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not. As we have therefore opportunity, let us do good unto all men, especially unto them who are of the household of faith.*

This is the message that we have heard from the beginning. It is our job as Christians. It is how we are to know one another. Not keeping to ourselves or seeking out own profit. Certainly not by hating our brothers.

1 John 3:10–11
*In this the children of God are manifest, and the children of the devil: whosoever doeth not righteousness is not of God, neither he that loveth not his brother. For this is the message that ye heard from the beginning, that we should love one another.*

This is the mind of Christ, to be servants, one to another. To delight in others.

The ultimate expression of humility isn't thinking less of yourself, but not thinking of yourself at all. And the humbleness of submission to God's righteousness should naturally turn to our service for others. Not to add to God's goodness our filthy rags, but to glorify His goodness in us.

teachings.title: Defend the widow and the fatherless
teachings.summary: God's call to defend and provide for the widow, the fatherless and the needy is the outward practice He expects of believers, and He desires this mercy rather than the vain rituals and sacrifices of works-based religion.
teachings.text:
The reoccurring theme of the Lord defending the widow, the fatherless and the poor, and our role in carrying out righteous judgment for them, is probably the most talked about doctrine outside of Who God is, and the doctrines of salvation in Christ.

More than anything else, we are to clothe and feed the truly needy, to make sure people don't take advantage of those who have no one to defend them. No husband, no father. To do unto the least of these, and in doing so, doing it for Jesus.

**James 1:27**
*Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.*

This is the ultimate expression of our faith. The outward practice God expects. Self-sacrifice for others, not the selfish sacrifice of the works-based religions of the world.

**Hosea 6:6**
*For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings*

All the penance and "Eucharist" sacrifices, and all the other rites and rituals men do to get the Lord to be pleased with them are vain. God wants us to exercise mercy and judgment.

**Proverbs 21:3**
*To do justice and judgment is more acceptable to the LORD than sacrifice.*

Jesus, reading Isaiah, gives us the mission statement for Christians;

Luke 4:18–19
*The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, To preach the acceptable year of the Lord.*

Amen

teachings.title: Biblical Christianity, not social justice
teachings.summary: God's justice and care for the poor and fatherless are Christian virtues done personally and through the church, not handed to government or hijacked as cover for the guilty.
teachings.text:
One thing that we see again and again in Proverbs is a call for God's justice. Righteous judgment. Equity for the poor and oppressed.

These are Christian virtues and values. But when a Christian Nation abandons them, when they hold vengeance and disdain for the poor as respecters of persons, then these ideas are hijacked by those seeking to defend the guilty. They are used as rhetorical cover for perverting Justice, by those who call evil good and good evil.

Right judgment doesn't mean weak judgment. Or lack of judgment. We should consider the poor with the understanding that it's often sin that brings them to poverty. That we should provide the opportunity for gleaning our fields. To be generous and hospitable, while maintaining the biblical truth; *that if any would not work, neither should he eat.*

We should plead for the fatherless, explicitly standing against the causes of fatherlessness, such as fornication and adultery and divorce.

Feeding and clothing the needy is an opportunity to do unto them and by doing so, doing it unto God. What we do to the least of our brothers, we are doing to the Lord. Therefore, it should be personal and local. Acts of charity and alms done discreetly, or by our churches. Not given off to the government to do for us.

Biblical Christianity, not "social justice."

teachings.title: Usury and forgiving our debtors
teachings.summary: God's people should not take usury or unjust gain from the poor but give cheerfully and forgive debts, as God has forgiven us.
teachings.text:
This even extended to making a profit on food sold to the poor;

**Leviticus 25:35-37**
*And if thy brother be waxen poor, and fallen in decay with thee; then thou shalt relieve him: yea, though he be a stranger, or a sojourner; that he may live with thee. Take thou no usury of him, or increase: but fear thy God; that thy brother may live with thee. Thou shalt not give him thy money upon usury, nor lend him thy victuals for increase.*

Land owners were expected to allow gleaning of their fields, that after a harvest, the poor should go through the fields and bring in anything left behind by the laborers.

Alms and feasts of charity are expected of the Lord's people. Forgiveness of debts. A cheerful giver, providing for those in need is praised.

**Proverbs 11:25-27**
*The liberal soul shall be made fat: and he that watereth shall be watered also himself. He that withholdeth corn, the people shall curse him: but blessing shall be upon the head of him that selleth it.*

As **Proverbs 28:8** promises;

*He that by usury and unjust gain increaseth his substance, he shall gather it for him that will pity the poor*.

The gain you may make is temporary. The Lord will make certain your wealth is distributed to the righteous, in the end.

Because God is so just to forgive us, we should love one another enough to be like Him.

**Luke 7:41-42**
*There was a certain creditor which had two debtors: the one owed five hundred pence, and the other fifty. And when they had nothing to pay, he frankly forgave them both. Tell me therefore, which of them will love him most?*

So, we should not seek unjust gain, and further, we should relieve those in our debt, as God has forgiven us.

**Matthew 6:9-13**
*After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil: For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen.*

teachings.title: Iron sharpeneth iron
teachings.summary: Christian friends sharpen one another and act as a mirror of our heart, as does scripture, and we should not forget what we see but be doers of the word.
teachings.text:
Following along in chapter **27:13**, we are again reminded to avoid guaranteeing the debt of someone unknown or unreliable, to take their coat or a pledge as collateral. This of course, is always wise, or to swear not at all for a stranger.

Verse 14, don't be an annoying neighbor. Even a good thing, such as blessing a friend, is counted a curse when done at an inappropriate or inopportune time.

*A continual dropping in a very rainy day and a contentious woman are alike. Whosoever hideth her hideth the wind, and the ointment of his right hand, which bewrayeth itself.*

It is clear that Solomon had issue with contentious women, and the Spirit confirms this plight. As annoying as a continuous dropping or rain, impossible to hide. Like holding back the wind or a handful of oil, her nagging and arguing is impossible to contain.

Don't be that woman. Don't be that henpecked husband.

Next, an often quoted verse, Iron sharpeneth iron. We in the Christian life should cultivate other Christians as friends. And as friends, we can help hone one another, as sharpening a blade, to improve each other.

**Hebrews 10:23-24**
*Let us hold fast the profession of our faith without wavering; (for he is faithful that promised;) And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works*

A friend can sharpen the countenance of his friend, then to, as the reflection of your face in water revealed your appearance, so too is your heart revealed when you deal man to man. In other words, our friends can be a mirror into our own heart.

When we have the opportunity to see ourselves as we are, don't ignore it or forget it. It's a means to improve. To sharpen our iron. The way we see ourselves without reflection, is often tainted and false. Built up by our own rationalizing and self-deception. But our heart is made known to us by our interactions with others. It is also reflected back at us in reading Scripture.

 **James 1:23-25**
*For if any be a hearer of the word, and not a doer, he is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass: For he beholdeth himself, and goeth his way, and straightway forgetteth what manner of man he was. But whoso looketh into the perfect law of liberty, and continueth therein, he being not a forgetful hearer, but a doer of the work, this man shall be blessed in his deed.*

We should relish the opportunity to see ourselves as we really are, unashamed because we are walking God's path. Being a doer or the word, not a hearer only. That when we see our heart, man to man we are not ashamed. And that others look at us and see the love of Christ.

teachings.title: It is a glory to pass over a transgression
teachings.summary: As Christ taught to turn the other cheek, it is a glory to defer anger and let slights go rather than react like a fool.
teachings.text:
Rounding out the chapter are true sayings and the promises of God.

False witnesses shall be punished. Liars will not get away with it. Ungodly witnesses hate judgment and devour iniquity. There are judgments prepared by God for scorners and stripes for the backs of fools. They will have their reward.

But those that seek wisdom and understanding show love to themselves and shall be rewarded with good.

A fool's delight is unseemly. It really is obnoxious and troublesome to see the happiness of a fool. It is usually found in nonsense or tragedy for others. God calls it as unnatural as a servant ruling over princes.

While I admit it is likely not an allusion to this, it is what that allegory reminded me of;

**Galatians 4:1-7**
*Now I say, That the heir, as long as he is a child, differeth nothing from a servant, though he be lord of all; But is under tutors and governors until the time appointed of the father. Even so we, when we were children, were in bondage under the elements of the world: But when the fulness of the time was come, God sent forth his Son, made of a woman, made under the law, To redeem them that were under the law, that we might receive the adoption of sons. And because ye are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father. Wherefore thou art no more a servant, but a son; and if a son, then an heir of God through Christ.*

We, as heirs are no longer under the governor of the law, no longer under its tutelage.  Princes don't serve the servants.

Solomon cautions discretion and temperance in the face of wrath. To let the small stuff go, to pass over transgression, to let go of a slight. Sometimes it is better to just ignore things that a fool would impulsively react to. As Jesus said;

**Matthew 5:38-42**
*Ye have heard that it hath been said, An eye for an eye, and a tooth for a tooth: But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also. And if any man will sue thee at the law, and take away thy coat, let him have thy cloak also. And whosoever shall compel thee to go a mile, go with him twain. Give to him that asketh thee, and from him that would borrow of thee turn not thou away.*

These examples aren't so-small slights for most men. Our pride and anger at being treated poorly or stolen from can be difficult to resist. But it is a glory to pass over such things, and defer our anger.

The sayings continue; *House and riches are the inheritance of fathers: and a prudent wife is from the Lord.*

Whatever inheritance you may receive from your fathers, the legacy they may leave is a good thing, but a prudent wife is a gift from God. A blessing He gives men, so appreciate it.

Another warning against sloth, that the lazy will suffer hunger. As we've noted before, God says if a man doesn't work, he shouldn't eat. *A slothful man hideth his hand in his bosom, and will not so much as bring it to his mouth again.*

Smiting a scorner teaches the simple to not be like them. Reproof of the wise is welcome and brings knowledge and understanding.

Above all, fear the Lord and give ear to wisdom and seek knowledge and understanding.

 *The fear of the Lord tendeth to life: and he that hath it shall abide satisfied; he shall not be visited with evil.*

*Hear counsel, and receive instruction, that thou mayest be wise in thy latter end. There are many devices in a man's heart; nevertheless the counsel of the Lord, that shall stand.* Amen

teachings.title: No respect of persons; lending to the Lord
teachings.summary: Man naturally favours the rich and forsakes the poor, but James forbids respect of persons, and having pity on the poor is lending to the Lord, who will repay.
teachings.text:
Other sayings in **Proverbs 19** add to the previous lessons in earlier chapters. The wealth of a man makes many friends. It is human nature to be respecters of persons. To favor the wealthy for what they could do for you, while the poor is separated from their neighbors, disregarded.

James warns of this in his epistle;

**James 2:1-12**
*My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons. For if there come unto your assembly a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment; And ye have respect to him that weareth the gay clothing, and say unto him, Sit thou here in a good place; and say to the poor, Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool: Are ye not then partial in yourselves, and are become judges of evil thoughts? Hearken, my beloved brethren, Hath not God chosen the poor of this world rich in faith, and heirs of the kingdom which he hath promised to them that love him? But ye have despised the poor. Do not rich men oppress you, and draw you before the judgment seats?*

Proverbs tell us again and again that the poor with integrity is better than a fool or a scorner. *Even though as respecters of persons, we will intreat the favour of the princes: and every man is a friend to him that giveth gifts.*

For a prince like Rehoboam, this understanding of flattery and false friends is essential. But for those of us who may not be in that position, it's also a warning against acting that way ourselves.

*All the brethren of the poor do hate him: how much more do his friends go far from him? he pursueth them with words, yet they are wanting to him.*

These truths are not just observations, but an insight to our own behavior, and the underlying idea that shows us why James' appeal to impartiality is needed.

*He that hath pity upon the poor lendeth unto the Lord; and that which he hath given will he pay him again*.

This is the mind of Christ. This is the work of the Spirit. This is the way of the Lord. We are to be kind. Not blindly enabling sloth and rewarding scoffers and fools, but having mercy on the poor. The widow left without honor. Taking care of our parents and judging the fatherless, caring for those without. Having mercy and love, without being perverted by wealth and title, and what they could do for me. We are lending to the Lord. He will repay. Amen

teachings.title: A friend born for adversity
teachings.summary: God tries the heart like a refiner, and a man of excellent spirit loves others as Christ loved us, being a friend and brother in adversity, forgiving and holding his tongue.
teachings.text:
*The fining pot is for silver, and the furnace for gold: but the Lord trieth the hearts.*

God is refining fire. He tries every man, knowing our hearts, examining our spirit. A man of excellent spirit is a man of understanding.

A man with an excellent spirit has a merry heart, and their joy is like medicine to others. This infectious spirit not only heals others, but brings them to glorify God.

**Matthew 5:16**
*Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.*

In that spirit, be a friend to others. Love them. Be as a brother, a help in trouble. Born for adversity. As Jesus loved you, so too love others.

**John 15:13**
*Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.*

In the extreme, this is truth and a love we should strive for, but often it really is just a softly spoken word or an ear to listen, that sows friendship and a bond of brotherhood. Forgiving transgressions, seeking love instead. Refraining from gossip and strife.

Be a man of understanding. Holding your tongue when necessary. Giving wise counsel when appropriate. But above all, having the spirit pleasing to God. Refined in time by His trials into the servant and brother He wants us to be.

teachings.title: He that hath mercy on the poor
teachings.summary: Remembering the poor is done unto Christ and lent to the Lord, and since righteousness exalteth a nation we should win souls so it becomes a nation of Christians, not Christian nationalism.
teachings.text:
Remember the poor. Do not despise them, as we are poor in spirit and God gave to us abundantly. As Jesus said;

**Matthew 25:35-40**
*For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in: Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me. Then shall the righteous answer him, saying, Lord, when saw we thee an hungred, and fed thee? or thirsty, and gave thee drink? When saw we thee a stranger, and took thee in? or naked, and clothed thee? Or when saw we thee sick, or in prison, and came unto thee? And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.*

And the promises of God to repay, that when we give to the poor we lend to the Lord.

**Psalms 41:1**
*Blessed is he that considereth the poor: the LORD will deliver him in time of trouble.*

And again, in verse 32 we see the gospel in **Proverbs**, the righteous has hope in our death. That blessed hope of eternal life in Christ Jesus. This is wisdom, to hear and believe the truth of God's mercy and grace, by the imputed righteousness of Christ.

Because righteousness exalteth a nation and sin is a reproach to any people, we should strive to win souls, instruct wisdom, have standards, that our nation would be blessed by our righteousness in Christ. Not Christian nationalism but a nation of Christians.

teachings.title: Love thy neighbour; strive not without cause
teachings.summary: Proverbs 3:27-32 is love thy neighbour, explained by the good Samaritan, and the froward, unyielding man who strives without cause is an abomination to the Lord.
teachings.text:
Verse 27-32 can be summed up; Love thy neighbor. Give to him his due, good when it is in your power, loan to him freely when you can. Don't devise evil against him. Our neighbors dwell against us, locally.

Jesus answers the question, "Who is our neighbor?" with the parable of the good Samaritan, leaning on this very wisdom. Our neighbors are those in our proximity who need help, and it is in our power to provide it. Love thy neighbor.

Strive not with a man without cause. In the NT, Paul writes;

**Romans 12:8** *If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.*

Love our enemies, certainly, but don't go out of your way to make one. Especially if they've done no harm to you. Don't be like the froward and oppressors, they are an abomination to the Lord.

**FRO'WARD**, a. L. versus: *turned or looking from.*

- Perverse, that is, turning from, with aversion or reluctance; not willing to yield or comply with what is required; unyielding; ungovernable; refractory; disobedient; peevish; as a froward child.

Implacable, unmerciful, disobedient. It is as much an abomination to unreasonable and unyielding as being a sodomite, to the Lord.

The Lord's curse will be on the house of the wicked. Vengeance is His. But the Lord blesses the household of the just. Those who work righteous judgement and show mercy. Peacemakers. The meek and lowly.

This is wisdom. And as the meek inherit the earth and peacemakers are blessed, the wise shall inherit glory.

While fools inherit shame.

teachings.title: Job restored when he prayed for his friends
teachings.summary: Job made peace with God by faith, but it was his forgiving and praying for the friends who wronged him, a picture of Christ the mediator, that led God to restore him double.
teachings.text:
Job, having seen the glory of God, His power and might, he says he has uttered what he understood not. In ignorance, he demanded of God the "why" to his predicament, and now sees the Who behind all things. He has gained understanding and repented towards the truth of the power of God. Left humbled in the dust and ash of his mourning.

This settled, Job has gained the the understanding that God does what He does, at a higher purpose and longer view than His creation can even comprehend.

The Lord then turns to Eliphaz and the two friends, saying they kindled His wrath, having spoken falsely about Him. Things that aren't right. Their prosperity gospel theology and their standing in judgment as if they were God Himself against Job was wrong.

And He tells them to make sacrifices and offer burnt offerings, and Job's prayers for forgiveness for them He will accept. This act of humiliation, seeking forgiveness through the man they had slandered, is done according to God's word, and the Lord accepted Job.

This, in a way is symbolic of Christ as the mediator between God and man, as Job is the mediator here for his friends.

And when Job prayed for his friends, the Lord turned the captivity of Job, the allowances of the devil to control his fate, and restored Job twice as much as he had.

In all these things Job never spoke improperly, but in ignorance demanded of God. But it was Job's forgiveness of others who had wronged him that led God to restore him, and bless him with more than he had.

Job reached peace with God just by his understanding and faith. But it was forgiveness of others that restored him. This is such an important point to remember.

Job first receives the comforting and support, from family and friends, that he needed. And their financial support to him that was without, allowed Job to restore his wealth. The love and respect Job had shown others paid off, as they loved on him with emotional support and alms. Gold and riches he used to make his flocks great again.

And God blessed him with 10 children, seven sons and 3 daughters. And Jobs delight in his daughters, naming them for peace, and fragrant spice and beauty, led him to make them co-heirs as their brothers.

teachings.title: Pure religion: service to others
teachings.summary: Caring for the widow, the fatherless and the poor was always God's will, not new in the New Testament, and a Christianity centered on serving others for God's glory is the goal (James 1:27, Luke 4).
teachings.text:
One of the things that we should take away from Job is his attitude towards service. Putting others first.

A lot of people seem to think that Jesus introduced all of these concepts of loving your neighbor, and caring for the poor in the New Testament. But again and again we see that this is how God wants us to be.

He took no pleasure in the blood of bulls and goats. He called people to mercy and judgment. To have discernment. To be so grateful for the things that we have that we have no problem sharing them with others. That we put others profit before ourselves.

Especially when it comes to the fatherless, the widow, the poor and feeble-minded.

**James 1:27**
*Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.*

When you reach the point where you're Christianity isn't about you at all, but about God, glorifying Him in service of others, you are reaching perfection. This should be the goal of all Christians.

I've talked about it before but, Jesus quoting Isaiah gives us a mission statement for our Christian walk:

**Luke 4:16-19**
 *And he came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up: and, as his custom was, he went into the synagogue on the sabbath day, and stood up for to read. And there was delivered unto him the book of the prophet Esaias. And when he had opened the book, he found the place where it was written, The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, To preach the acceptable year of the Lord.*

Let this mind be in you as it is in Christ.

teachings.title: Clothed in righteousness, a father to the poor
teachings.summary: Job's respect came from delivering the poor, the fatherless and the widow and wearing righteousness and judgment, and this should be the goal of every Christian man.
teachings.text:
Job's monologue continues, building upon the stipulations and understanding of God and His judgment, to how it applied to Job's life.

He laments again his current situation, wistfully thinking about his life before the tragedy. Job in all his ways acknowledging the Lord, and letting His light direct his ways.

The secret of God, I believe is the gospel. The mystery of salvation to those that believe God and it is counted for righteousness. The Almighty was with him, Job was blessed with children and prosperity and had the respect of the men at the gate.

This is the patriarchal rule of the day. The men of means and power sat in the street of the city and heard matters, and offered wisdom. They judged.

The young men feared Job, the elders gave him deference. Even the princes, the governors of the city gave him his due. They listened and watched what Job would say and do. His influence was such, that he had everyone's respect and attention.

Why? Job tells us. He delivered the poor and the fatherless. Those that had no man. He blessed the dying and gave to the widow in her need.

Because he clothed himself in righteousness and wore judgment like a crown.

This should be the goal of all Christian men. To have this mind in them as it was in Christ, to start with the Lord, and to lead others in His wisdom, for His purpose and other's profit.

Job not only was as a father to the poor, seeing the hungry and feeding them, as Jesus commands us, but further seeking out causes to take up that he hadn't known yet. Going out of his way to help others.

Note Job also did this soberly, with seriousness. That when he smiled upon someone in need, they couldn't believe their luck, they delighted in the light of his countenance.

teachings.title: Comfort the broken hearted, don't berate them
teachings.summary: Bildad's curses on grieving Job show what not to do, since a friend's suffering is a chance to let God's light shine by comforting him.
teachings.text:
Imagine being the father of 10 goodly adult children, and losing them all at once, and then having the man you thought came to comfort, now berating you.

*His roots shall be dried up beneath, and above shall his branch be cut off. His remembrance shall perish from the earth, and he shall have no name in the street.*

What a wicked thing to say to anyone suffering this loss.

When bad things happen to friends, it is an opportunity given by God to show His love. His light, on the darkness they are in.

**Matthew 5:16** 
*Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven*.

We are to comfort the broken hearted, with the love of God that His glory may be shown from Heaven.

Not make it about ourselves.

Bildad finishes his cruel screed by accusing Job of being wicked and not knowing God.

*Surely such are the dwellings of the wicked, and this is the place of him that knoweth not God.*

All to a broken man, laying in dirt made mud by his tears.

teachings.title: Though he slay me, yet will I trust
teachings.summary: Job rebukes his friends as worthless physicians, teaching that silent love is better than lectures, while he trusts God and asks only why.
teachings.text:
Job continues his rebuke of the 3 friends-turned accusers. He says he heard them and understands them, he knows what they know and isn't inferior, not a novice that needs their theory that his suffering is because his sins are great. He is lamenting because he wants to reason with God, not men.

He calls them liars and physicians with no value. They should be comforting the broken hearted, not castigating him.

He says if they'd only remained silent, that would have been wiser than the things they had said.

**Proverbs 17:28**
*Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise: and he that shutteth his lips is esteemed a man of understanding.*

When dealing with someone in grief and inconsolably miserable, it is better to sit in silence and love them, than seek to explain away their feelings, and lecture them what to do.

Many well meaning people, afraid of sitting in silence need to fill the air with words, and those overcome by sympathetic fear, seek to project those fears of their own misdeeds onto the person suffering. Like Job's friends.

Job pleads to God, and says they don't have to reply for Him, especially when their entire premise is based on a lie. He lets them know in no uncertain terms that they will have to answer to God for their temerity in speaking for Him, in unrighteous judgment.

Judging the appearance, not the spirit;

**John 7:24**
*Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.*

He puts the fear of God in them, reminding them that they are just mortal men, so they should hold their peace, shut up and let Job speak out to God, and if Job is in the wrong before the Lord, let God judge and take his life.

*Though he slay me, yet will I trust in him: but I will maintain mine own ways before him.*

We often quote the first half of this verse, to show our faith being absolute, especially in tribulation. But this is Job not only proclaiming his faith, but accepting God's judgement against him for asking, "Why?"

To Job's understanding, he had put off the sin of his youth, and was upright and perfect in his ways, having trusted God. He isn't a hypocrite (as some are) and he reiterates his conviction that he is a saved son of God. He knows that he is justified by his faith before God, so why all this?

He asks of God two things. To lift His hand from against him, to stop the mounting evil that has befallen Job, and to answer Job's question, Why?

If it is sin, tell him that he may turn from it. Does God see job as an enemy? If so why, that he may get right.

He compares himself to leaves in the wind, the stubble of the wheat, fanned into the air, as bitter things are against him. As of he's been put into stocks, marking his feet with their bonds. Permanently disfigured, physically and spiritually. As rotten meat or a motheaten garment.

Job has humbled himself before the Lord, he just wants to know the cause.

teachings.title: Quoting scripture without comfort
teachings.summary: Eliphaz quoted true proverbs but misapplied them to blame Job, warning us not to judge by appearance and lecture the afflicted.
teachings.text:
Eliphaz's monologue continues, directly from chapter 4, and he continues to paint a picture blaming Job for his own suffering. Implying secret sin that has led him to his current condition.

He says to call upon the righteous, and see if any man would answer him. Some Catholics use this verse as a proof text for praying to saints. Because they will strip verses from context, and ignore that God completely rebukes everything that is said by Job's friends.

But Eliphaz is not encouraging Job to pray to the dead, but to appeal to the stories of the righteous to find if any ever suffered as he did, If any holy one had ever been down so low.

He then begins to list off parables, about the foolish being cursed, their children killed, their harvest spoiled, their things taken by thieves. He says that this trouble doesn't come up out of nowhere, but that men are born into trouble and that it comes up like sparks flying out of a fire. As embers. That the destruction that comes naturally follows the life of a foolish man.

He advises his friend to seek God and to commit his cause to God Who is mighty and punishes the wicked. But saveth the poor.

He then gives the proverb that a man should be happy when God corrects him and to not despise the chastening of the Almighty.

**Proverbs 3:11**
*My son, despise not the chastening of the LORD; neither be weary of his correction*.

So he is quoting scripture, and some of what he is saying is true. But he's misapplying it by assuming that that is the cause of his friends misery.

And worse, he mentions children being crushed at the gate, knowing that Job's own sons and daughters were killed by a collapsing house. He insensitively talks about having his things spoiled and stolen.

He's clearly indicating that he believes Job acted foolishly in some way and deserved everything he got. And in his own judgment he thinks he's giving good advice.

It's something we should be aware of because, far too often we judge a matter by its appearance. And we have a ready verse to give. And we pride ourselves in it when we should be comforting the afflicted. Not forgiving sin, not excusing it, but when we don't know the circumstances or the situation, or even more, we know the person is honorable and upright in their ways, we shouldn't assume or presume to lecture.

But you can tell Eliphaz really thought he was cooking here, giving these great words of wisdom to a man laying in ash, with a shaved head for mourning, scraping the oozing sores on his flesh.

Telling him to hear it now and know that it's for thy own good, is the last thing Job needs to hear.

teachings.title: Who ever perished, being innocent?
teachings.summary: Eliphaz accused grieving Job of hidden sin, but Jesus taught that tragedy is not proof of greater sin, so we should comfort rather than lecture.
teachings.text:
So, to recap: Job, devastated by the loss of his children, wealth and health, and wishing he was never born, while yet not sinning against God or cursing Him, sits in ash, scraping his sore-covered flesh, in agony.

He had been blessed by these three well meaning friends, who traveled afar, and patiently, in love, sat mourning in silence for a week. But with the silence broken by Job's lamentation, Eliphaz the Temanite now speaks up.

He starts by asking that, if they attempt to talk with him, will it offend Job? And then immediately, before Job can answer, Eliphaz gives himself permission by saying "Who can withhold themselves from speaking?"

We have all likely, at one time or another been on the receiving or delivering end of this. "I know you're going through a lot, so I don't want to offend you, but I can't help myself..."

As well intentioned as this sentiment can be, what follows it rarely is a help to the person hearing it. Ultimately, the motivation behind it is self-centered and doesn't come from sympathy for the aggrieved, but out of an impatient empathy, where the friend sees it from their detached view, and thinks their opinions and musing can fix what's broken, or even just make the person stop complaining.

Many times, after having given our two-cents, we can feel comfortable washing our hands of any obligation to be bothered by a friend's burdens. "Well, if they'd just listen to reason...Oh well, I tried."

Better to have remained silent than to do this.

Eliphaz the Temanite barrels along right into it. He begins by pointing out the example Lot has been for many, that his faith and council have helped those in troubled times. Strengthening the weak. But...it is never good to follow a compliment with a "but," but now that it has come upon Job, he faints and is troubled.

Rather than encouraging Job to embrace the same strength and hope that he gave others, Eliphaz uses this good quality of his friend as an indictment. As an accusation of weakness.

I would doubt that any of the people Job had encouraged had gone through anything even remotely touching the tribulation that he found himself in. But even so, rather than repaying the favor and encouraging Job, Eliphaz makes an accusation out of it.

*Is not this thy fear, thy confidence, thy hope, and the uprightness of thy ways?*

He says, isn't your religion, your trust in God, your piety and righteousness, shouldn't that all be enough to console you? If all of that was sufficient for Job to preach to others in their moments of doubt and pain, why isn't it enough for him?

And rather than waiting for a reply to his condescending "tough love," Eliphaz answers his own question in the least charitable way possible; by accusing Job of hidden sin.

*Remember, I pray thee, who ever perished, being innocent? or where were the righteous cut off?*

This is the crux of his argument, That Job deserves what has happened to him. That he is reaping what he has sown.

Eliphaz uses the truth that God's wrath is revealed from Heaven against the ungodly, to say that this is evidence enough that so great a temptation has befallen Job, because his piety was vanity, and hid the truth of his sin.

"What goes around comes around," even when true, is the last thing we should say to another when we're trying to comfort them. Especially considering the grace God has extended to us.

 In **Luke 13**, Jesus answers his disciples, who suggest that recent tragedies that happened to others was a direct result of their sin, that it was karma, by asking "*Suppose ye that these Galilaeans were sinners above all the Galilaeans, because they suffered such things?*" Jesus says, nay, and that something evil can happen to anyone by chance, but if men don't repent, everyone will likewise perish. Stuff happens. The rain falls on the just and the unjust alike.

teachings.title: Heap coals of fire on his head
teachings.summary: Unlike Jonah, believers must show mercy to enemies, including giving them the bread of life and water of the gospel, remembering the mercy God showed them.
teachings.text:
**Matthew 5:44-45**
*But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you; That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.*

**Romans 9:15-16**
*For he saith to Moses, I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy, and I will have compassion on whom I will have compassion. So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.*

**Proverbs 25:21-23**
*If thine enemy be hungry, give him bread to eat; and if he be thirsty, give him water to drink: For thou shalt heap coals of fire upon his head, and the Lord shall reward thee. The north wind driveth away rain: so doth an angry countenance a backbiting tongue.*

Perhaps the hardest thing in the Christian life, showing mercy to those who hate us and whom we hate. But if God chooses us to be a blessing to another, it isn't on us to question why. We shouldn't be as Jonah.

And if they are hardened against us, that's on them. Our mercy will be as hot coals upon their head.

**Romans 12:20**
*Therefore if thine enemy hunger, feed him; if he thirst, give him drink: for in so doing thou shalt heap coals of fire on his head.*

Note the spiritual application of this. Your enemy hungers and thirsts. For what? Food and water? Or truth and the repentance unto faith in Christ?

Will the coals of fire make them angrier and dug in against you? Or remind them of the Hell that awaits them?

Will you withhold that bread that came down from Heaven? The waters of life that you've drank?

Are there many who don't know their right hand from left?

Only God knows.

Remember the mercy God showed you, and let that be what guides your spirit. Don't be as Jonah, and let your anger consume you.

teachings.title: Deal courageously: judging righteously as to the Lord
teachings.summary: Jehoshaphat's charge to his judges to judge without respect of persons in the fear of the Lord is the calling of every Christian to serve justly, seek others' profit and obey authority.
teachings.text:
But despite that lapse of judgement (one he would commit again) Jehosaphat's faith was great and he did lead a revival in Judah.

He preached the Lord throughout the land, placed faithful judges over the people and encouraged and empowered the priests of the Levites to fulfill their role before God for the people.

Jehosaphat calls to the men he placed in judgment over Judah to do right judgment with fear of the Lord. Not as respecters of persons. Serving the Lord faithfully and with a perfect heart. And proclaiming the righteousness of the Lord, warning against trespass, that His wrath not be kindled against them or the land.

D*eal courageously, and the Lord shall be with the good.*

This is our calling as Christians, to be just servants over those in our responsibility. To seek others profit more than our own. To deal fairly. To work as to the Lord. To obey authority.

It is an Old Testament lesson of leadership that we see throughout the New Testament applied to all Christians.

We are to judge righteously. Serve as to God.

**Hebrews 13:17**
*Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls, as they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you.*

**Romans 13:1**
*Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God.*

teachings.title: All things come of Thee: giving willingly
teachings.summary: Beyond the tithe, all we have is God's, so we should give to the church, the brethren and missions cheerfully and willingly with thanksgiving.
teachings.text:
Here in **1 Chronicles 29**, the final chapter, we come to the transition of power between King David and his son Solomon. David has, in obedience to the Lord, organized the Kingdom, set up the leaders of men and the chain of command in the various roles and responsibilities. He has given Solomon the plans for the house of God, the pattern given by the Spirit, and laid up treasure and provisions to see it built.

And the people all willingly gave treasure to build up the house of the Lord and to do His work. Free will offerings.

David calls them to prayer and to bless the Lord God of Israel, to give Him all glory and honor. David's prayer reminds us that whatever we give to the service of God is His to begin with.

Tithing, the practice of giving the first of the flock, the tenth of the wealth and harvest, etc...these are commands in the Old Testament, that we honor today in the New.

But the free will offerings here are a reminder that all we have *cometh of Thine hand, and is all Thine own.* Not just 10%, pretax income, itemized and listed on our taxes. All of it. Everything we have is His because it is by His grace we have it at all.

For all things come of God. And when we give, it is of God's own.

When we approach giving towards the church, or to help the brethren, or missions and church plants and soul winning trips...whatever it may be, give cheerfully, willingly.

Because riches and honor come from God. It is His power to make us great, and blessed by whatever riches He provides. We can't take it with us; there are none abiding.

So give joyfully, knowing it's not yours but the Lord's. And rejoice in it, praising Him in thanksgiving, that you have abundance wherewithal to give.

teachings.title: He that is chief, as he that doth serve
teachings.summary: Like David's mighty men and the disciples striving for position, believers may strive to do great things for the Lord, but first must seek to serve, counting the cost of suffering while pressing toward the prize.
teachings.text:
This chapter reminds me of the Apostles, constantly competing for position and favor and honor in the Kingdom of Heaven.

**Luke 9:46-48**
*Then there arose a reasoning among them, which of them should be greatest. And Jesus, perceiving the thought of their heart, took a child, and set him by him, And said unto them, Whosoever shall receive this child in my name receiveth me: and whosoever shall receive me receiveth him that sent me: for he that is least among you all, the same shall be great.*

**Luke 22:24-30**
*And there was also a strife among them, which of them should be accounted the greatest. And he said unto them, The kings of the Gentiles exercise lordship over them; and they that exercise authority upon them are called benefactors. But ye shall not be so: but he that is greatest among you, let him be as the younger; and he that is chief, as he that doth serve. For whether is greater, he that sitteth at meat, or he that serveth? is not he that sitteth at meat? but I am among you as he that serveth. Ye are they which have continued with me in my temptations. And I appoint unto you a kingdom, as my Father hath appointed unto me; That ye may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom, and sit on thrones judging the twelve tribes of Israel.*

**Mark 10:35-45**
*And James and John, the sons of Zebedee, come unto him, saying, Master, we would that thou shouldest do for us whatsoever we shall desire. And he said unto them, What would ye that I should do for you? They said unto him, Grant unto us that we may sit, one on thy right hand, and the other on thy left hand, in thy glory. But Jesus said unto them, Ye know not what ye ask: can ye drink of the cup that I drink of? and be baptized with the baptism that I am baptized with? And they said unto him, We can. And Jesus said unto them, Ye shall indeed drink of the cup that I drink of; and with the baptism that I am baptized withal shall ye be baptized: but to sit on my right hand and on my left hand is not mine to give; but it shall be given to them for whom it is prepared. And when the ten heard it, they began to be much displeased with James and John. But Jesus called them to him, and saith unto them, Ye know that they which are accounted to rule over the Gentiles exercise lordship over them; and their great ones exercise authority upon them. But so shall it not be among you: but whosoever will be great among you, shall be your minister: and whosoever of you will be the chiefest, shall be servant of all. For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a ransom for many.*

The Apostles and chief disciples of Jesus were as the mighty men of David. And we are called honor as well. We can do great things for the Lord, even strive with one another to out do each other. We can run the gauntlet of Philistines to bring water for our Lord, but first we should seek to serve. First we should seek to be a good judge for the children, the fatherless, the widows. A servant to our brethren.

And we should be cautious in what we strive for, as the sons of Thunder, James and John sought. The baptism of pain and persecution may be the price for glory. The cup of tribulation and suffering for His name. But even so, we should reach for the prize set before us;

**1 Corinthians 9:24-27**
*Know ye not that they which run in a race run all, but one receiveth the prize? So run, that ye may obtain. And every man that striveth for the mastery is temperate in all things. Now they do it to obtain a corruptible crown; but we an incorruptible. I therefore so run, not as uncertainly; so fight I, not as one that beateth the air: but I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway.*

**Philippians 3:13-14**
*Brethren, I count not myself to have apprehended: but this one thing I do, forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.*

teachings.title: Forgive as God has forgiven us
teachings.summary: Having been reconciled while we were God's enemies, we should show our enemies the same grace and forgive others as we ask the Father to forgive us.
teachings.text:
The Lord tells us love our enemies. That we who are saved, that have received the atonement through Jesus Christ, Who died for us while we were yet sinners, who were His enemies now reconciled in the blood of the lamb, because God is kind to the unthankful and to the evil, should judge our enemies with the same spirit of grace, longsuffering and mercy that God has shown us.

His mercy is such that we are promised by the Lord Jesus Christ that though we suffer loss, are despised for His name's sake, will be blessed. We are poor, and ours is the kingdom of God. We hunger, but we shall be filled. We weep, but we shall laugh. And when we are persecuted, we should leap for joy, because we are rewarded in Heaven.

And here on earth, our generosity, our putting others needs before our own, even to the thankless and those that seek to do evil, we shall be rewarded greatly, here on earth as well as in Heaven. *For with the same measure that ye mete withal it shall be measured to you again.*

It can be hard to not lose sight of the mercy of God that has been given to us. To take for granted so great a gift as Christ. To forget the pattern of prayer Jesus taught us, asking the Father to *forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors*. Why?

*For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.*

teachings.title: David the king as servant
teachings.summary: David's last words confess the Psalms were inspired and show him as a servant king, a picture of Christ and an example of esteeming others better than ourselves.
teachings.text:
The end of David's life is come, and the final words of the King are recorded, and they begin with a beautiful recitation of faith and doctrine.

David, the anointed of God of Jacob, the sweet psalmist of Israel, acknowledges that he was inspired by God, Who spoke through him in the Psalms. In case there was any doubt about the inspiration of the Psalms of David, which were quoted throughout the New Testament by Jesus and the Apostles. *The Spirit of the Lord spake by me, and His word was in my tongue*.

David goes further to say the God of Israel, the Rock of Israel, spake to him and advised that he as King must be just, ruling in the fear of God. This is the truth, and a standard that David, being human didn't always achieve.

But it is undeniable as we read his life story that he strove to rule as a God fearing judge, with mercy and faith. An example in patience and longsuffering for Christian believers. He tried to be as the light of the morning, which is how Jesus is described in scripture, that the people of Israel would be as the tender grass covered in dew springs forth at the light. Putting the profit of others before himself, something we are commanded to in scripture;

**Philippians 2:3-5**
*Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves. Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others. Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus*

David is a picture of the king as servant. A picture of Christ, and an example for us who follow after Jesus.

teachings.title: Leave vengeance to the Lord
teachings.summary: Taking vengeance for oneself is sin in God's eyes, but forgiving, seeking peace and trusting the Lord to judge is the path of faith that delivered David.
teachings.text:
Once again we see that the judgment of the world, taking vengeance for themselves, seeking favor by slaying David's enemies, is a sin in the eyes of the Lord. But forgiving and trying to make peace, trusting the Lord to judge, is the path we are told to take.

*As the Lord liveth, who hath redeemed my soul out of all adversity...*This is the faith we should have when we are beset by our enemies. They will either come to be friends or their own actions will be judged by God, but it is not our place to seek their hurt. We are supposed to love them, and pray for their well-being. Seeking peace.

This is considered weakness by the world, but we see in the story of David how well it served him. The Lord delivered him out of all adversity, in His time, in His way.

It is one of the hardest lessons of faith and longsuffering we can learn.

teachings.title: Blessed are the peacemakers
teachings.summary: The most peaceful solution should always be sought, especially between brothers, because peacemakers are called the children of God.
teachings.text:
First, we see David, a man after God's own heart, inquire of the Lord if he should go unto Judah, into Hebron. And the Lord answered saying yes.

David further sought peace with the men of Israel, specifically Jabeshgilead who had honored Saul by retrieving his body from the enemy, and informing them all that Judah had anointed him king. A peaceful offer to do the same. Letting them all know he was willing to honor them.

We see even though Abner's plans were different, that he took sought an outcome that was as peaceful as possible. They agree to a battle of champions, 12 vs 12. When that doesn't go his way, and he flees, Abner seeks peace with the one pursuing him. When the men of Judah arrive and see the gathered forces of Benjamin, again he cries out for peace.

There is an honor in being a peacemaker. Regardless of the righteousness of the cause or the bitterness of the disagreement, or whatever else has been done to wrong the different parties. Especially between brothers.

The most peaceful solution should always be sought, even when that solution is rejected and more forceful action is required. Even if peace creates an uneasy result, it is preferable than brothers going to war with one another.

**Matthew 5:9**
*Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God.*

If a brother is your enemy, and you have defeated him and he offers you a chance to let it go, you should consider it. Asahel did not. Joab did. And while both are heroes, one lived to fight another day. The other paid the price.

teachings.title: How are the mighty fallen: forgiving in death
teachings.summary: David's lament for Saul shows Christians should forgive those who wronged them, even in death, leaving judgment to a just God.
teachings.text:
*How are the mighty fallen* is yet another wildly used phrase in popular culture, that comes from the beauty of the King James Bible translation. As an idiom, it has come to mean that someone once in power has been toppled.

The song of David's mourning is far more valuable and insightful than just this poetic turn of phrase.

We see David demonstrate true sadness at the loss of Saul. Forgiveness that he extended to someone who had been his bitter enemy for years. Someone who had tried to kill him multiple times. We expect the future king to mourn the loss of his beloved friend Jonathan, but his kind remembrance of the fallen first King of Israel, recalling his valiance and goodness to the daughters of Israel, shows the forgiveness that Christians should have towards one another. Especially in death, knowing that we ourselves will be transformed as fully new men, and our past sins forgotten and forgiven by the Lord.

David strived to make peace with Saul while the king was alive. And in death, honored the Lord's anointed. No resentment or bitterness.

But more; In the death of those who've hurt us, or were against us, we should also offer this spirit of forgiveness and let go of any enmity to those who may not have been saved. To our unsaved parents who've wronged us, to family we've felt betrayed us. To friends and neighbors and coworkers who may have done us wrong, without cause. We should let go of the animosity and hurt feelings we may have had, because we know that they have their punishment. That God is just and He will repay. We should only lament that they weren't won to Christ in life, and let go of the pain of the past.

This attitude of forgiveness is one of the key aspects of Christian life. It is part of what allows us to live peacefully with all men. To have a productive life filled with love, joy and longsuffering. Building our faith.

If you have animosity towards a brother or sister in Christ, let it go. And if they've passed on, joyfully look for them in the resurrection.

And if it be that they never believed, rest easy knowing that the Lord is just.

teachings.title: Love your enemies and let God avenge
teachings.summary: By sparing Saul and leaving judgment to God, David shows the perfecting faith Jesus commands: love your enemies, trusting the Lord to deliver you.
teachings.text:
The living God is the God of judgment and vengeance, delivering His sons and bringing his wrath on our enemies. As followers of Christ, we are called to love our enemies and give them a chance to repent of the evil they seek to do to us. Even to support them in their need, and to forgive them if they turn away from their anger.

**Matthew 5:44-48**
*But I say unto you, Love your enemies, bless them that curse you, do good to them that hate you, and pray for them which despitefully use you, and persecute you; That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust. For if ye love them which love you, what reward have ye? do not even the publicans the same? And if ye salute your brethren only, what do ye more than others? do not even the publicans so? Be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father which is in heaven is perfect.*

This is one of the hardest doctrines to accept for many Christians. It can be the thing that snares them and keeps them from being perfect, complete, in their faith.

Of course, to be saved, we must have trust in God's promise of salvation and eternal life in Christ Jesus. We have to believe that He can deliver us from wrath.

We may believe that He can heal us of our sins, removing thorns from our heart and conforming us to His purpose. We will pray for our physical well-being and the safety and health of our loved ones, trusting His tender mercies and that He will help us in our affliction.

We might even develop faith deep enough to not fear when hard times come, when money is tight, when we need food or clothing or shelter. That He will provide.

But when we are wronged by another, when we are unfairly persecuted, or others hold us in contempt and seek our harm, it is often difficult to trust in the Lord to deliver us. To bring to nothing their schemes. We want to fight back, answer railing for railing, to protest and proclaim our righteousness loudly, to all who will listen, so they know that our enemies cause is not just.

But what sayeth scripture?

When David has the opportunity to end this one-sided feud with King Saul, he chooses to let God judge. To allow the Lord to deliver him.

By his kindness to Saul, humiliating the paranoid king by showing that mercy and his good intentions to all the men present, Saul was left no choice but to withdraw. David's faith in God and the righteousness of obedience to His word, not only saves his life and the life of his men, but heaps coals upon his enemy's head.

And as we know, God's vengeance against Saul is coming, his destruction is assured. Saul knows it too, and asks favor from David, to spare his seed after David is king, a covenant David had already made with Jonathan.

By trusting in the Lord, without a single blow, David has been delivered and his enemy made weak. Saul, with 4,000 men surrounding the cave, could have easily turned and destroyed the upstart and his small band. Instead he slunk away in defeat.

This is the kind of faith that makes us perfect, Jesus says. The lack of fear, trusting in the righteousness established in us by Christ, testified of by the Spirit, knowing the power of the Father to deliver us. With that sure knowledge, loving your enemies becomes our strength. It is a mercy given them by victors, even if that victory hasn't been seen yet. A victory we have already received in Jesus, having overcome the world.

teachings.title: Doing right against peer pressure
teachings.summary: When friends urge vengeance as if it were God's sign, we must do what is right in the Lord's eyes as David did, rather than please men as Saul did.
teachings.text:
*And the men of David said unto him, Behold the day of which the Lord said unto thee, Behold, I will deliver thine enemy into thine hand, that thou mayest do to him as it shall seem good unto thee.*

We may have friends and family that don't have the faith to understand this strength. They may see the opportunity to exact vengeance as a sign from God, as David's men did. They may be afraid, and look for the easiest way out, and push you into taking it with the best of intentions.

It can be hard to do the right thing in the presence of that kind of peer pressure.

It is notable that while Saul consistently bowed to that sort of pressure, choosing to please man rather than do as God said, David does the right thing and silences his men by keeping to the principles of righteousness as God has given us.

Had he done as they thought best, doing what seemed good to him, rather than what is good to the Lord, who knows what may have happened, but it's a good bet that they'd be in worse straits, surrounded and outnumbered and without the protection of God, having not trusted in Him.

So take heart. Faint not. Trust in the Lord. Do what's right in His eyes. The rest takes care of itself.

teachings.title: Jonathan and David's covenant in the Lord
teachings.summary: The covenant of Jonathan and David sworn in the Lord's name pictures salvation, and Jonathan's love above his own father and kingdom shows how we should love Christ and our brethren.
teachings.text:
It is impossible to read this chapter, and miss the number of times both Jonathan and David appeal to the Lord in their communication with each other.

*God forbid; thou shalt not die*...

*David sware moreover...truly as the Lord liveth, and as thy soul liveth, there is but a step between me and death.*

*And Jonathan said unto David, O Lord God of Israel, when I have sounded my father about to morrow any time, or the third day, and, behold, if there be good toward David, and I then send not unto thee, and shew it thee; The Lord do so and much more to Jonathan: but if it please my father to do thee evil, then I will shew it thee, and send thee away, that thou mayest go in peace: and the Lord be with thee, as he hath been with my father. And thou shalt not only while yet I live shew me the kindness of the Lord, that I die not...But also thou shalt not cut off thy kindness from my house for ever: no, not when the Lord hath cut off the enemies of David every one from the face of the earth.*

*So Jonathan made a covenant with the house of David, saying, Let the Lord even require it at the hand of David's enemies...*

*If I expressly say unto the lad, Behold, the arrows are on this side of thee, take them; then come thou: for there is peace to thee, and no hurt; as the Lord liveth. But if I say thus unto the young man, Behold, the arrows are beyond thee; go thy way: for the Lord hath sent thee away. And as touching the matter which thou and I have spoken of, behold, the Lord be between thee and me for ever...*

*And Jonathan said to David, Go in peace, forasmuch as we have sworn both of us in the name of the Lord, saying, The Lord be between me and thee, and between my seed and thy seed for ever.*

The parallel with salvation, calling upon the living God, the Lord God of Israel, literally of the seed of David, and these paths sworn between Jonathan and David are obvious. Saul, like the remnant of unbelieving Jews, having the kingdom taken from him, and given to another, and so he seeks the son of Jesse's life. Just as they sought Christ's.

But Jonathan loves David more than his own father, more than his own earthly reward, more than even inheriting a kingdom of man. No greater love. We should love our brothers in Christ this much. We should love Jesus like this and more.

teachings.title: Help thy neighbour in his need
teachings.summary: The laws on lost property and helping a neighbour in a bind are simply love thy neighbour, doing to others as we would have done to us.
teachings.text:
Here in **Deuteronomy 22**, the statutes of the Lord continue with what seem to be things self-evident to us, but that in practice we know are not. Of course we help a neighbor with lost property. Of course we help another we see in a bind, along our way. But yet...

How often have we seen something lost and turned our heads and walked away? Or been tempted to take it and hide it away? Finders keepers, losers weepers? Our conscience should pang us, pricking our hearts and yet... God makes it clear what the right thing is that there be no mistake, and no temptation. Love thy neighbour.

Do we pull over to help a person with a flat tire? Do we stop and help a stranger carry something burdensome? Do we find someone's wallet and return it, intact? If we do unto others as we would have done to ourselves, we will.

teachings.title: Proclaim peace, then fight
teachings.summary: He teaches godly people should first offer peace to enemies as a mercy and a show of strength, knowing our victory is already won in Christ.
teachings.text:
Continuing, the word of God tells us that, when we confront our enemies, prepared for war, confident in our deliverance, to proclaim peace unto them.

For the children of Israel, this is literally the case. And for godly people in general, in matters of war and confrontation with our enemies, those who seek to do us harm, we should lead with an offer of peace. This is the same principle as turning the other cheek. It isn't a show of weakness to extend the offer of peace, to give our enemies a chance to lay down their weapons and live peaceably with us. It is a show of strength. It is a mercy.

Because we have already won, as we are God's, and He fights with us. And if they slap the other cheek, if they reject an offer of peace, then we are to go to war, knowing the Lord is with us.

This faith in God to deliver us from tribulation and the evil of other men is often maligned by the world. Our steadfast hope that even if we are slain, we have won. Our victory being in Christ, Who has overcome the world. Unregenerate men don't like this. They see it as foolishness.

**1 Corinthians 1:25-29**
*Because the foolishness of God is wiser than men; and the weakness of God is stronger than men. For ye see your calling, brethren, how that not many wise men after the flesh, not many mighty, not many noble, are called: But God hath chosen the foolish things of the world to confound the wise; and God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the things which are mighty; And base things of the world, and things which are despised, hath God chosen, yea, and things which are not, to bring to nought things that are: That no flesh should glory in his presence.*

teachings.title: Every man shall give as he is able
teachings.summary: Blessed by God, believers give back as they are able in two main ways, winning souls and executing right judgment for the fatherless and widow.
teachings.text:
*Every man shall give as he is able, according to the blessing of the Lord thy God which he hath given thee.*

What a concisely phrased explanation of the Christian life, and God's expectations for us. He blessed us, His children. He asks in return that we give to Him as we are able, according to those blessings.

The giving isn't required for the blessing. But the blessing asks for the giving. And we know that there are two main ways the Lord asks us to give unto Him; winning souls and right judgment.

What a day when we are bringing in the sheaves! When the fullness of man has come in, and to the Lord is given the increase.

As the parables of the sower, the wise servant, and others told by Jesus, picturing the Kingdom of God and the fruit that we are called to bring forth, after our kind. The winning of souls through the gospel.

And in judgement, knowing; *Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted.*

It's no coincidence that the reminder of keeping the feasts, bringing the gifts, remembering the blessings given by the Lord to us, is followed immediately by;

*Judges and officers shalt thou make thee in all thy gates, which the Lord thy God giveth thee, throughout thy tribes: and they shall judge the people with just judgment.*

That we are to be unspotted, blameless in our judgement. Not being a respecter of persons. Not showing favor to one over another, but executing right judgment. Not taking bribes, which would pervert out judgment. That we be just in our ways that we may live.

The two things we are separated unto God's ministry in the Gospel to do, linked forever in the feasts that are Christ's.

teachings.title: Remember thou wast a servant in Egypt
teachings.summary: Remembering we were servants to sin freed only by grace, believers should show the same mercy to others, even strangers, that they may come to Christ.
teachings.text:
*And remember that thou wast a servant in the land of Egypt, and that the Lord thy God brought thee out thence through a mighty hand and by a stretched out arm: therefore the Lord thy God commanded thee to keep the sabbath day.*

The spiritual application of this understanding, that Jesus is the Sabbath, that our works contribute nothing to our salvation should be coupled with remembering that we were servants to sin. That we were in bondage in Egypt. That before God brought us out from the ministry of death and into eternal life by His mighty hand, we were as slaves, just as the Hebrews were.

And the extension of the Sabbath to those who are our sons and daughters, our employees, and even to strangers, is to show the same mercy given us who were once servants, that they may come to know the truth in Christ.

Never forget that we were servants in Egypt, and only are free by the grace of the Lord. Have charitable love for the unsaved that they may be lifted out of bondage as well.

teachings.title: The gift of helps
teachings.summary: The gift of helps or ministry is serving one another as members of one body, as Paul praised his fellow laborers in Romans 16.
teachings.text:
**Mark 9:35**
*And he sat down, and called the twelve, and saith unto them, If any man desire to be first, the same shall be last of all, and servant of all*.

In discussing the gifts of the Spirit given to believers as part of the body of Christ, Paul mentions "helps;"

**1 Corinthians 12:28**
