*Above when he said, Sacrifice and offering and burnt offerings and offering for sin thou wouldest not, neither hadst pleasure therein; which are offered by the law*.

Just as the Pharisees had the OT sacrifices, we have the once and for all sacrifice of Christ, and total remission of sins.

**Hebrews 10:17–18**
*And their sins and iniquities will I remember no more. Now where remission of these is, there is no more offering for sin.*

Just as He says to His people That he isn't seeking to add more sacrifice to those that they are already, God isn't asking us for additional acts of atonement. He remembers our sins no more. There is no more sacrifice to be had.

**Hebrews 10:26–27**
*For if we sin wilfully after that we have received the knowledge of the truth, there remaineth no more sacrifice for sins, But a certain fearful looking for of judgment and fiery indignation, which shall devour the adversaries.*

Just like Israel in **Psalm 50**, we are covered by the blood. We are his people. But are we bound by the formalism and outward appearance of being clean, while failing to maintain the good work that God has saved us for? That gives Him glory?

Or are we looking over our shoulder, expecting a similar charge to be made by God against us as He is making here?

If we're not declaring his righteousness and glory in Thanksgiving, and showing mercy and judgment to others, loving our neighbor, how are we taking his covenant in our mouths? How are we telling the world that we are Christians when we aren't acting like it? Who does it benefit?

**James 2:14–17**
*What doth it profit, my brethren, though a man say he hath faith, and have not works? can faith save him? If a brother or sister be naked, and destitute of daily food, And one of you say unto them, Depart in peace, be ye warmed and filled; notwithstanding ye give them not those things which are needful to the body; what doth it profit? Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone.*

teachings.title: Judge not means no hypocrisy, not no judgment
teachings.summary: Judge not warns against hypocrisy, not right judgment; like David we ask God to judge us first, separate from false believers, and enter the congregation with a clean conscience.
teachings.text:
**Matthew 7:1–2**
*Judge not, that ye be not judged. For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.*

Jesus' words are often twisted by others to mean a Christian should never judge another person, no matter how wicked they are or what sins they do. But, we know the warning is against hypocrisy, not right judgment.

**Psalm 26** gives us a picture of what Jesus is actually teaching, where David asks the Lord to judge him by his doings, according to his faith, in comparison to the wicked around him.

The understanding of proper judgement is key to good Christian living. It allows us to be separated, to be holy as God is holy, to put away the filth of the flesh and walk in the Spirit. To seek to be a disciplined servant of the Lord.

We walk in integrity, and trust in the Lord alone, that we shall not slide. Firmly on His rock, not backsliding to live as the world does.

It is not an automatic transformation. We are sanctified by the Spirit by the inward man, the new man, but our flesh is still prone to lusts of the eyes and the pride of life and we can stumble and fall.

But if we seek the judgment of God, asking Him to try us and see that our heart is right, we are opening ourselves to correction and refinement, to better be used by God.

Walking in His truth, keeping ourselves pure and humble, seeing others in the way God does, with grace and mercy and lovingkindness, we can make our case to the Lord, and compare ourselves to the wicked without the leaven of the Pharisees, hypocrisy.

David lists the things he has not done, to separate himself towards God.

He has not sat with vain persons, false believers. He has not had ecumenical fellowship with the dissemblers, the false prophets who teach lies. He has avoided the congregation of evil doers. The bitter fruit of the false religions of this world. He has not yoked with unbelievers.

Instead, knowing he is innocent of these things, and sanctified, he is able to come before the altar of the Lord. To gather with the assembly of God's people. To walk into church without the burden of unresolved sin, with a good conscience towards God.

He doesn't do this to be haughty, or to puff up himself in comparison to the wicked, but that he may proclaim the goodness of the Lord in the midst of the congregation, without hypocrisy.

Meekly seeking God's judgment in our lives that we may be a better testimony is a good thing. Judgment that leads to repentance and forgiveness of others, that we may love the habitation of His house, that we may know how to behave in the church, as a pillar and foundation of truth, is a good thing.

Asking the Lord to remember us, that we aren't caught up in His judgment of the wicked, but rather walk in our integrity, waiting for His redemption out of His wrath, seeking His mercy in our obedience.

*My foot standeth in an even place: in the congregations will I bless the LORD.*

This should be our guiding principle. To rightly judge, beginning with ourselves that we may purge ourselves, be separated unto the Lord that we may boldly proclaim His mercy and bless the Lord in the congregation. Amen.

teachings.title: Who art thou that judgest another man's servant
teachings.summary: Accusing a fellow believer of his failings accuses his Master, so we should edify one another in meekness and remove the beam from our own eye first.
teachings.text:
Continuing **Proverbs 30:10**
*Accuse not a servant unto his master, lest he curse thee, and thou be found guilty.*

The practical application of this is to guard against accusing the master through his proxy, his servant, especially false or exaggerated claims, that expose hypocrisy and deficiency in your own life. An accusation against another man's servant is an accusation against the master's stewardship. If the servant did wrong, dealt dishonestly, was slothful, the implication is that the master can't oversee his own, or is lax in some way.

Spiritually, Paul uses this proverb to warn against brothers in Christ accusing one another for their failings in their Christian walk.

**Romans 14:4**
*Who art thou that judgest another man's servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth. Yea, he shall be holden up: for God is able to make him stand.*

We are answerable to God. If one is falling down in some area, weak in the faith, God will correct them. Accusing them accuses Him, and opens yourself up to being called out and chastened for your own deficiency before God.

It isn't an excuse to enable, and standards and church discipline still exist. Fellowship can still be broken. But encouraging speech, edifying one another with fear and admonition of the Lord, is what we should use. Not accusations of being less holy than thou. Meekness and humility, with the grace to understand you're not perfect either, is the key.

As Christ taught;

**Matthew 7:3-5**
*And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye? Or how wilt thou say to thy brother, Let me pull out the mote out of thine eye; and, behold, a beam is in thine own eye? Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye.*

So, we must be cautious that we aren't projecting, that we who also serve the Lord aren't falling down in our own way. To not be a hypocrite, least He curse us and we be found guilty.

teachings.title: It is not good to have respect of persons
teachings.summary: In judgment we must not favour the rich but weigh a man by his words, character and the full matter, and woe to those who call the wicked righteous.
teachings.text:
*These things also belong to the wise. It is not good to have respect of persons in judgment.*

Final entry in the **Proverbs 24** study, and we are again reminded to show no partiality or preference in dealing with people, especially under our judgment. If we have to determine truth, decide someone's date, or even just how we interact with each other, don't be a respecter of persons. God isn't. The rich or the lords among us should be subject to the same treatment as the lowly and poor.

Note that we are also given other things to judge a man with over station; the words they speak, are they wise or froward? Do they have a reputation for wisdom? Generosity? Are they diligent or sluggards? Do they give their parents honor or woe? Are they drunkards? Do they plot wickedness and sow to themselves iniquity? Have you heard the matter fully, before witnesses? Is there mercy that can be shown?

These are the factors we are to consider, but not favoritism that causes us to overlook right judgment. Not by appearances, as Jesus said. But right judgment.

And for the judge, there is a warning;

*He that saith unto the wicked, Thou are righteous; him shall the people curse, nations shall abhor him: But to them that rebuke him shall be delight, and a good blessing shall come upon them.*

**Isaiah 5:20**
*Woe unto them that call evil good, and good evil; that put darkness for light, and light for darkness; that put bitter for sweet, and sweet for bitter*!

If you pervert justice and promote the wicked and cast your lot with the rich man over the widow or fatherless, if you justify the works of mischief, woe unto you. It is a blessing to call it straight and to rebuke that which is evil, and a curse to give cover to evil.

teachings.title: He that answereth a matter before he heareth it
teachings.summary: Saints who will judge angels must judge righteous judgment among brethren, hearing the whole matter and the other side rather than the first story told.
teachings.text:
Continuing the chapter, **Proverbs 18:13** is an often quoted verse; *He that answereth a matter before he heareth it, it is folly and shame unto him.*

As in our recent **Job** series, the idea of right judgment is one God demands. Hearing the facts, witnesses and filtering it through the discernment and Wisdom that comes from being His sons. As Paul writes to the contentious church at Corinth;

**1 Corinthians 6:3**
*Know ye not that we shall judge angels? how much more things that pertain to this life?*

We who are joint-heirs with Christ will rule and reign with Him in the Kingdom. Petty matters between brethren shouldn't be a problem for us to resolve. Most don't require the splitting-the-baby wisdom of Solomon, that even the least esteemed among saved believers should be able to determine a matter. As Jesus says;

**John 7:24** 
*Judge not according to the appearance, but judge righteous judgment.*

To that end, Solomon provides guidance;

*He that is first in his own cause seemeth just; but his neighbour cometh and searcheth him.*

The first to complain or to seek judgement on a matter might seem the obvious plaintiff, and just. But his neighbor may have something to say about it. Others may come forward. We should not judge a matter before hearing the matter, and that includes questioning claims, and not going with the first story you hear.

And, again Solomon brings up an arbiter men can use to end many contentions; the lot. The simple roll of chance, and giving it up to God.

*The lot causeth contentions to cease, and parteth between the mighty.*

teachings.title: The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination
teachings.summary: God hears the prayer of the upright but the wicked's show of piety and self-made sacrifices are an abomination, since they go about to establish their own righteousness instead of submitting to God's.
teachings.text:
The constant reminder from God to heed the wisdom of your father, to incline your ear to instruction, to prudently regard reproof continues to be hammered home.

Following after the way of righteousness is wise, but those that have forsaken the way of God despise correction and hate reproof. Scorners hate being reproved of their ignorance. They won't seek after the wise. They feed on foolishness, are destitute of wisdom, their plans come to naught for lack of counsel, those greedy of gain and their pride brings destruction to their house.

*The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the Lord: but the prayer of the upright is his delight.*

*The Lord is far from the wicked: but he heareth the prayer of the righteous.*

Having God on your side, accepting your prayers, working in your life is a treasure beyond measure. The wicked and their public display of piety, their self-righteous works and so-called fasts, the "sacrifices" they make, be it the Old Testament animal offerings, or the vows made today to "cut out sweets," or to "drink less" or whatever, are an abomination to the Lord.

*The fear of the Lord is the instruction of wisdom; and before honour is humility*. The wicked may have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. They lack the humility that comes before wisdom.

**Romans 10:3**
*For they being ignorant of God's righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God.*

The humility of submitting to His righteousness, the fear of the Lord, that we may gain understanding, being willing to receive reproof and correction, to seek after knowledge and study to be approved before God, that we may have a ready answer to all for our hope, this is the wisdom and the way we must seek.

*The way of life is above to the wise, that he may depart from hell beneath.*

teachings.title: Phylacteries and binding the word on the heart
teachings.summary: Binding God's word on the heart means living it and letting it guide us day and night, not the Pharisees' literal phylacteries worn to be seen of men.
teachings.text:
*My son, keep thy father's commandment, and forsake not the law of thy mother: Bind them continually upon thine heart, and tie them about thy neck.*

This appeal to listen to the good and Godly word, given by your parents, the instruction in righteousness, and to keep them in your heart, and allegories like it are found frequently in **Proverbs**. It is a source cited by Jews to defend their practice of "phylacteries."

**Matthew 23:4-5**
*For they bind heavy burdens and grievous to be borne, and lay them on men's shoulders; but they themselves will not move them with one of their fingers. But all their works they do for to be seen of men: they make broad their phylacteries, and enlarge the borders of their garments*,

Pharisees and scribes exaggerated religious symbols, specifically phylacteries (small leather boxes with scripture inside them, worn on the forehead and straps with scripture worn on their shoulders and wrapped in their arm, called tefillin) and garment tassels (tzitzit) to appear more pious and draw attention to themselves, rather than truly living God's law. They made the command literal, rather than in the spirit of how it was given. They lose sight of the words and living them, not being doers of the law.

Being led by the law, on God's paths, going His way, is the meaning behind it. That when you sleep, when you wake, His word talks with you.

This is so true. When we wake in the night, if we walk in the Spirit and stay in the word, our idle thoughts become more focused on Him, and prayer and pondering His word. When we don't it is easy to have the cares of this world and fear and sin knocking at the door.

The commandment is a lamp, a light to your feet. Reproofs of instruction are the way of life. The way, the path, the road God wants us to walk on, that we may live.

teachings.title: Playing church versus mercy
teachings.summary: God is not pleased with outward acts of religion, ritual and showy worship but with a humble heart and mercy to the lost, the poor and the widow.
teachings.text:
Today, many Christians worry more about the outward acts of religion over the spiritual things of God. They play church, and make a long pretense of prayer, and get into "worship services," getting ecstatic over worldly sounding music, or engaging in fasts and other rituals, that satisfy their needs and excite the flesh, but do nothing for honoring God or doing what He has commanded us.

Dead works and vain traditions, but no mercy or judgment for the lost, the poor, the widow, the fatherless.

**Luke 18:12-14**
*I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess. And the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner. I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other: for every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.*

**Hosea 6:6**
*For I desired mercy, and not sacrifice; and the knowledge of God more than burnt offerings.*

**Matthew 12:7**
*But if ye had known what this meaneth, I will have mercy, and not sacrifice, ye would not have condemned the guiltless.*

God doesn't care about where you sit in church, sitting in the chief seats, or your religious acts that show everyone else how holy you claim to be. But He cares about what's in your heart and how you treat others.

You can be the most separated person in the pews, but if you look down on others, and hold yourself as better than, you're separated unto yourself. Not the gospel of God. Like these men who inquired of the Lord.

teachings.title: Doers of the word, not hearers only
teachings.summary: Like Ezekiel's hearers who enjoyed his preaching as a song, many churchgoers hear without doing, but the word should change us.
teachings.text:
Finally, the Lord brings to Ezekiel's attention those that were listening to his preaching, who gathered in their doorways to hear him whenever he spoke. Who called others to hear the burden of God placed on the prophet.

The Lord says, they come and listen but do not do what is told them. For with their mouth they show much love, but their heart is full of covetousness.

**Isaiah 29:13**
*Wherefore the Lord said, Forasmuch as this people draw near me with their mouth, and with their lips do honour me, but have removed their heart far from me.*..

**Matthew 15:8**
*This people draweth nigh unto me with their mouth, and honoureth me with their lips; but their heart is far from me.*

God compares their vain pleasure im hearing the word of God preached to those listening to a song. It's got a good beat, and the singer is talented, but it has no deeper meaning than that for them.

How many professing Christians, even in solid fundamental churches, are there just to enjoy the show? For the ambiance and the vibe? How many Sunday morning-glories show up to a service, check the box, hear the word, and let it drip off them like water off a duck?

The Bible says in **James 1:22-25**
*But be ye doers of the word, and not hearers only, deceiving your own selves. For if any be a hearer of the word, and not a doer, he is like unto a man beholding his natural face in a glass: For he beholdeth himself, and goeth his way, and straightway forgetteth what manner of man he was. But whoso looketh into the perfect law of liberty, and continueth therein, he being not a forgetful hearer, but a doer of the work, this man shall be blessed in his deed.*

Are you like those that attended Ezekiel's preaching, but took nothing from it? Whose hearts continued in covetousness? Like those who play church and see it as a social occasion, and aren't transformed by the hearing of the word?

Spending time with God's word should change you. We should have ready hearts and open ears and not just be there for the fellowship. But to be a doer of the work, that we may be blessed.

But when destruction comes to pass, (and lo, it will come), they shall know that a prophet has been among them. That the word of God is true. But they will be caught sleeping. Unprofitable servants. It will come as a thief in the night, and they will not be prepared.

Ready your hearts and be attentive listeners and doers. Amen

teachings.title: The fast that God has chosen
teachings.summary: God rejects public fasting to be seen of men; the fast He chooses is to loose burdens and serve the needy in secret.
teachings.text:
*Cry aloud, and spare not...*one of the most quoted verses in scripture, used by pastors and preachers, lifting their voices like a trumpet to sound out the people's sins and transgressions.

And those sins are many. Even among the church crowd. *This people draweth nigh unto me with their mouth, and honoureth me with their lips; but their heart is far from me*, the Bible says. They seek God daily. Here, going before Him at the temple. Reading His ordinances and fasting. But we see it's in vain.

They boast about these works, bragging about their fasts. Publicly proclaiming these fast days, that God has no part in giving.

**Matthew 6:16-18**
*Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward. But thou, when thou fastest, anoint thine head, and wash thy face; That thou appear not unto men to fast, but unto thy Father which is in secret: and thy Father, which seeth in secret, shall reward thee openly.*

But they fast for strife and debate, to lord over others. To place burdens on people grievous to be born. The Catholic Church and its harlot daughter, the Orthodox, spent much of the past weeks doing this. But that is not a fast God has chosen. To afflict themselves, publicly. To be seen of men and to guilt those who aren't as "holy."

The fast the Lord has chosen is to comfort the afflicted, to loose the bands of wickedness, the burden of the law, especially the doctrine of men taught as commandments. To free men from every yoke, by faith in Him.

To feed the hungry and to clothe the naked. To give comfort to the poor. Especially those of your own flesh. Your own family. Your nation.

The same that Jesus asks of us.

**Matthew 25:35-40**
*For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in: Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me. Then shall the righteous answer him, saying, Lord, when saw we thee an hungred, and fed thee? or thirsty, and gave thee drink? When saw we thee a stranger, and took thee in? or naked, and clothed thee? Or when saw we thee sick, or in prison, and came unto thee? And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me*.

This is the affliction, this is the sacrifice God asks of us. Not doing without to be seen of men. To justify us before God as we continue in sin and pride. But sacrifice of our time and talents and wealth to help others in need. Without fanfare. And our light will so shine.

**Matthew 5:16**
*Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.*

*Take heed that ye do not your alms before men, to be seen of them: otherwise ye have no reward of your Father which is in heaven...But when thou doest alms, let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth: That thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly.*

teachings.title: What confidence is this wherein thou trustest
teachings.summary: The world respects ornate high places and Rome's trappings, but humble trust in the Lord in weakness is the believer's strength.
teachings.text:
Here in **Isaiah 36** we have the third telling of this historical event, where the captain of the Assyrian horde has come down through Samaria, along the Jordan, from Lachish, the city of Dan in the north, unto the plains before Jerusalem in the South.

Hezekiah is king over Judah, and while not a good king in the tradition of David, but he has trusted the Lord, preached by Isaiah, with his illness and been healed, being granted 15 years to his life by God. He had taken down altars to the false gods, in high places. And here the city is under siege.

The Assyrian Rabshakeh, speaking in Hebrew, calls out to the King's advisors on the wall, telling them of the futility of their position and asking *What confidence is this wherein thou trustest?*

What a question, and one our adversaries in the world, mockers and scoffers and those seeking us harm may ask. One our spiritual adversary, Satan, may corner us into answering.

Rabshakeh says who will you trust? Egypt, a broken reed, nothing one could put their confidence in. For us, God uses Egypt as an example of the bondage to sin and the world.

Or do you trust in the Lord? But notice it isn't the Lord God, but his natural man understanding of what God is, and what religion of the believers looks like.

*But if thou say to me, We trust in the Lord our God: is it not he, whose high places and whose altars Hezekiah hath taken away, and said to Judah and to Jerusalem, Ye shall worship before this altar?*

The false religion of worshipping God in high places and idols and altars, which the world sees vs our worship in our hearts, at the Temple of God's choosing. Hezekiah had done right, and Rabshakeh is mocking it.

The world sees the Roman Catholic Church, or any of its splinters this way, as the true religion of Christianity. If we reject those trappings, they think we weaken God, or doubt our faith.

We see this all the time, when the world makes fun of "Pastor Bob" with a strip mall church. The world respects the high places, the ornate temples made of hands. They don't fear the god of these places, but they understand it, the carnality of elegant churches, idols, altars.

To the world, trusting the Lord humbly, and in weakness is foolish. But to us, strength.

**2 Corinthians 12:8-10**
*For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me. And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me. Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ's sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong.*

teachings.title: Once you begin, you are without excuse
teachings.summary: Starting to do right (Bible reading, church, separation, witnessing) obligates us to continue, and though people will mock, we must be doers of the word and accept it as the Spirit working in us.
teachings.text:
One of the biggest hurdles to overcome in doing the right thing, is that if you begin, you know you will have to continue.

If you begin reading the Bible every day, you're admitting that you should. And if you know that you should, you know it's wrong if you don't. And now you are without excuse.

If you haven't been to church in a while, and you go once, you are admitting you should be going regularly, and now you don't have an excuse.

If you haven't been living a separated life, as blameless as you can, and you try to clean it up, and get rid of worldly things in your life, you will have to continue in it.

If you begin to testify for the gospel, people who know you will judge all those sins they've witnessed you do. And now you're forced to show genuine faith and a change.

This can be terrifying. It makes us make rationalizations. Or empty promises and vows to "do better tomorrow." While living for today.

But we are to be doers of the word, not hearers only. We are supposed to let our light shine.

A prophet is not without honor, except in his home country. We will have family and friends who aren't Christian who will roll their eyes. Who will feel threatened by your newfound dedication to the Lord. Who will look for chinks in the whole armour of God you try to put on.

You will fail sometimes. It's ok. God's mercies are new every morning.

Yes, you will be making yourself obligated to doing the right thing by acknowledging it is the right thing. That is the Spirit working in you. Accept it. Accept people will be put off by the change. Accept some will make fun of you, mockers. It's ok.

Because this tribulation is nothing compared to eternity. God will bless you in this life and the next.

teachings.title: Samson's one line
teachings.summary: Like Samson keeping only his hair while breaking the rest of his vow, Christians set an arbitrary line to feel right with God while sinning around it.
teachings.text:
Samson's story ends with a bang. His weakness revealed; Women.

He is nearly caught because of his visit to a harlot in Gaza. And just as his riddle was given away to the daughter of Timnath for her pleading, Delilah the Philistine manages to get Samson to tell her his heart, and his belief that the Lord was with him due to his hair, kept unshaved due to his lifelong vow.

Women, and their persistence with him, was Samson's undoing.

The lifelong vow of the Nazarite that he violated so often, being unclean with dead bodies, eating from carcasses, drinking from bloody bones, and laying with harlots, included not taking a razor to his hair. And that's where he drew the line.

Many times as Christians, we do the same thing. We know what we ought to do and that which we should not. And we set an arbitrary line around one particular thing, that we fool ourselves into thinking we are right with God so long as that one thing isn't violated, even as we sin all around it.

And God is patient and longsuffering.

But when our heart, our trust, is in that one thing, especially under a vow, and not Christ, He will punish us when we break it. Delilah was the means. The hair she shaved, the 7 locks he had, was just the thing, the vow, he used as a fig leaf. Once gone, the Spirit given strength he had was gone.

Samson was made blind. Tied to posts and mocked. And even with stubble growing back, was still weak. Led around by a boy.

But Samson called upon the Lord for deliverance. *O Lord God, remember me, I pray thee, and strengthen me, I pray thee, only this once, O God, that I may be at once avenged of the Philistines for my two eyes*.

And the Lord answered his prayers, and sacrificing himself, Samson killed 3,000 Philistines including their lords, gathered to offer sacrifices to their false god.

In the end it was faith that delivered Samson. In the end God was the source of his strength. Amen

teachings.title: Phinehas heard them before judging
teachings.summary: Distance breeds misunderstanding, and Phinehas shows right judgment by asking and listening before acting instead of accusing.
teachings.text:
But the story has applications that we can learn from, as does the entire Bible. But here we see the tendency of distance and absence from among one another often leads to misunderstanding.

We can see it in our own experiences, where a sibling moves away to the city, or a brother from church takes a job in another state, or even coworkers who don't share an office or a site, but question the ethic of those working remotely...distance and absence stir up questions, and an innocent act by one can spark a potential conflict between the two.

Godly parents worry about whether their children who leave the nest are living godly themselves. For example we see Job offering sacrifices for his children, just in case they weren't;

**Job 1:5**
*And it was so, when the days of their feasting were gone about, that Job sent and sanctified them, and rose up early in the morning, and offered burnt offerings according to the number of them all: for Job said, It may be that my sons have sinned, and cursed God in their hearts. Thus did Job continually.*

It is a natural feeling to have, but it can also lead to paranoia and rash action.

Phinehas, who in his zeal for the Lord acted decisively in Moab, taking a spear and ending the judgment against his people with the deaths of the fornicator and the whore, shows discernment, judgment and mercy here, at Ed. Rather than impulsively allowing his hatred of every false way lead to violence, he asks of them the altars purpose. And rather than accuse, he reminds them of why he has concerns. That not only would this be bad for them if they'd fallen away to Baal, but that God's judgment is upon nations, and all of Israel could suffer. Phinehas asks them to return cross the Jordan if it meant repenting of their possible sin, a chance to get right. And, most importantly, he listens to their answer, not deciding the matter before hearing them out.

This is a pattern we can all learn from. Especially in situations where we don't know the intent of the heart. The same right judgment he showed in Peor, he shows here.

And of course there's an innocent explanation. And the explanation made by men of the 2.5 tribes who had just demonstrated their honor by keeping their word in settling Canaan is accepted. And all of Israel rejoiced at the news. Crisis averted.

teachings.title: Inquire meekly, then rebuke false ways
teachings.summary: Believers should hate every false way but meekly ask professing Christians what they mean, testing them by the gospel before rebuking or accepting them.
teachings.text:
Now, the other application is that we should hate every false way, and there is no harm in asking someone professing to be Christian to explain their apparent behavior or statements that seem contrary to the Gospel.

As we see online especially, there are many who hold damnable heresies and doctrines of devils, claiming to be of Christ. There is no profit in blind ecumenicalism, and accepting everyone calling themselves Christian regardless of their beliefs. But we should trust someone who claims to be a believer, giving them the benefit of the doubt unless there is a sign that concerns us. And then, remembering Phinehas, inquire what they meant, meekly and with care. It could simply be a misunderstanding or a different way of phrasing something, perfectly innocent.

Yes, if they announce their beliefs in a false gospel or a different god, or some vain traditions and dead works, we should confront them with scripture and rebuke them. But there are times brothers as set at variance, when the truth is there are only surface differences caused by distance and absence of fellowship.

Thankfully, God's word has a shortcut to finding out if we share a common foundation; asking "What must one do to be saved?" Paul repeatedly uses the gospel as a way of assurance of common mindedness with the churches he writes to. That we all share the same foundational belief. As Jesus says of testing the spirit of a teacher, we shall know them by their fruits, by the beliefs of their followers. If they are saved by the gospel or if they believe some false way.

We need to meekly and humbly seek to know, before either grabbing a javelin or declaring peace, and always ready to provide a way out should they prove to be going the way of Balaam, and heading to the destruction of Baal-Peor. By giving them the true gospel in love. Amen

teachings.title: A copy of the law for kings and heirs
teachings.summary: As kings were to copy and read the law, believers who will reign with Christ must learn scripture to judge rightly, turning neither to the political left nor right but to God's way.
teachings.text:
*And it shall be, when he sitteth upon the throne of his kingdom, that he shall write him a copy of this law in a book out of that which is before the priests the Levites: And it shall be with him, and he shall read therein all the days of his life: that he may learn to fear the Lord his God, to keep all the words of this law and these statutes, to do them: That his heart be not lifted up above his brethren, and that he turn not aside from the commandment, to the right hand, or to the left: to the end that he may prolong his days in his kingdom, he, and his children, in the midst of Israel.*

This command for kings, for those that rule over others in judgement, holds the most application for us today out of the other warnings for future kings.

We who are saved are heirs to the Kingdom. Admonishments and advice given throughout the OT, and New, are given that we may know right judgment. Not only in this life, but in the Millennial Kingdom, where we are to rule and reign with Christ.

This is an often overlooked aspect of our Christian life. We will judge angels. We are called to be part of the hierarchy of God's divine plan. As husbands, wives, parents, children, servants. As men over thousands, hundreds and tens. To judge the fatherless and advocate for the widow. And as princes of His Kingdom.

And the administration of His Kingdom requires men and women of understanding. This is the most important thing about Bible study, learning scripture and committing the word of God to our hearts. That we may know His will and execute His judgements with mercy, grace and longsuffering. With understanding.

God told whomever would be king of Israel to make a handwritten copy of the law, that they may know it. That he may keep the statutes and in doing so, serve with a humble heart. This applies to us so much today, and it is as neglected as Solomon neglected it in his day.

God's promise is that we will prolong our days on this earth, that would be well with us and with those who he is given us authority over. And authority under.

When we know his commandments and try to keep them, and we understand his judgment and try to see things the way God does, We will turn neither to the left hand nor the right.

We've been trained all our lives to use the left and the right as shorthand for two diametrically opposed philosophies. But the truth is we as Christians are supposed to embrace a third way; God's way. What is right in His eyes rather than our own.

Many of us identify with the so-called right? Because they are correct in many of their assessments of what's wrong and seem to be moving towards a godly return to tradition. But that can only carry us so far. In the end we are not to turn either to the left or the right, but to maintain the straight paths He has set before us. We would do well to remember that as princess of the Kingdom. Sons of the King.

teachings.title: Fasting and outward piety cannot save
teachings.summary: Judah fasted while under God's judgment, but outward acts of piety cannot cover a sinful heart, as Jesus taught of the hypocrites and the Pharisee.
teachings.text:
It is also worth pointing out that when the words of the book are read, it is during a fast to the Lord. The people were called to the temple for the fast, and yet this is a prophecy of judgment against them. God took no account for this act of piousness. Their sin of Judah was too great in His eyes. The judgement had been made, Babylon would have her for her adultery, that the children of Israel would turn to God from their whoredoms.

There are times when people, who knowing the judgment of God against them, do religious acts of outward piousness. They fast, make long prayer. Act holier than thou.

As Jesus says in Matthew 6;
*Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.*

We see how the hypocrites have that outward appearance to be seen of men. Like Jesus says, they are whited sepulchers, beautiful on the outside, but inside, stinking of death.

**Luke 18:10-14**
*Two men went up into the temple to pray; the one a Pharisee, and the other a publican. The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican. I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess. And the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner. I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other: for every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.*

The people who heard the word of God through Jeremiah believed in vain that their performative acts of penance and fasting would offset the sin in their hearts, their trust in idols, their adoption of the customs of the heathen. Their sin and degeneracy. They needed to repent, to think again, to know God's judgment is real and there is only one way, God's way. And all the beating of their chest and sackcloth and ashes, fasting and outward signs of religion couldn't save them.

teachings.title: The shewbread and the Lord of the sabbath
teachings.summary: The lamps and shewbread picture God's truth and word, and religion that forgets their meaning becomes rote practice used to condemn, as with the Pharisees.
teachings.text:
**Leviticus 24** begins with the command to have the lamps of the Tabernacle burn continually, dusk to dawn. A statute for ever. That there is light in the place of God.

And God commands that there be bread baked as a memorial, continually, as an offering before the Lord, and eaten by the Levitical priests. This is called the shewbread, concentrated by the Lord.

The light symbolizes the truth of God throughout the Bible, and so it is never dark before Him. The bread is both the life given the people by God's grace and His word.

This shewbread becomes a means of feeding David and his men as they flee Saul, who was in a murderous rage against the future king. Even as it was offered to God and holy, but to the Lord's purpose, it fed His favored in a time of need.

Likewise, as Jesus rebukes the Pharisees when He and His disciples gleaned corn on the Sabbath to eat, Jesus points to how these things are the Lord's, and not just blind tradition and meaningless ritual. That He is the Lord of the sabbath.

Often religion becomes rote practices, that forget the meaning behind them as the Pharisees had. Using these things to condemn. Jesus says had they understood who He was, that He was present for mercy in His death and resurrection to come, that the sacrifices of the temple were a picture of Him who had come not to condemn but to save, that they'd understand why it was acceptable for them to eat of their work, as the Levites were allowed on the sabbath. Because they did the work of God.

teachings.title: Mind not high things
teachings.summary: Believers must be of one mind and humble, not wise in their own conceits like Calvinists and trad Catholics, patiently guiding those less mature.
teachings.text:
*Be of the same mind one toward another. Mind not high things, but condescend to men of low estate. Be not wise in your own conceits.*

This admonition, to be of the same mind, is repeated in the epistles, that the churches which receive them understand that we all share one goal. Serve one Gospel. Look forward with certainty, the same hope.

It is why one of the 7 things God hates is a sower of discord among the brethren. It is why church discipline exists. But a church that is of one mind can do great things for the Lord.

But more so, see that the same caution to be of one mind, not at variance and strife, is coupled with the warning to Mind not high things, to not put ourselves as better than others, but rather condensed to the lowly. To not be wise in our own conceits.

Don't be a special boy.

If you have wisdom, if you have knowledge, it came from God and isn't yours. Be humble. If facing someone who isn't as far in their Christian walk as you, be patient and longsuffering and offer guidance, because that is why God gave you that knowledge. Don't be high-minded. Don't get caught up in theologies and intellectual pursuit, thinking you're better than the unlearned.

Special boys, your Calvinists, reform types, trad Caths, etc, full of vanity and the wisdom of the world, hold themselves up as better than others, full of hypocrisy.

But we shouldn't be. Rather knowing that we serve God and love others, seek their profit, not our own vainglory.

teachings.title: Condescend to men of low estate
teachings.summary: Do not think yourself above the poor and broken, who are often most receptive to the gospel, remembering Christ humbled Himself for us.
teachings.text:
This is also speaking of not being a respecter of persons in a material sense. Understand that the more lowly and sinful and broken a person is, there's a strong likelihood that they will be receptive to the Gospel. Don't think better of yourself because someone is poor, uneducated, simple, not of your class or status. They aren't beneath you. Be their servants, ministering the Gospel in love.

Jesus Christ who is the holy Son of God, was made flesh, subject to the corruption of the world, made sin for our sakes, suffering the humiliation of the cross, pain and death, the fires of Hell, all for our benefit, while we were yet sinners.

Keep that in mind.

teachings.title: Present your bodies a living sacrifice
teachings.summary: Doctrine must be applied by presenting ourselves holy in service, not conformed to the world, each using his gifts to edify the one body.
teachings.text:
Having established all things, Paul now begins the practical application of the doctrines he has laid out. My favorite sermons are those that really tear into the meat of the word and then give practical application, how that doctrine can change your life and make you more able to work for God.

Knowledge and wisdom.

It isn't enough to know the word or have understanding of how it all connects, without taking the implications and applying it to our lives. How to be doers of the word and not hearers only.

Paul, in the letter to the Romans, lays out some heavy doctrine in dense language, the revelation of God, the reprobate doctrine, salvation by grace through faith alone, to the Greek and Jew alike, the understanding of God's grace and the purpose of our salvation. And the understanding of a spiritual Israel, not of the flesh.

But what then?

Chapter 12, in clear and concise language tells us.

That we present our bodies as a loving sacrifice, without blemish, which is our service, separated to the Gospel. Be holy that we may be better able to be of service to God. Vessels fitted for glory. Blameless.

This isn't an appeal to hit the gym and not eat poorly. Our bodies are corruptible, and flesh is going to lead us to sin. It is about walking in the spirit that we may not fulfil the lusts of that flesh, and by example bring others to Christ.

He writes, *be not conformed to this world: but be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind*, which comes from walking in the spirit. To know the will of God. Proving, testing to see what is acceptable.

We are to remain humble, understanding that to every man of faith God has shaped to a purpose. Not all have the same gifts, the same talents, but all are members of the same body, which is Christ. None more important or less important. A similar theme Found in **1 Corinthians 12**:

*But now are they many members, yet but one body. And the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee: nor again the head to the feet, I have no need of you.*

And so each of us should seek to use the talents we have to edify the whole of the body of believers.

*Having then gifts differing according to the grace that is given to us, whether prophecy, let us prophesy according to the proportion of faith; Or ministry, let us wait on our ministering: or he that teacheth, on teaching; Or he that exhorteth, on exhortation: he that giveth, let him do it with simplicity; he that ruleth, with diligence; he that sheweth mercy, with cheerfulness.*

So, to our measure, we all make perfect the will of God. And we see too, that attitude is everything.

teachings.title: The fathers have eaten sour grapes
teachings.summary: Ezekiel 18 teaches that God judges each man on earth by his own sins, so we cannot blame our troubles on our fathers but must walk righteously ourselves.
teachings.text:
It's important in understanding this particular prophecy of God that this is not about salvation, it is about life on this earth, and soul in this sense means the person. Spirit and body together form a soul.

Now with that understanding, let us consider the opening verse. *What mean ye, that ye use this proverb concerning the land of Israel, saying, The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the children's teeth are set on edge?*

The saying refers to the idea that the children of Israel are claiming that God is judging unfairly by punishing them for what their parents did. What their immediate forefathers got up to. That they ate sour grapes but it's the children whose teeth are on edge.

It's important to keep this chapter of Ezekiel in mind when we're looking at the boomer question. God judges us fairly on this earth, saved or unsaved. We may suffer from the sins of a father, but our own inequities are what we are punished with.

Just as a just man may have an unjust son, so too can an unjust man have a just son. It is the keeping of the statutes and doctrines of God that prolongs ones life and brings blessings to it. It is being mired in sin that brings ruin and physical death, regardless of your faith in Christ.

If anything you're chastised even more so as a child of God.

So while it is well and good to point out the sins of the father, that we may learn from them and not do them, we can't blame our troubles on God punishing us for our father's sake. It's entirely up to us to forge ahead in a righteous life.

teachings.title: We are the elder son
teachings.summary: The prodigal son parable is addressed to the Pharisees as the resentful elder son, and many long-saved Christians likewise despise new converts and add works to the gospel of grace.
teachings.text:
Here in Luke chapter 15 we see that again, the Pharisees and scribes murmured amongst themselves, judging Jesus for the publicans and sinners that were drawn to hear His preaching. And again, Jesus shows them in parable that He is come to bring the lost sheep home. He has come to bring sinners to repentance towards God, not the righteous. A physician treats the sick.

And Jesus tells how much joy there is in Heaven when one sinner turns towards God that they may be saved. He offered the example of the lost sheep, and another of a lost piece of silver, and the rejoicing of those who had found what was lost, comparing that to God the Father and His angels rejoicing over every saved believer, even the most wicked and wretched.

To drive the point home, Jesus tells what has become one of the most iconic parables in scripture. The Prodigal Son. This story of falling and forgiveness, the love of a father for a son thought lost to the world, and the joy at his being restored home is well known even outside of Christian circles. It is an archetype used in secular stories, referred to throughout the culture, and the phrase "prodigal son" part of our lexicon.

The tearful joy of the Father at having his son returned to him, all that he'd done forgiven in an instant, has been a moving inspiration to millions seeking redemption in Christ. The lesson that no matter how far we fall, we are still welcome home by God, Who celebrates our return with joy has helped heal so many similarly lost, and brought them home through Christ.

It has moved me to tears to read it over the years. First as a sinner, come to God saying "Father, I have sinned against heaven, and before you, And am not worthy." But especially as a father of grown children, being able to relate to that kind of heartache and love. The shift in my life's perspective, changing the meaning and adding depth to my appreciation of Jesus' words.

But that's not who the parable is addressed to here. It's not addressed to the repentant sinner. It's not addressed to God the Father, for certain. It's addressed to those Pharisees and scribes, ostensibly righteous men, who are casting judgment on the sinners who're called by faith to Christ.

They are the elder son. The son, who by nature didn't rebel and stayed, doing the work on the farm for the father, who was there while his brother went after whoredoms and drunkenness. Who stayed true. And who, feeling entitled by his works came to anger at his father, resenting his brother and refusing to celebrate his return.

How many saved Christians today are like the elder son? Many who grew up in Christian homes, given the advantage of hearing the Gospel regularly, attending church where the Bible was preached, seeing the testimony of their own family, their parents, friends and congregants living out their Christian walk before them, and who, seeing new converts coming into the church, babes in Christ saved from a life of indulgence and sin, often scarred and broken, traumatized by the damage done in their lives and seeking to be healed, and came to resent them? To be holier than thou? Hypocrites? Fruit inspectors?

It's happened. It was the case of the Pharisees, many of whom were not saved by faith but being so immersed in the culture of the religion believed they were righteous by their own works and in a place to judge others. The beam in their eye blinding them.

Even those long-saved, but grown prideful, forgetting their previous state and losing sight of the mercy God showed them, the grace given to their undeserved salvation. Thinking they are better than.

These are often those who seek to add works to the gospel of grace. Who push Lordship and outward signs of turning from sin before things like longsuffering, charity, instruction. Who have the leaven of the Pharisees in their hearts, which is hypocrisy.

teachings.title: He that hath ears to hear, let him hear
teachings.summary: Having ears to hear means choosing to be fertile ground, doers of the word who live out the Isaiah 61 mission rather than letting cares of the world choke the seed.
teachings.text:
I would add to the points made about the parable of the sower in the other Gospels, that before explaining it to His disciples, as Jesus ended the preaching to the people who'd gathered to see Him, He cries out, "He that hath ears to hear, let him hear."

We have talked about how Jesus used parables that those seeking truth would hear, and understanding come to accept the Gospel, but those with hardened hearts were deaf to it. Unable to understand. They were like the well worn and compacted dirt of the pathway that the seed never takes to.

But if we truly have ears to hear, it isn't enough to understand the meaning of the parable. It isn't simply "getting it" but understanding it and being pricked in the heart to be that fertile ground that produces abundantly, rather than the more worldly and unfruitful Christians. Hearing should compel us to be more than just saved. To whom much is given, much is expected. We are to prepare our hearts that we be fertile, to water the growing spirit inside us with the word. To grow deep roots in scripture and to branch out higher and higher as we seek the light.

It is up to us whether we be the rock or the thorny ground, or if we are fertile soil. It's not just happenstance. It isn't just what it is. We have a choice. We can hide the light under a bushel or on the highest candlestick that others may see and be drawn in. We do that by obeying the word. Not being hearers only, but doers.

Remember, to obey is better than sacrifice. Abstinence and fasting and not sinning in a manner we aren't prone to anyway is all well and good, but it is the keeping of the law, which Jesus boiled down to Love of God shown by keeping His commandments, and loving your neighbors which is the means by which we keep them.

I keep coming back to Jesus' use of **Isaiah 61** as a mission statement for Christian life, but it is key and given us for a reason:

*The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he hath anointed me to preach the gospel to the poor; he hath sent me to heal the brokenhearted, to preach deliverance to the captives, and recovering of sight to the blind, to set at liberty them that are bruised, To preach the acceptable year of the Lord*.

If we seek to be fertile ground, we need to make this our mantra. Our founding principle. We who are saved have been given the gift of having the Spirit of the Lord upon us. Are we frittering it away? Hiding it under a bushel? Do we allow the cares of the world to choke it out? Do we fall away having no roots?

Do we live up to the ideal that to whom much is given, much is expected? Or, will we see it taken away, being only hearers of the word and never growing past that?

It is impossible to spend time with Jesus and not have it change you. The more we diligently seek Him, the more we are given. And the more knowledge and understanding we are given, the harder and harder it becomes to live in sin. To not love others. To be lazy in our Christian life. To be afraid. To be blown away by the wind or choked out by the thorns, the cares of this world.

Let him who has ears to hear, let him hear.

teachings.title: Is this the fast that I have chosen
teachings.summary: In Isaiah 58 God condemns self-afflicting fasts done for strife and show, and says the fast He chose is to loose bands of wickedness and do works of mercy, the sabbath being rest that pictures Christ.
teachings.text:
This chapter of Isaiah is incredibly relevant here. The opening verse, one of the most famous lines used by preachers for millennia. The LORD tells the prophet Isaiah, preaching in the Spirit to cry aloud, to tell His people, the house of Jacob of their inequities. To reprove them of their sins.

 God, anticipating the protests of the people who may resist the idea that they are guilty before Him, says yet they seek Me daily and delight in my ways, they do the ordinances of the law, the works. The sacrifices and the offerings and the dietary laws and carnal ordinances. They delight in doing these things.

They may say, Didn't we fast? Lord didn't you notice? We afflicted ourselves, and you didn't see? Didn't we fast on your day, Lord?

And God answers this rhetorical question for us; He doesn't regard their fasting and self affliction, because they are doing it for themselves selfishly, while they are openly oppressing others. It's not a spiritual act of humility, but arrogant and prideful.

God says to them that they fast for strife and debate. To hold it over others. To judge the righteousness of others. To hold the people bound to a yoke of works-based self-righteousness, not the liberty found in faith.

God asks, is this a fast I have chosen? Did He order them to do these acts of penance on the Sabbath? Is it part of the ordinances given in the Old Testament, the covenant in effect at this time? He asks incredulously, "*a day for a man to afflict his soul? is it to bow down his head as a bulrush, and to spread sackcloth and ashes under him? wilt thou call this a fast, and an acceptable day to the Lord?*"

Basically God is saying, is that what the Sabbath was made for? To afflict yourselves with fasting and ashes and sackcloth? To burden the people? Is this what you call an acceptable day to the Lord?

God continues to berate them, again asking rhetorically, "Isn't the fast I chose to loose the bands of wickedness? To undo the heavy burdens? To let the oppressed go free? "*And that ye break every yoke?*"

The Sabbath was to be a day of rest, that pictured the rest found in Christ. A day without labor, that people could understand that God did all the work so that they could share in His rest. A picture of salvation. Not to bind people to doctrines of devils, abstaining and fasting and weeping and wailing in sackcloth, covered in ashes.

God is like I never told you to do any of this. It is sin.

God continues, saying He gave us the Sabbath that we may do things that a workday prohibits getting done. Feeding the poor, going out and finding them that you may give them shelter in your home. To see the naked and give them clothes. To do the works of charity and mercy that we are called to do as His people. Not self flagellation and misery. Not heaping these carnal ordinances and requirements on to the people who are meant to be free to do His will.

He promises if they do those things he actually asks of them, He will bless them and their light will shine, the glory of God our reward. The multitudes of blessings that would come upon them span the next several verses.

But these false acts of piety aren't it, chief.

God tells us, directly, in no uncertain terms, exactly what His stance on all these made up fasts and acts of communal suffering in His name is. It is inequity and sin. Doctrines of devils.

And God promises us directly, the benefits of doing His will in this, and not our own:

 *If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath, from doing thy pleasure on my holy day; and call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the Lord, honourable; and shalt honour him, not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words: Then shalt thou delight thyself in the Lord; and I will cause thee to ride upon the high places of the earth, and feed thee with the heritage of Jacob thy father: for the mouth of the Lord hath spoken it.*

teachings.title: Of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh
teachings.summary: A tree is known by its fruit, and what we say and do reveals whether our hearts treasure God's grace or our grudges and envy.
teachings.text:
*For a good tree bringeth not forth corrupt fruit; neither doth a corrupt tree bring forth good fruit. For every tree is known by his own fruit. For of thorns men do not gather figs, nor of a bramble bush gather they grapes. A good man out of the good treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is good; and an evil man out of the evil treasure of his heart bringeth forth that which is evil:*

True servants of God bring forth good fruit. Others brought to salvation.

False prophets, bad fruit. Damned.

What is it your heart treasures? The mercy and grace of God? Or your petty resentments and grudges? What does what you say and what you do speak of you? ...*for of the abundance of the heart his mouth speaketh.* What do you treasure in your heart? It is revealed to all by your behavior. By what you say. By our grace and love to others, and our patience having faith in our reward. Or by our petty hypocrisy. Our wrath and fear and envy. Do we produce good fruit, or cultivate evil around us?

teachings.title: Built on the rock: doers of His sayings
teachings.summary: Those who hear Jesus' sayings and do them build on a rock and will not be moved, while hearers only build on sand.
teachings.text:
Finally, Jesus challenges His disciples, and by extension those of us who call ourselves His followers. He asks pointedly:

*And why call ye me, Lord, Lord, and do not the things which I say?*

He is giving us the truth. The word of God. But are we hearers of the word, or doers? Do we, in pride, in shortsightedness, despise the gift we've been given, or look to live like we understand the blessing it is?

God has given us His word that we may know His will.

Whosoever cometh to me, and heareth my sayings, and doeth them, I will shew you to whom he is like: He is like a man which built an house, and digged deep, and laid the foundation on a rock: and when the flood arose, the stream beat vehemently upon that house, and could not shake it: for it was founded upon a rock. But he that heareth, and doeth not, is like a man that without a foundation built an house upon the earth; against which the stream did beat vehemently, and immediately it fell; and the ruin of that house was great.

This is a promise. One we can count on, if we do it. If we live by His word, which is like a foundation of rock, we will not be moved.

If we don't, but lean into our own understanding, we are building on shifting sands. To be washed away.

Therefore let us build on that rock.

teachings.title: When ye fast, not as the hypocrites
teachings.summary: Jesus came to call sinners, not the self-righteous Pharisees who boasted of fasting and tithes; fasting is not a sign of righteousness but a seeking of God in times of trouble.
teachings.text:
Returning to **Luke 5**, we pick up with Jesus calling a publican named Levi, who we know as Matthew, who we're told, *left all, rose up, and followed* Jesus.

Now publicans, who worked for the occupational governments of the Roman empire collecting duties and taxes, were looked down upon by the the people under their jurisdiction, who naturally resent their fellow countrymen serving the foreign state against them, and were often as corrupt and crooked as they still are today. Further, Matthew was of the tribe of Levi, who were called to be the priesthood under the Old Testament, and so must have been particularly a pariah in these times. But by faith he answers the call and leaves all to follow Christ.

And for him, as it is for us, his salvation is a cause for celebration. He has wealth and status among others in his profession, and calls those he knows together a feast, inviting Jesus and His disciples.

To this, as is often the case throughout the Gospels, the envious and bitter Jews, in this case the Pharisees, see the opportunity to criticize Jesus, asking why he is hanging out with sinners like Levi/Matthew. To which, Jesus replies "*They that are whole need not a physician; but they that are sick. I came not to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance.*"

This is the purpose of Christ's ministry and our commission to give the Gospel to the poor. To the heartbroken. To those in bondage to sin. To set them at liberty with the good news of salvation. Just as Jesus stated in His reading of **Isaiah 61** that we just covered; It is the mission statement of the Lord.

Also detect a hint of rebuke, in that Jesus mentions the righteous in this saying somewhat sarcastically to give a ribbing to the self-righteous Pharisees. They, of course respond with another accusation, questioning why Jesus' disciples don't routinely fast as they do. (They lump John the Baptist's followers in there to lend themselves some of his credibility.)

But, Jesus knows their hearts, that they are vipers. Hypocrites. As He tells in a parable later on in **Luke 18** that seems based on exactly this encounter:

*Two men went up into the temple to pray; the one a Pharisee, and the other a publican.*

*The Pharisee stood and prayed thus with himself, God, I thank thee, that I am not as other men are, extortioners, unjust, adulterers, or even as this publican. I fast twice in the week, I give tithes of all that I possess. And the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner. I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other: for every one that exalteth himself shall be abased; and he that humbleth himself shall be exalted.*

Note that the Pharisees took pride in their ritual fasting, as well as their tithing and temple attendance and all the rest. They saw themselves as righteous by their works and better than, holier than, the humble publican, a sinner who may not have done these rituals and rites but who understands his place and the undeserved mercy and grace of the Lord.

There are commandments of the Lord that we are given, things He tells us we must do. We must believe the Gospel. We must share it with others, for example. Then there are things we are expected to do, but not commanded as such. We are not told we must fast, but Jesus tells us how to when we do;

**Matthew 6:16-18**
*Moreover when ye fast, be not, as the hypocrites, of a sad countenance: for they disfigure their faces, that they may appear unto men to fast. Verily I say unto you, They have their reward.*

Notice He says "*when* you fast." It is assumed we will fast, at the appropriate time, called by the Spirit, when we have a need to align ourselves to God's will and build our faith. Fasting in the Bible wasn't a sign of righteousness or a way to get God to do our will, but usually done at a sign of trouble or turmoil in the person's life. A death in the family, a tough or perilous time. At the beginning of a trial.

teachings.title: True fasting and prayer, not to be seen of men
teachings.summary: Jesus prepared with real fasting and prayer to God, while those who deny every word of God and pray to men cannot resist temptation and fast to be seen of men.
teachings.text:
It should be mentioned that before beginning His earthly ministry, Jesus sought to purify himself with prayer and fasting. Legitimate fasting, denying Himself not personal taste and treats, preference and privilege, but actually sacrificing physical necessity that He may focus on the things of God. The word. In prayer and supplication.

How can those who deny that we have "every word of God" and that don't read it daily, allowing other men to be an intermediary, how can they resist temptation? If their prayers are to other men, not boldly going before God the Father with supplication?

They can't.

That's why they often seek worldly power. It's why they fast and pray to be seen of men, and not locked away as God commands. Not going into the wilderness but proclaiming their "sacrifice" to the world. It's why they tempt God.

teachings.title: Faith Without Works Is Dead
teachings.summary: Justified before God by Christ's blood, believers show their faith before men by works, while those who make works their justification damn themselves.
teachings.text:
Now, the expression of faith is found by obeying the will of God. By this a man's faith is justified before men. Just as the OT saints listed in **Hebrews 11** believed and their faith was counted for righteousness, and by faith their works showed to others the power of God's promises.

So too, we are to live our faith. For faith without works is dead, being alone. We may be justified by the blood of Christ before God, but if we hide that faith under a bushel, or we bury that which we've been trusted rather than gain an increase for the Lord, our faith is fruitless. Dead.

The exhortation of James 2 to live out our faith and in doing so, help those in need, sharing that faith that they may come to the same and live, is a beautiful reminder of our calling.

Those that twist it to make works their means of justification before God, damn themselves and put Christ to an open shame, for their dead works are without faith. Disobedient to the Gospel. Perishing.

teachings.title: What cometh out of the man defileth him
teachings.summary: Sin comes from within the heart, so the believer must walk in the Spirit, the word and prayer to fill the heart with Christ's righteousness rather than the flesh.
teachings.text:
In **Mark 7**'s version of this event, we get greater clarity on Jesus's preaching to the people of the hypocrisy of the Pharisees and then, further explanation to the Apostles, where He is exasperated at their lack of understanding;

*Are ye so without understanding also? Do ye not perceive, that whatsoever thing from without entereth into the man, it cannot defile him; Because it entereth not into his heart, but into the belly, and goeth out into the draught, purging all meats?*

*And he said, That which cometh out of the man, that defileth the man. For from within, out of the heart of men, proceed evil thoughts, adulteries, fornications, murders, Thefts, covetousness, wickedness, deceit, lasciviousness, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride, foolishness: All these evil things come from within, and defile the man.*

It is what is in our hearts, our old man's mind of the flesh that wars with the new man created of the Spirit within us. When we are born again, we have the benefit of a quickened spirit, and the indwelling of the holy Ghost, but we still struggle with sin because it is in our thoughts and feelings, still taken by the flesh. By what comes out of us, what originates inside us.

And while this is also a rebuke of continuing dietary laws meant to instruct Israel on the law and the ways of Christ, or similar traditions of man today, like the silly "no meat on Fridays" thing, the important lesson is in how our nature is regarding sin.

We will have foolish thoughts our entire life on this Earth. Thoughts of envy and wrath, fear and lusts. Unbidden. And saying things of strife and contentions, *for out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaketh.*

The key is to walk with the Spirit, in God's word and in prayer, that the heart be filled with His righteousness and not our own sinful flesh. It doesn't stop us sinning but it makes it less out of our control, giving it over to Christ.

teachings.title: The sabbath was made for man
teachings.summary: Jesus taught that the sabbath pictured rest in Him and that what defiles is the heart, not outward ritual, a higher standard than the Pharisees' outward show.
teachings.text:
The chapter ends with two more challenges by the scribes and Pharisees to Jesus and His correction of their error.

First, they accuse Jesus and His disciples of not being pious enough to fast, and use the austere ministry of John the Baptist and his followers fasting to lend more credence to their own self-righteous fasting. To build a stronger "got ya" against Christ. And once again, Christ answers them with unassailable doctrine. How can they fast in the presence of the bridegroom? They celebrate while He is with them, and will fast once He's gone.

Jesus says one doesn't patch an old garment with new cloth, or place new wine in old skins, as a parable to what would happen. The cloth would rend from the inflexibility of the new cloth. The wine, fresh juice would ferment and tear the old skins. So to, He is saying He isn't there to "patch" the old failed ways of the Pharisees, to mend the old law. He's there to fulfill it and make it new again.

Mark shifts to another instance of the so-called holy men challenging Christ and the behavior of His disciples, as they glean corn in a field to eat on a sabbath. Jesus uses the example of David and his men when they were fleeing his enemies, eating the shew bread of the temple, despite that being reserved for the priests. That the sabbath was made for men, not men to the sabbath.

The Sabbath was designed to picture the rest we have in Jesus after salvation. It was meant to give rest to the weary. To teach as a schoolmaster the truth of Christ to the Hebrews. It wasn't meant to be a way of showing super righteousness by how closely you followed the tradition of man that sprung up around it. As a pups exercise to be seen of others.

That the rest we have in Jesus is the same. It's not our actions that sully us, but the context and spirit by which we commit them.

*All things are lawful for me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but all things edify not.*

It is similar to the story in **Matthew 15** where the Pharisees again question Jesus and His disciples, when they don't wash their hands in the ritual way before eating.

*Do not ye yet understand, that whatsoever entereth in at the mouth goeth into the belly, and is cast out into the draught?*

*But those things which proceed out of the mouth come forth from the heart; and they defile the man. For out of the heart proceed evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, thefts, false witness, blasphemies:These are the things which defile a man: but to eat with unwashen hands defileth not a man.*

A common teaching of Christ is emphasis on the spirit and heart by which we sin, the same as the spirit and heart of how we have faith. That it is the thought of wrath that is murder, thought of lust that is adultery. What our intent and what is in our hearts that God judges when we are His.

This is a higher standard than the Pharisees' outward displays of righteousness, while inwards they are ravenous wolves, full of sin.

However it cuts both ways, where in the trappings of what man sees as outward signs of sin may well be just their idea of what righteous looks like. Who put appearance over substance. Who sin in their hearts, polishing the outside of the cup, but defile themselves inwardly by their hearts.

As Jesus said to these hypocrites “*Woe unto you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites! for ye make clean the outside of the cup and of the platter, but within they are full of extortion and excess."*

 It is perspective we should all keep in mind.

teachings.title: Bodily exercise profiteth little
teachings.summary: Every creature is good to eat being sanctified by the word and prayer, and godliness, not the flesh, is what profits, since God is the Saviour of all men, specially of those that believe.
teachings.text:
Now to edify Timothy in his role as evangelist to the Ephesians, Paul gives yet more advice as to the doctrines he should be certain to instruct the churches.

That every creature is good to eat, *For it is sanctified by the word of God and prayer*, just as God told Adam and again to Noah. The dietary laws and carnal ordinances given to Moses for a season, done away with in Christ. This understanding will help the men of the church "be a good minister of Jesus Christ," not because of the food they eat, but rather the understanding of prayer and God's blessing. That, as Jesus said, *the flesh profits nothing,* rather they will *be  nourished up in the words of faith and of good doctrine.*

And so, avoid old wives tales, similarly, Jewish fables, and be about exercising godliness, their spirit, not the flesh.

*For bodily exercise profiteth little: but godliness is profitable unto all things, having promise of the life that now is, and of that which is to come.*

We the saved, *having*, present tense, the promise of the life that now is and the eternal life that awaits, must exercise and grow, spiritually. Godliness is our gainz, for our eternal life will be built upon that, not our PRs at the gym.

*This is a faithful saying and worthy of all acceptation.*

And therefore, because of this doctrine of faith, living Godly, in the spiritual rather than the flesh, the *faithful sayings* Paul writes unto Timothy, he warns they will both labor to teach others, and be rebuked by those of this world, *because we trust in the living God, who is the Saviour of all men, specially of those that believe.*

(Note to calvinists, God is the savior of all men, specially those who believe. Christ died for everyone, especially to those who believe and are saved)

teachings.title: Render unto God the things that are God's
teachings.summary: Jesus turned the tribute question to show the Pharisees did not give God His due, and the worldly fixate on the Caesar half while the spiritual see the call to render unto God.
teachings.text:
Now, offended by His preaching, the Pharisees attempt to trap Jesus in sedition against Rome. They send their disciples and the Hellenistic Jews, the Herodians, who with flattery ask Jesus to judge whether it is right under the law to give tribute to Caesar. For Jews to pay taxes to the empire that occupied them.

Jesus annoyed at their deception, knowing the wickedness they sought to do, says;

*Why tempt ye me, ye hypocrites?*

*Shew me the tribute money. And they brought unto him a penny. And he saith unto them, Whose is this image and superscription?*
*They say unto him, Caesar's.*

*Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar's; and unto God the things that are God's.*
