*He that is faithful in that which is least is faithful also in much: and he that is unjust in the least is unjust also in much. If therefore ye have not been faithful in the unrighteous mammon, who will commit to your trust the true riches?*

teachings.title: Jesus isn't Joel Osteen
teachings.summary: Jesus preached no gospel of comfort and wealth, and the more we read the Bible the more we see what is required of us before we grow comfortable in our salvation.
teachings.text:
This is a hard saying. This is difficult to hear. We are so caught up in touting our own righteousness that we missed the point of having it entirely.

Jesus isn't Joel Osteen. He doesn't preach a gospel of comfort and wealth.

If we seek to grow in our Christian life, we need to recognize the cost asked of us for following Him. And that starts with daily Bible reading and prayer.

And the more we read the Bible, the more we understand what is expected of us. With more knowledge comes more expectation. To whom much is given much is required.

The more you know, the more you realize you're half-assing it. Some will count the cost and fall away, castaway. Like the seed that falls on unfertile ground. Few will strive for the faith and contend for the crowns incorruptible. To produce fruit a hundredfold.

We should consider this before feeling comfortable in our salvation. That we are prepared to do all for Christ.

teachings.title: Take up the cross: the call of discipleship
teachings.summary: Beyond salvation, discipleship means being willing to forsake family, possessions and life itself for Christ, a cost Jesus increasingly preached as the cross neared.
teachings.text:
Another message Jesus began mentioning increasingly as His time drew near, was that of discipleship. Of not just salvation by faith, and the fulfilment of the promise made of God for a Christ, but that of those who would pick up their cross and follow Him. Those who would, for love of Him, forsake everything to serve Him, and what that would mean.

He called Peter, Andrew, James and John to be fishers of men, to forsake family and the family's business as fishermen, and they left all. Due to Jesus' intervention, they filled their nets so much so the boats began to capsize. They had the richest catch of their lives, and left it behind on the beaches of Galilee for others, in order to become disciples of Christ.

This wasn't for everyone who believed. And it certainly divided off those who were there only for the spectacle; the signs and wonders, the miracles performed, the fiery sermons preached, the dead brought back to life and demons cast out.

Jesus frequently warns there's a cost for following Him. His hard sayings brought division, and offended many that they no longer followed. His telling them that they'd be persecuted, brought before magistrates and beaten in synagogues for His name's sake, that they would see prison, and possible death for preaching the Gospel.

Jesus told those who were faithful to follow Him and be His disciples that they should go out, among the highways and hedges, with nothing but the clothes on their back and the sandals on their feet, and want for nothing, to live on faith that God would provide. To leave their family, friends, the towns they knew, the sins they were comfortable in, the ways of their former life, that they may seek rewards in Heaven, afar off, ministering to the the poor in spirit, that they may come to know the truth of God. To do more than simply believe and be saved. To do more than be in the Kingdom of Heaven, but to help reign over it. To be willing to live for Christ and not themselves.

This wasn't for everyone. Many in the crowds who believed fell away. Like the seed that falls on rocky soil that grows up with shallow roots and fades away in the heat of the sun.

Some, in the joy of their salvation and the hope they were filled with tarried longer, seeking to do some service for Christ, only to fade by and by, consumed by the cares of this world.

Many are called but few chosen. The harvest is ripe but the laborers few. The spirit willing, but the flesh weak.

It is in this context that we see Jesus, on the road to Jerusalem and the looming weight of the cross already heavy on His shoulder, and He turns to the masses that are behind Him, some saved. Some already having given up much to follow Him. Some who believed unto salvation and others unsure. And gadflies and haters of God, seeking that He fall in some way that they could accuse Him. These same sort of mixed multitudes that had been with Him throughout His ministry.

And it is in this context that He speaks to them, recorded here in Luke chapter 14.

Jesus says essentially, if anyone comes to Him, to be His disciples, and hates not his family, not only his father and mother and wife, but his brothers and sisters and his own children, and more than that, his own life, he cannot be His disciple.

Understanding that Jesus doesn't mean that we should hate them, or ourselves, but that we be willing to give them up and more, our very lives because we love Him all the more. That if the choice was given between them and Him, a disciple would choose Christ.

He says of you're not earnestly expecting to bear your cross, the implement of death used by the Romans, the equivalent to this first century group of people, pre-crucifixion, pre-resurrection, to saying a firing squad, an electric chair, lethal injection. If you're not willing to be hung from a tree in public, a gazingstock in death for those passersby, a horrific sight they may have seen themselves as it was common, Jesus says, if they would follow Him they must be prepared to face.

teachings.title: Count the cost; salt that loses savour
teachings.summary: Jesus urged the crowds to count the cost before following Him, for a disciple who falls away is mocked and like salt without savour is cast out.
teachings.text:
Jesus turns to this mass of people and says, sit down first and count the cost. Consider the price. For if they begin their discipleship and fall away in due time, they will be mocked. Ridiculed. Their faith doubted. The cause of Christ given a bad report, but more, they themselves would be seen as foolish. Taken by a trend, their service just a fad. That they didn't mean all they said.

Like a king, knowing he faces overwhelming odds, would sue for peace having scouted and reckoned the cost of war, Jesus is begging they likewise consider if they can follow after Him.

Jesus says; *Salt is good: but if the salt have lost his savour wherewith shall it be seasoned with?* You may be useful to the Lord. You may, with the best of intentions and the fullest of desire seek to be a minister, serving Him. This is good. But what if in time you lost that usefulness? Salt without savour is not only not useful, but it can't be dumped on the land for nothing there would grow, not even the dunghill, because it would ruin a compost pile. It has to be cast out.

teachings.title: Discipleship, not salvation: count the cost
teachings.summary: The hard sayings on discipleship are not about salvation, which is by grace, nor are they automatically true of every believer; forsaking all for Christ is a serious calling every saved person must weigh.
teachings.text:
This passage can be a downer. Jesus gets real, and many people misunderstand what's being said. Many mistakenly think this passage and others like it are about salvation, not discipleship. This error cuts two ways.

Some believe that He is describing a works-based salvation, that the works of discipleship are a way to earn righteousness and sanctification, and by this false belief fail to achieve either.

But even more common mistake, including among saved Christians, is that Jesus is describing the saved, just as they are. That by belief unto redemption that they have picked up that cross. That by nature of their being given eternal life by God's grace they have forsaken the world. That discipleship comes naturally with being born again, and they have nothing left to do but maybe go to church once in awhile and read some scripture-poasts on Telegram here and there. (Or arguing with heretics online). These passages become meaningless self-congratulatory "inspirational quotes." That when they give up some sin or another, they've picked up their cross.

It is deeper than that, and far more serious a matter to be willing to forsake everything for Christ. To be His disciples. And we should count the cost, soberly and with great care.

This isn't an admonition, I am in no position to judge, I am really only coming to count the true cost of this myself, after many many years of being saved. It is a place that some never come to, or try in youthful exuberance only to fail, but later, in maturity successfully achieve. Jesus wasn't trying to discourage us from being His disciples, but dividing the chaff from the wheat, being honest with those of us who remain.

Every born again believer is called to be in service to Christ. It is time to consider the cost.

teachings.title: Blessed are ye poor; rejoice when persecuted
teachings.summary: Jesus told His disciples, unlike the fickle crowds seeking healing, that the poor and hungry who follow Him are blessed and should rejoice when persecuted for His name.
teachings.text:
For those that may have missed it, this weekend we went over the first two sections of **Luke 6**, scroll up if you missed it, they are important studies on the sabbath and other ordinances of the old and new covenant, and how Jesus' prayer life can inspire us to be more diligent in prayer to ascertain God's will. Here in the last 30 verses of Luke 6, we are given a lot of red-letter preaching from Jesus, and it's all important, and much of it is self explanatory. Jesus is the truth and speaks it here without using dark sayings and parables, as He begins addressing His disciples directly.

You'll notice the section begins with the masses, the multitudes, coming to Jesus to be healed. His fame has grown, the miraculous events being even more people who seek to be made whole of their infirmities, and the "virtue flowed out" of Jesus to heal them. Again, a focus of Luke, being a physician, is the nature of Jesus as a healer.

Note what the Bible says;

*And he came down with them, and stood in the plain, and the company of his disciples, and a great multitude of people out of all Judaea and Jerusalem, and from the sea coast of Tyre and Sidon, which came to hear him, and to be healed of their diseases; And they that were vexed with unclean spirits: and they were healed. And the whole multitude sought to touch him: for there went virtue out of him, and healed them all.And he lifted up his eyes on his disciples, and said...*

Now, to increase the reach of His ministry and to serve those He can with the multitudes coming, Jesus had prayed and appointed of His disciples 12 Apostles, ordained of the ministry He was about, finding the lost sheep of Israel. Disciples, those who followed Him to learn, many who were saved believers, some were not (Judas for example). The 12 Apostles would be joined by 70 or so more at a later point in His earthly ministry, were those qualified to be sent out, to the highways and hedges, to preach and heal in His name. These disciples had left their lives and professions behind to follow Christ. They were poor, often hungry (earlier they were gleaning a field for some corn to eat), they moved about with His ministry, walking the wastes between towns and cities. God provides, but they were sacrificing to be Jesus' students.

But the multitudes, we are told repeatedly, flocked to see Jesus that they may be healed by proximity, to take the virtue that came out of Him. To witness a miracle or to see a sign. Of these mobs, most didn't come to a saving faith, despite what they witnessed, even those affected first hand. Some did to be sure, but most didn't as we are reminded at the crucifixion where the same people who lauded the coming of the son of David with palm fans and hosannas, days later called for His blood. They were there, like many transient "Christians" today, just there for the show.

In this context, the transition here in Luke chapter 6 is interesting. The mob presses on Jesus to be healed of their ailments, but Jesus looks from His work to address directly His disciples with this sermon, and the first topic is on humility.

He says blessed are you who are poor, hungry, in tears now, because you will be inheriting the Kingdom of God, your needs will be met. This application is not only for them that followed Christ then, but a comfort to us as well, today.

And with that comfort, comes a warning. He says to His disciples that they will also receive persecution, just as the prophets did, and from the very people that surrounded them as Jesus healed. The Jews' fathers treated the prophets like criminals and often killed them for the truth they preached. In a like manner they will be persecuted, but, Jesus say "*Rejoice ye in that day, and leap for jo*y," when this happens to you. It's a blessing to be persecuted for His name's sake.

And you can sense that Jesus then begins speaking loudly, turning His voice to the crowds. Still talking to His disciples, but addressing those surrounding them:

teachings.title: Endure hardness as a good soldier of Christ
teachings.summary: Timothy is charged to endure as a soldier, athlete and husbandman for the elect's sake, who become elect by believing rather than by Calvinist choosing, and to rightly divide the word against cankerous false teachers.
teachings.text:
Paul continues his impassioned appeal to his young charge Timothy, written near the end of his life, from chains. Under house arrest in Rome. Unsure of his future but confident in his fate, Paul seeks to put his son in Christ firmly on the rock of the gospel, and in chapter 1 had recounted that many in Macedonia that he'd won to Christ had turned their backs on him in his tribulation, and turned from the truth of the gospel.

Paul charges Timothy to be stedfast in the faith that won him, unashamed of Christ and the promise of God. Holding fast to the scriptures.

He begs Timothy to be strong in the faith that Paul had won him by, with many witnesses, that is others who believed and were born again, those saved by the word, so as to be able to teach it to others.

To endure hardness like a solider, as he's been called by God to be. Not entangled with any other cause or cares, but the one he's been drafted to.

To strive for mastery, like an athlete. Earning crowns for his victories, without cheating, but with excellence.

A husbandman, enjoying the fruits of his labor, souls won to Christ.

He then impresses upon Timothy these doctrines that he feels are most important, beginning with the truth; *Jesus Christ of the seed of David was raised from the dead.* For preaching this is what brought Paul to be in bonds. Scourged and stoned. Now facing the end of his race, he says he's endured all these things for the elects' sake. For the souls won by the same Gospel he's been persecuted for. That it was worth it all for their sake, that they may obtain salvation in Jesus Christ.

(Note that he is saying they believed the preaching to be elect, and that he endured that they may have believed. Not that they were going to no matter what. Not that they were picked to believe, but having believed, become elected to the promise. This is not calvinism, but how the truth of the good news and the light of the Holy Spirit works in men to bring them to repentance and towards faith in God. That we must endure tribulation to share, that all men might be saved.)

Paul continues. This is a faithful saying, that he charges Timothy to teach others;

*For if we be dead with him, we shall also live with him: If we suffer, we shall also reign with him: if we deny him, he also will deny us: If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself.*

He writes that the vain babblings and striving, arguments about the law and doctrines not of scripture serve no other purpose but to subvert those who hear them. To keep people from the faith and salvation. It continues the theme of his previous letter to Timothy, about instructing church leaders at Ephesus to be first and foremost good witnesses to the word that men might be saved. Here too, he is seeking to reinforce this idea, especially where there are those like Hymenaeus and Philetus, teaching false doctrines and damnable heresies such as the resurrection having already been past. (Hymenaeus is the same heretic who Paul said he had given over to Satan for his blasphemy in 1 Timothy 1:20)

Like Phygellus and Hermogenes, who ashamed of Paul's bonds, abandoned him and the calling, weakening the power of the Gospel for those who witnessed their shame and fear.

These false teachers and weak leaders, subverting and deserting, are like cankers. Their striving and arguments like sores that fester and eat away at the word, leading men to damnation.

Instead he charges Timothy to study to be approved by God rightly dividing the word that he may be able to stablish the faith of many, where these heretics overthrow the faith of some.

*Nevertheless the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his. And, let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity.*

Again, God knows who are His, but he lets, allows, every one that calls upon the name of Christ be saved.

teachings.title: Whosoever will lose his life for my sake
teachings.summary: Believers should take up the cross willing to die for Christ, because our blessed hope is eternal life and reward at His coming in glory.
teachings.text:
Jesus again admonishes those of his disciples who sought for him to avoid earthly persecution, which they in turn would receive for their faith, to not be afraid to pick up their cross and follow him. To be willing to be crucified and like manner, laying down their earthly life, because we have eternal life as our reward:

*For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it. For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul? For the Son of man shall come in the glory of his Father with his angels; and then he shall reward every man according to his works.*
*Verily I say unto you, There be some standing here, which shall not taste of death, till they see the Son of man coming in his kingdom.*

This is our hope as believers, this is our blessed assurance. We'll not taste of death, but rather we will live to see the son of man coming into his glory, and the coming of the Kingdom of Heaven. Our flesh may parish but our spirit has eternal life and our glorified bodies will be risen on that day, and our works for Him will be weighed and rewarded. Amen.

And so, with this promise, we shouldn't care for our life in this world. We should take up our cross willing to die for Him, just as He was for us.

teachings.title: Not peace, but a sword
teachings.summary: The gospel brings division even in our families, and loving Christ above parents and children means taking up the cross and bearing their hatred for His name.
teachings.text:
Jesus continues His instructions, telling them that God is watching over them, and what we preach, fearlessly from the rooftops as it were, may bring condemnation by men, division within even our own families.

The peace of God given by His Son to those that believe will not bring peace on earth between men. They will hate us for His name's sake. Those that accuse Jesus of being Beelzebub will accuse us likewise. If you have been born again for any length of time, you have experienced this. Especially within family. Those that know us best and who refuse the truth, resent and turn on us, accusing our every deed, hating us for His grace within us. Our sins thrown against us, and lies used to accuse.

That's why Jesus says if we love our parents or siblings or children more than Him, we aren't worthy. We must carry the cross, despising the shame, just as He did. Not caring for our very life, willing to die for God's will, just as Jesus did.

teachings.title: Lamps in earthen pitchers: Gideon's 300
teachings.summary: Gideon's men breaking pitchers to reveal lamps pictures Paul's treasure in earthen vessels, where God works through weak believers so that He alone gets the glory.
teachings.text:
This verse about earthen vessels with the light inside reminds me of the story of Gideon's 300, from **Judges 7**, where God tells Gideon to send home most of his troops before a battle, so that when the enemies were delivered unto them they couldn't take the glory for themselves, he tells the remainder to put a light, a lamp, in earthen pots.

*15 And it was so, when Gideon heard the telling of the dream, and the interpretation thereof, that he worshipped, and returned into the host of Israel, and said, Arise; for the Lord hath delivered into your hand the host of Midian.*

*16 And he divided the three hundred men into three companies, and he put a trumpet in every man's hand, with empty pitchers, and lamps within the pitchers.*

*17 And he said unto them, Look on me, and do likewise: and, behold, when I come to the outside of the camp, it shall be that, as I do, so shall ye do.*

*18 When I blow with a trumpet, I and all that are with me, then blow ye the trumpets also on every side of all the camp, and say, The sword of the Lord, and of Gideon.*

*19 So Gideon, and the hundred men that were with him, came unto the outside of the camp in the beginning of the middle watch; and they had but newly set the watch: and they blew the trumpets, and brake the pitchers that were in their hands.*

*20 And the three companies blew the trumpets, and brake the pitchers, and held the lamps in their left hands, and the trumpets in their right hands to blow withal: and they cried, The sword of the Lord, and of Gideon.*

*21 And they stood every man in his place round about the camp; and all the host ran, and cried, and fled.*

The faint of heart and fearful are sent home, thousands are sent to their tents. Those 300 who remain placing lamps in earthen vessels, that are then broken to reveal the light and lead God to triumph over the enemy. This is such an amazing parallel to our lives, and an illustration of Paul's point.

teachings.title: Blessed beyond measure, and still we complain
teachings.summary: Like Israel, Christians who take God's blessings and liberty for granted and are not thankful invite His judgment, while today we still have unprecedented freedom to serve Him.
teachings.text:
So another tale of Elisha, the siege of Samaria by the Syrians. A host of Syrians lay encamped about the city, to starve the king out. And the people were so desperate for food they boiled the heads of asses, and ate the dung of the birds. Even boiling their own children to eat, as one grieving mother tells the King. She was tricked into offering her own child with the promise of another woman to then cook her own.

We cannot imagine such tribulation and hunger. We are blessed beyond measure. And still we complain.

We have food in abundance, clothing, shelter. Relative peace and security.

We are free to worship God, to attend church, to read the Bible, free to give the gospel to the lost...All things denied Christians for hundreds of years. Things that could be a death sentence in the past. Yet how many people claiming Christ do them? How many exercise the liberty we have?

One of the reasons Israel was so often afflicted was, that when they knew God, *they glorified him not as God, neither were thankful; but became vain in their imaginations, and their foolish hearts were darkened.*

They turned to the worship of idols and worse. They held the truth of God in unrighteousness.

But first, they took for granted the blessings of the liberty they had from the Lord.

As longsuffering and merciful as God is, the Lord's patience runs out. With individuals, and with a nation.

How many Christians spend their time complaining about how bad they have it, how fearful they are about the state of things, and yet do not pray everyday in thanksgiving, glorifying God for what they have?

How many neglect their Bible? How many forsake the assembly? How many make excuses as to why they don't have to go to church, they don't have to live separated lives, they don't have to win souls and be a light?

And the excuses always are ridiculous. "There are no good churches! No good pastors! The Bible is hard to read! It's easier to listen to a podcast or to watch YouTube debates!" Itching ears, taking every rationalization they are fed, while rejecting the word preached, and complaining all the while.

America may end up as Samaria. Under siege and eventually overrun. But today we have unprecedented freedoms to turn to the Lord and to make an impact with His light so shining.

We don't have to wait until it's too late because of fear.

teachings.title: From glory to glory by the Spirit
teachings.summary: Believers are at liberty and not judged by the law, yet beholding God's glory they are changed by the Spirit if they choose, not by rules men use to lord over others.
teachings.text:
I wanted to note that the order of things is to love God and then we keep his commandments, that it be well with us and that we live long and prosper, so to speak. But it makes people then go "see? You have to keep the law too!" or "See? If you believe you will follow the law automatically!" But that's not what it says, especially in the NT.

*Now the Lord is that Spirit: and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty. But we all, with open face beholding as in a glass the glory of the Lord, are changed into the same image from glory to glory, even as by the Spirit of the Lord.*

We have the Spirit of the Lord so we are at liberty. We aren't judged by the law.

But even so, in liberty, and beholding the glory of God towards us, by walking in that Spirit, we see our own selves transformed by His glory. We are changed by it if we choose to be.

And that change is in ourselves, observed by us in our own spiritual reflection, from glory to glory. We feel God working in us, and as we feel it, His Spirit works in us even more.

People overcomplicate these things and want to make hard and fast rules of how this works and how it can be observed in others, usually for the express purpose of lording over those who we feel aren't walking the Christian walk the way we do, being holier than thou. Hypocrites.

teachings.title: Jeremiah 10 is not about Christmas trees
teachings.summary: Jeremiah 10 condemns carved idols, not decorative trees, so believers may celebrate Christ's birth in good conscience and others should not judge them.
teachings.text:
**Colossians 2:16-23**
*Let no man therefore judge you in meat, or in drink, or in respect of an holyday, or of the new moon, or of the sabbath days: which are a shadow of things to come; but the body is of Christ. Let no man beguile you of your reward in a voluntary humility and worshipping of angels, intruding into those things which he hath not seen, vainly puffed up by his fleshly mind, and not holding the Head, from which all the body by joints and bands having nourishment ministered, and knit together, increaseth with the increase of God. Wherefore if ye be dead with Christ from the rudiments of the world, why, as though living in the world, are ye subject to ordinances, (touch not; taste not; handle not; which all are to perish with the using;) after the commandments and doctrines of men? Which things have indeed a shew of wisdom in will worship, and humility, and neglecting of the body; not in any honour to the satisfying of the flesh.*

There are many false teachers, Reddit theologians and sincere but misled believers, who have taken **Jeremiah 10** out of context, to make the claim that this chapter isn't about graven images, carved, fashioned and decked with plated gold and silver, idols that are being worshipped and feared as if they have power, and saying that it is explicitly about the tradition of the Christmas tree.

That it is, preaching against decorating your house with a plant while celebrating the birth of Christ Jesus. That the practice of having house plants and decorative trees is itself paganism. But what does God instruct?

**Isaiah 60:13**
*The glory of Lebanon shall come unto thee, the fir tree, the pine tree, and the box together, to beautify the place of my sanctuary; and I will make the place of my feet glorious.*

The Bible doesn't teach against use of plants as decoration. It shows us God uses evergreen trees to beautify His temple.

No one bows and serves a decorative house plant, they beautify their homes with them. No one worships a pine tree except pagan "druid" LARPers.

Even the most secular reprobate consumerist, who strips Christ from Christmas and makes it entirely about snowmen and reindeer and coveting things, doesn't look at the plastic tree covered in lights and tinsel in the corner of their living room and thinks, "I shall worship this." They don't even "venerate" it.

But that hasn't stopped some from judging believers in respect to holy days, and teaching doctrine of men for commandments.

There are plenty of reasons to not want to participate in traditional Christmas trappings, especially as they have become in the modern, consumerist world of greed. The lie of Santa, the works-based system that you have to be good, "repent of your sins or you don't get a present!" The profane and the blasphemous way our Jewish-subverted culture has secularized it all.

But most believing Christians see the season as simply a feast celebrating the miracle of the birth of our Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ.

Most take the season to reflect on scripture, give thanksgiving to God the Father for His Son, to sing Psalms and hymns praising Him. And decorating their homes, eating special meals with family. And giving gifts in the spirit of grace, just as God has given to each of us.

If you don't want to worship Jesus this way, and if you are convinced of yourself that it is a sin, then you should not do it.

And regardless of your conviction, **Romans 14** should apply;

*1 Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations.*

*2 For one believeth that he may eat all things: another, who is weak, eateth herbs.*

*3 Let not him that eateth despise him that eateth not; and let not him which eateth not judge him that eateth: for God hath received him.*

*4 Who art thou that judgest another man's servant? to his own master he standeth or falleth. Yea, he shall be holden up: for God is able to make him stand.*

*5 One man esteemeth one day above another: another esteemeth every day alike. Let every man be fully persuaded in his own mind.*

teachings.title: Let no man judge you in meat or holy days
teachings.summary: Sanctification is not automatic or required for salvation, and believers must not be beguiled by philosophy, traditions or asceticism that pass for holiness.
teachings.text:
I would that all who believe on Christ for salvation come to the understanding that, as befitting a quickened spirit, a new man, we put off the lusts of the flesh and put on the things of God. Mortifying our members, being dead to sin.

But as Paul explains, this isn't automatic. It isn't even a necessity to salvation, as he is writing we who are saved by faith in Christ.

And because it is not automatic, and yet our new man cries out for us to be holy, many men take advantage of this conflict, warning within our members. They come with philosophy and vain deceit; that is the ideas of men that claim to know truth, often that is hidden, that doesn't come from scripture. Or from traditions of men, that things that come from the vain beliefs, and are adopted as religious practices, must be followed. These things aren't of Christ.

Christ in whom we not only have died with and been quickened, and redeemed, our sins done away with and the ordinances taken away. Nailed to His cross.

Therefore, we should not allow any man to judge us in meat, or in drink, or in respect to an holiday, or new moon, or sabbath, all of which were shadows of Christ, or any other condition that they teach for doctrine that are commandments of men and offered in their place.

This means that the vain philosophy of men, as well as the old testament strictures, have no power over we who are saved by faith in Christ. And men who place these things as stumbling blocks and snares are attempting to beguile us. Trapping us into things like voluntary humility, that is sackcloth and ashes. Self-flagellation. Aestheticism, the denial of self for the purpose of self-righteousness (*Touch not; taste not; handle not; Which all are to perish with the using)*.

Weird doctrines like the worship of angels (or saints). Things that they haven't seen themselves, but imagine in their fleshly mind. Things other than Christ who is the head of us who are saved.

Don't be misled by people who indeed seem holy, who may be able to make an argument of men in the wisdom of how they worship in their humility and neglecting things of the body. Unsaved and even reprobates, can fast for example. They may live without gluttony or abstaining from alcohol. They may be even living "cleaner" than some saved Christians. They may refuse to celebrate certain holidays or feasts, citing earthly reasons and the denial of themselves as a form of righteousness. But these are all lies and not of Christ, in whom is liberty.

Chapter 3 goes into details of how a saved Christian *should* seek to clean up their lives. These things that should be done because we are free in Christ and dead to the flesh. Not because man tells us to. Not to show our own holiness but to put off these deeds as new creatures, not beholden to the things of the flesh. But renewed in the knowledge of Christ, as the elect of God. Using the wisdom of His doctrines to teach and rebuke one another. Giving thanks to God through Christ Jesus.

It is the subtle difference between legalism and rejoicing that we are free in grace. And discernment is required.

teachings.title: Receive the weak in faith, not to doubtful disputations
teachings.summary: Romans 14 teaches believers not to judge or argue with brethren over matters scripture leaves open, but to bear with weaker consciences and not put stumbling blocks before them.
teachings.text:
Romans chapter 14 is Paul giving particular application to these things regarding the consequences of our faith, turning it inwardly onto brothers in Christ; our role in edifying one another rather than debating and striving in doubtful disputations about things not clearly taught in scripture.

Something we see ourselves in any church or fellowship with other churches or individual Christians.

The Bible says we are to be a *whole body fitly joined together*, repeatedly stating we should be of one mind regarding the Gospel and the ministry of it. That if there are disputes between us, or trespasses against us, that we work it out within the congregation. Even unto church discipline. But in all things we are to strive together for the Gospel, and because of this, and loving one another, we shouldn't judge one another over things the Bible isn't firm on.

Understand that the Bible is the final authority on all matters of faith and practice. All scripture is given by God that we may be throughly furnished to all good works. Perfect. Complete. Especially with the catch-all, love each other as you love yourself. Putting others needs before your own. And the profit of others before yours. As much as possible live peaceably with all men.

And so, chapter 14 begins with a hypothetical situation to illustrate the point Paul is building to.

*Him that is weak in the faith receive ye, but not to doubtful disputations.*

This caveat  is important to understand what he is proposing; A person weak in the faith may hold themselves to a higher standard than the Bible calls for, that we being more stable in the faith may see as silly.

Right up front Paul is warning not to use the occasion to argue with them. Especially of they are so weak of faith, or babes, that either may dig in their heels at rebuke, and add to the Gospel their opinions. Doubtful disputations, arguments about unimportant things that ultimately rest on "if you disagree you aren't saved."

Get the picture here. We can assume these are both saved Christians who simply disagree on a matter of separation and sanctification that aren't spelled out, explicitly or implicitly in scripture. Paul uses eating of meat vs vegetarians, but He also applies it to celebration of holidays, even the first day of the week as sacred.

Other than the strong admonishment against eating meat sacrificed to idols in 1 Corinthians for example, even if you don't think the idol is anything but wood or molten metal, is clear. And the giving to us that all food is clean and good to eat, that is blessed in Christ by our thanksgiving, there is nothing that says we have to eat meat. Just as there's nothing against abstaining.

But one weak in the faith and consumed by guilt at eating an animal, or who sees holidays as unnecessary or even wrong in their conscience, we should be patient with. We shouldn't push them to do what's wrong in their mind, to stumble. Even if you think they're fools.

To love them, we shouldn't place stumbling blocks but rather edify them. Our job isn't to judge one another who believe and are not in open sin regarding clear teachings, over petty matters.

An example may be something like *The woman shall not wear that which pertaineth unto a man*, and applying it to all things, even specifically women's attire that has a shared element to what the male version is. Tee-shirts. Sweatshirts. Hoodies. Taking it beyond not crossdressing and wearing modest apparel as scripture teaches, but extending it to a higher level.

Just because they have a higher standard than the Bible calls for doesn't mean you should mock it or ridicule it, and by God if it is in your church and it is their standards and it isn't being placed as a work of righteousness, than not only remain quiet about it, but hold to it. Better to dress in the manner that is greater than the Bible calls for than to sow discord among the brethren and bring others to sin.

teachings.title: Do not judge another man's servant
teachings.summary: In matters of liberty such as holidays, both the stronger and the weaker believer must stop judging each other, since each gives account to God.
teachings.text:
And by the same token, those weaker in the faith should learn not to judge another's walk, if it is keeping with the spirit of the law, but maybe not to your liking.

We are to build each other up.

Stand fast for what's true, in love. If the Bible says it and they are against it. Correct them.

If the Bible gives us liberty to determine for ourselves what's right (again outside clear teachings) then don't worry about others who don't see it yet.

If you celebrate Christmas or Thanksgiving, and do it to Christ, giving thanks to God, and someone else doesn't, it shouldn't bother you. Or vice versa.

We will give account to God. Don't judge His servants by your own terms. If some brothers see it as unclean and you don't, both being fully persuaded, let the matter settle, but the onus is on both to not give the other occasion to stumble at their own conscience.

teachings.title: Encourage, do not scorn, those weaker in the faith
teachings.summary: Believers who take sanctification seriously should edify rather than scorn those who are weaker or fearful, speaking the truth in love and saving rebuke for clear doctrine.
teachings.text:
This can be very hard for many. Especially those who, despite being saved and understanding their righteousness is as filthy rags, take their sanctification in all things very seriously. They see some, in their mind, abuse the liberty we have been given in Christ. Those who do not strive as they strive. Who don't go to church as much as they do. Who don't read the Bible sufficiently enough for them. Who go soul winning sporadically, if at all when you're out there grinding.

Those people need your encouragement. Not your scorn, least we think better of ourselves than we ought. Becoming hypocrites. Edify them and show them the blessings of the work that they may emulate you.

People who take matters of this life and this world too seriously, who worry about money. Who worry about politics. Who, being weak in the faith feel like we have to be active in supporting candidates to keep "evil from gaining" or something. Who are prepping a bunker and are terrified of persecution, stocking up on ammo and freeze dried food. These to me are people weak in the faith, and I try not to judge. I have been there myself.

And while it is important to be ready for things that may happen, and aware of what's going on, to be afraid and give in to the troubles of the world is wrong. But many weak in the faith do it and believe they are serving God when they do. We should receive them, but not to doubtful disputations. Not in strife. I am using examples of how to apply this, and if they aren't perfect don't judge me.

*But speaking the truth in love, may grow up into him in all things...*

Try saying something like "I'm not judging you, but I can show you from the Bible what the word says." But don't argue. Save admonishment for actual clear doctrines, not your opinions, and not to lord over someone who isn't as far along in their Christian walk as you. (Or who. Being stronger in the faith, acting in that faith but to you, seems wrong)

teachings.title: Liberty, but not at the expense of others
teachings.summary: Our liberty in Christ is not a license to sin, so we forgo things that would hinder others from the faith, which is loving our neighbour and not weakness, though it never means accepting wickedness.
teachings.text:
Now Paul having established this, gets to the heart of the matter; eating sacrifices.

As he's already said it is nothing to a Christian, knowing that the gods they are sacrificed to are just dead stone and wood. And knowing that all things are fine for us to eat as blessings from God as long as we acknowledge that. Again all things are lawful to us, but not all things edify others.

And just as we sit in common with our Brothers and sisters in Christ and are told, by Jesus, on those occasions that when we break the bread and drink the wine we are to remember him, Paul says that by being partakers in this, we shouldn't be partakers of the meat sacrificed unto idols. That although we could do it, there are reasons why we shouldn't.

He draws the analogy between the communion of saints, the Lord's supper, symbolic act when we come together and bless the food we consume together in God's name, in remembrance of Jesus, we are like the levitical priests who partook in the sacrifice of the altars in the Old Testament. And where Christ died once for all men, the sole propitiation for our sin, we partake in the food and drink God has provided us in remembrance of him and that sacrifice.

And if we so partake, how does it look to other people whether they not be saved yet, or maybe babes in Christ, and they see us sit down at the table of idolatry to partake in those sacrifices?

And so we do not exercise our Liberty at the expense of others. We do not seek our own comfort and fortune, we should seek others. We should be pleasing to all men in service of the gospel. We should do without rather than offend.

This aspect of Christianity, that we are both free from all sin in the blood of Christ, and the knowledge that most things people think of as sin is a sin of the heart, because what goes into the mouth doesn't defile us, but what comes out. And out of the abundance of the heart the mouth speaks. It is our intent, it's the adultery we commit in our hearts. And the knowledge of that is the Liberty we have in Christ. But it is not a license to sin. Because if what we do in our Liberty hampers another person's ability to believe or come to faith, or makes them struggle with the loss of their own flesh which turn to sin when exercised by them, then we must do without.

This is what Paul means by pleasing others. This is what loving your neighbor entails. We are to be weak to those who are weak that they might be strong.

And unlike the Jew who is contrary to all men, we are to be agreeable with all men in God. That's not going along with earthly sins and lusts of the flesh, but it's being cognizant of how our actions on matters can be a snare or a stumbling block for others.

There are many who criticize this as being a Christcuck. That it is this a good natured Christian impulse to not offend that has left us defenseless against those who would subvert and destroy us. That this is a slave mentality of sorts.

But that's not what's being said here at all. When we act agreeable to others to win them to the gospel that is not the same as accepting wickedness in our presence or going along with these abominable people when they seek our destruction.

Being mature enough in the word to understand the distinction is one of the goals of consuming the word daily. Rightly dividing the word of God.

teachings.title: Meat offered to idols and the weaker conscience
teachings.summary: Knowing idols are nothing, the believer is at liberty to eat, yet should forgo that liberty if it causes a weaker brother or an unbeliever to stumble, seeking to build others up rather than please himself.
teachings.text:
In chapter 8 of First Corinthians, Paul gets into an often misunderstood doctrine. It's regarding eating food sacrificed to idols in heathen temples and homes, but it can apply to many other things in our Christian life. Things that aren't explicitly sin, in our knowledge and understanding of both our salvation, and the liberty that's in Christ, and of God's law in our conscience, which is bulwarked by the Spirit.

As Paul says, we who are saved should understand that there is only one living God, and that idols are dead, made by man and have no power, being graven images. But the unsaved man or a babe in Christ, still superstitious of the things of this world, may stumble or be snared by seeing our eating of the sacrifice. Knowing it's nothing but meat, and the pagan practice silly and stupid, we could, in good conscience eat the sacrifice and laugh at how silly the pagans are and give all blessing and honor to God. But if that thing done in our knowledge were to cause the weaker man to sin or not come to the faith of the one true God, we shouldn't do it. It is offensive.

This can apply to the circumcision. Maybe to other practices not forbidden by the scriptures, or that is sinful only in intent of the heart, not in the doing for one at liberty.

I would list a few things, but in doing so I risk offending a weaker conscience.

Ultimately, we should be mindful of others and their infirmities, and seek to build up their faith, not please ourselves.

teachings.title: Romans 14: the weak brother's conscience
teachings.summary: Romans 14 is not about works salvation or licence to sin but about brothers not judging or stumbling those who hold themselves to higher standards in conscience.
teachings.text:
Romans 14 is often confused by the unsaved with works salvation, but it's addressing those with faith, brothers in Christ, weak in the faith they may be, who add as sin things not inherently sinful, to their own judgement in service to God.

It's also twisted by some who take the liberty found in Christ as a license to sin, saying "The Spirit hasn't convicted me on that" as they engage in wickedness clearly commanded against in the Bible.

What Paul is speaking to is holier than thou judgments of those with higher standards than even God's, or the mocking of those who see it as vain and foolish, knowing the liberty we have, obeying commandments but not adding things like not eating meat.

Both serve God and are acting in their conscience, and to get a brother to stumble in his belief is to occasion them to sin, even if the thing itself objectively isn't sinful.

Basically, not being a fruit inspector and minding your own business when someone holds themselves to a higher standard to the glory of God and their service to Him, even if you know it's a little silly.

teachings.title: All things are good for meat
teachings.summary: Jesus and Paul show dietary laws are vain carnal ordinances, yet the greater good is to love the weaker brother and not give him occasion to stumble.
teachings.text:
Dietary laws amended to the sanctification process of the believer often end in the place where "Pharisees were offended" having made those carnal ordinances into works of righteousness themselves.

Jesus declares the vanity of these carnal ordinances and dietary laws. Paul reminds that in Jesus all things are good for meat (meat means food to eat in the Bible, not just flesh of animals). But the greater good is loving your brothers and not tempting them to betray what they see as separation and sanctification. To not offend their conscience to please yours. To not be spiteful to those weaker in the faith. To not give them occasion to stumble in their walk.

teachings.title: Giving occasion to the enemies of the Lord
teachings.summary: God chastened David chiefly for giving the enemies of the Lord occasion to blaspheme, so believers must live blameless before others.
teachings.text:
It is important to note that God primarily punished David for *given great occasion to the enemies of the Lord*.

We who are professing believers are supposed to live like it. To be blameless before others. Not sinless, which is an impossible standard while we live in the flesh, but blameless. Trying to do the right thing, being a good example. Living like we have eternal life. Princes of the Kingdom.

Keeping that perspective can be difficult at times. But forgiveness, mercy and grace, charitable love, meekly displaying the joy we have in the hope of Christ, goes a long way towards bringing others to the truth of Jesus. His light shining through us.

And so when we wilfully sin, and bring shame on the gospel, giving *great occasion to the enemies of the Lord* *to blaspheme,* do not be shocked when you are chastened by the Lord.

teachings.title: Rejoicing in hope, patient in tribulation
teachings.summary: Christians should be cheerful in hope, patient in trouble and constant in prayer, as Paul and Silas singing in prison won the Philippian jailer.
teachings.text:
*Rejoicing in hope; patient in tribulation; continuing instant in prayer.*

Be cheerful. Not a doomer. You have the hope of Christ, act like it. Not fearful, but let that joy come off of you. It is contagious.

Be patient in tribulation. This applies obviously to the persecution for our faith, in Christ. But it is more than that. Try not to let the petty frustrations of this world get to you, lead you to wrath, being a bad report to the Gospel we live by.

Continuing in prayer, always. Talk to God throughout the day. Give Him thanks and praise. While we shouldn't make a show of prayer, as is the habit of some, we shouldn't be ashamed to ask God's blessings for others and praise for when He answers or blesses.

Think of the Philippian Jailer, who was saved by Paul and Silas, and the church planted there that did great things for the Lord. It all came about because, despite being in chains and captive, they sang hymns and Psalms and cheerfully held themselves out as content even in tribulation.

**Philippians 2:1-5**
*If there be therefore any consolation in Christ, if any comfort of love, if any fellowship of the Spirit, if any bowels and mercies, Fulfil ye my joy, that ye be likeminded, having the same love, being of one accord, of one mind. Let nothing be done through strife or vainglory; but in lowliness of mind let each esteem other better than themselves. Look not every man on his own things, but every man also on the things of others. Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus*

teachings.title: Moses' face shone
teachings.summary: Time with the Lord changed Moses so His glory shone, and Christians who walk in the Spirit reflect God's glory and must not hide their light though the world hates it.
teachings.text:
And so we see, after 40 days upon the mount with the Lord, Moses having fasted and prayed and recording all God commanded, he returns to the people and his face shown in the reflected glory of God, so much so that the sinful people couldn't stand to look upon Moses.

We know that here the veil was placed upon them that they may not look upon the glory of the Lord, but in Christ Jesus we may boldly go before God, the veil torn in twain. Removed that we may see Him in His word.

We see in Moses that his spending time with the Lord changed him, and the glory of God shone through him.

We who are saved Christians who walk in the Spirit, reading His word, praying ceaselessly, spreading the Gospel to others, feeding the new man, we are similarly changed. We have the same glory, magnified and reflected in us, shining as a light unto the world.

And sinful man can't bear to look at us. They get angry. Resentful. They call for a veil to cover our faith. And sadly, many Christians today hide our light behind a bushel.

But Jesus said to let our light shine.

*Let your light so shine before men, that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father which is in heaven.*

teachings.title: Give no occasion for the enemy to blaspheme
teachings.summary: Sound doctrine makes believers sober and blameless so the word is not blasphemed, and God chastens His children, as with David, for giving His enemies occasion to blaspheme.
teachings.text:
Chapter 2 is a direct continuation of the same thought in chapter 1 (reminder that these divisions we're not in scripture and often seem clunky and forced). The "But" sets in contrast the reprobates being talked about at the end of chapter 1, to provide counterpoint to what Titus should teach and preach instead. Sound doctrines.

That Christian men be sober and grave, clear minded and serious. Temperate, not given to wrath or over emotional, but instead being calm and measured. Sound in faith, trusting God, and in charity and patience, reflecting the love, mercy, longsuffering and grace God gave them, on to others.

That women do likewise, behaving in holiness, not false accusers, drunken, but teachers of good things. Women being the teachers at home of the children, especially young women, so they may know how they ought to behave and that the young men learn to be sober minded as well. And that they all are given to doing good works out of the abundance of their heart, because of the sound doctrine they have been taught.

This is all to serve the glory of God, to make us blameless that we may share His Gospel. That the word of God be not blasphemed.

We are at Liberty in Christ. We aren't going to be judged by our works for justification before God, but we are judged of man. We are to be good witnesses to others, for the unbelieving's sake. That they may be called by the light of truth we magnify. To become the vessels of gold and silver, meet for the master's use. To be more perfect in our faith. To earn glory in the Kingdom which we are joint heirs.

The Bible says everything else is vanity.

But the occasion to blaspheme God by being a bad witness should also motivate us. That the devil is an accuser of the brethren. A ravenous lion seeking whom he may devour. By our sin as believers, we give him cause to blaspheme God.

When Nathan reproaches David in his sin with Uriah the Hittite and Bathsheba, he says that David's sins of murder and adultery are already forgiven, as David was saved by faith. But *because by this deed thou hast given great occasion to the enemies of the Lord to blaspheme,* God punishes David with the death of his newborn son.

We too face reproach and punishment by God for being a bad witness to His power. He scourges His children for giving His enemies reason to blaspheme. For bringing dishonor to His house.

*In all things shewing thyself a pattern of good works: in doctrine shewing uncorruptness, gravity, sincerity, Sound speech, that cannot be condemned; that he that is of the contrary part may be ashamed, having no evil thing to say of you.*

This ties in with the much-abused James 2, and the exhortation of believers to do good works, that their faith be profitable to others, knowing that a man may judge their faith by their works.

And again it's in furtherance of spreading the Gospel.

We obey the commandments out of love and do good works out of love, that we being honor to the house of our Lord, and build His congregation with new believers. Edifying the church. This is our calling. All else is vanity.

teachings.title: Content in our station, humble before God
teachings.summary: Servants are to be honest and diligent, content in their station and humble, since God resists the proud, so they may win even their masters to Christ.
teachings.text:
Paul continues, again as he has in other epistles, instructing that servants, indentured or employed, be honest and diligent. That they may show through their behavior the glory of the grace of God, who is not a respecter of persons.

*God resisteth the proud, but giveth grace unto the humble.* The lowly and the high status are all judged the same. *When pride cometh, then cometh shame: but with the lowly is wisdom. Humble yourselves in the sight of the Lord, and he shall lift you up.*

This is a difficult saying, but it is found all through scripture. We are to be satisfied with our station, and be joyous in our salvation.

*Surely men of low degree are vanity, and men of high degree are a lie: to be laid in the balance, they are altogether lighter than vanity.*

Knowing this, and knowing it is God's grace that sets us free, we shouldn't resent our station, and instead be thankful for what we have, blameless that we may win even those who we serve to Christ.

teachings.title: Servants honouring masters for a good witness
teachings.summary: Scripture repeatedly commands obeying earthly authority and being the best of workers so God's name is not blasphemed, while always keeping God as the higher authority and leaving wrath to Him.
teachings.text:
The final chapter in 1st Timothy, and it is building on the theme of being able to give a good testimony for Christ to others by living like you have the gift of eternal life, not stuck in the cares of this world but growing in spirit.

The admonition to obey earthly authority, to please God and make His glory seen of man that you may give a good witness is repeated throughout the New Testament, from Jesus rendering unto Caesar, to Romans 13 and 1 Peter 2, and elsewhere. This is one of the hardest doctrines for most American Christians today, spoiled by the supposed promises of "Liberty" from the Constitution, and missing the liberty we have in Christ.

We bristle with pride at the idea of being good servants at work, living agreeably with all men as much as possible, paying taxes, tribute to whom tribute is due, custom to whom custom. Honor to parents and elders. This doctrine is seen as being a "Christ cuck." Seen as weak by those lacking understanding. Missing that while we defer to authority, we have roles of authority in God's hierarchy ourselves, and that we are instructed to always place God and His word as our final authority.

Often those who cry loudest about supposed persecution and calls for riot and seditions, have abandoned their own roles, or are derelict in their own responsibilities. They care more for their comfort than for their testimony. They live in fear rather than faith. They see wrath as theirs, not God's.

They, not being satisfied with what God has given them, and impatient with His longsuffering, are unable to bring others to believe and so, shoot themselves in the foot and worsen their own condition.

We have one means to lead a nation back from wickedness, and that is the Gospel. Soul winning. Revival. And that requires our being good witnesses to the power of the Spirit and faith that God, who is holy and just, and will keep His promise and restore us.

Paul is writing to Timothy who, living in Macedonia, a slave/caste society, will have gotten both masters and slaves saved, and in the same congregation. We are blessed not to be living in a society that openly enslaves people. But the same admonition applies to us as wage-slaves.

Be the best employee at your job. Even if your boss is terrible. Your employer, even if he despises religion and doesn't know Christ should still be forced by your witness to see Christians as good employees. The best, because we work for God not them. Those of us *under the yoke count their own masters worthy of all honour, that the name of God and his doctrine be not blasphemed.*

We represent Christ to the world. We are to be a light that draws men near.

And again, this isn't to say if a manager calls on you to do something that is contrary to God's word that you have to submit. We defer to the higher authority and there is none higher than God. But we do it peaceably, and with humility and meekness, trusting in God to save us should it lead to persecution.

We don't obey to avoid being persecuted, but to please God, and with the full expectation that we might face tribulation when we defer to God's will over earthly authority.

Paul uses Jesus' own example before Pilate, which by His meek silence led to Pilate confessing He was blameless, and leading to the Glory of God in the crucifixion.

*But godliness with contentment is great gain. For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out. And having food and raiment let us be therewith content.*

teachings.title: Pray for all men and live peaceably
teachings.summary: Believers are to pray for all men and rulers and live peaceably without fear or wrath, through the one Mediator, so their testimony brings others to the truth, with men and women each keeping their God-given roles.
teachings.text:
Paul, having laid out his instruction to Timothy, and his role in establishment of churches of the Ephesians, and giving some basic commands in that regard, and a warning against reprobate false prophets, moves therefore to spell out a broader doctrine that applies to all Christians. It is how to develop the men to have the temperament that will produce those fit for the office and called to that ministry, and how to edify the church, bringing in more believers.

The first point, praying for all men, supplications, or asking of God for favor, thanksgiving for the blessings He bestows, intercessions that the Spirit may work to bring about outcomes that give glory to God.

This is our instruction for the rulers of this world as much as the beggars, that we may live peaceably. Not given to fear or wrath. This causes many to bristle, but as much as possible we are to live peaceably and without offense, with all men, so we may in all godliness and honesty, bring others to the truth.

*For this is good and acceptable in the sight of God our Saviour; Who will have all men to be saved, and to come unto the knowledge of the truth. For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;*

We are to be a testimony to the truth of this. That our prayers and faith be lived out in a way that brings others to this truth. Doubt and wrath show a lack of faith and offends others from the truth. Simple as.

The spiralling people do when it comes to the cares of this world, or their fearful outbursts show a lack of faith in the same God who they are supposed to be magnifying and giving glory to, as witness to others.

Note that Jesus is our sole mediator for intercession with God. Not spirits of men. Not idols or priests. When we pray for others it is asking Jesus to intercede, God in His name to bless, the holy Spirit to give comfort.

Also, the Bible says the will of God our savior that ALL MEN come to believe. It isn't a select few as Calvinism would claim, and it is our calling to help make God's will manifest.

So men should be holy, in prayer, without fear, peaceable, without doubt and wrath. Praying for all men to come to the truth, even for the government that God may grant us peace, allowing more to be saved.

In a similar manner, women have a role as well. Just as men who are unruly and fearful offer a bad testimony so to do women who dress immodestly, who are ostentatious in their appearance. Not only because of the obvious temptations, but as speaking to their character as Godly women. The two admonitions, one for men and one for women, have the same root context. That we show outward signs of the faith that is saved us to better bring others to salvation.

It's often the men who are most fearful and wrathful, who have the loudest voice in pointing out to women not to dress shamefully. In this regard they are hypocrites. Women should do that which is pleasing to God, but so should men, we have an equal role in winning souls to Christ.

Wear those rolls differ, the Bible says women aren't to teach, because, like eve, they are prone to being deceived regarding God's word. This is just the truth of it, and it is a sentiment found throughout the Epistles, and borne out by experience. This is not to excuse Adam and condemn eve, but rather just clarifying rules and natural tendencies to better demonstrate God's will.

Paul goes on to say that it is in bearing children, and raising them up in a Godly way, that women have the greater influence than men leading the church. That they are saved, preserved and protected, by the generations of children that they bring into the world and give witness to God to, that they may be His.

Too many cherry pick these verses and create an artificial men versus women divide. It is about roles and responsibilities, understanding there are differences between men and women. And we have different deficiencies and negative tendencies that can trip us up in our walk with God.

teachings.title: An excellent spirit like Daniel
teachings.summary: The Sermon on the Mount calls us to excellence beyond the minimum, and like Daniel we should be so blameless that enemies can only accuse our faith, trusting God to deliver us.
teachings.text:
One of the messages of the sermon on the mount, in fact it's primary theme, is achieving excellence. Going above and beyond the bare minimum, striving for perfection, which means being complete. Whole.

That if we think it's enough to not commit adultery, it isn't, for even the thought of adultery is sin. Even hate in your heart is murder. If someone compels you to walk a mile with them, go two. If they take you coat, give them your cloak. Loving your enemies, not just the brethren. Going the extra mile, excelling, being perfect.

We see in Daniel that he had the spirit of excellence within him. He was blameless in his work. He did more, meekly and humbly, in God's name, serving Him. And it paid dividends with blessings from God and promotion over others. This of course led to their resentment, but they couldn't find anything to accuse Daniel of, except for his faith. And they had to trick the king into signing a law to persecute Daniel for that faith.

This is what we should all strive for. Make them come at us for our faith having nothing else with which to attack you. Being blameless and excellent. Working diligently on everything you do. Going that extra mile. Heaping coals on your enemies by praying for them and meekly and honestly dealing with all. Giving tribute to whom tribute is due. Rendering custom.

Make those that hate and resent you for your faith persecute you for it. Make it the only thing they can lay charge to you with.

And when you are thrown in the lions den, or put in the fiery furnace, put you in bonds like Paul, or whatever else they use to attack your faith, believe that God will deliver you.

teachings.title: An example of the believers
teachings.summary: When loved ones are perishing, believers should stay steadfast and peaceful as an example, since no one will believe our hope if we are as fearful as everyone else.
teachings.text:
A common lament of the believer is that their friends and family are perishing, damned without faith. The worry and stress of having that knowledge and their inability to convince them of the truth leaves many feeling impotent and frustrated. But this is all the more reason to remain steadfast. To magnify God's love for us, reflecting it to those we care about. To be the rock that they can turn to when they are troubled, and maybe coming to see the truth of the word though our example. The reason for our hope. To be *an example of the believers, in word, in conversation, in charity, in spirit, in faith, in purity.*

Why would someone believe someone telling them of the peace that passes all understanding found in Christ when we are as miserable and fearful as everyone else?

teachings.title: Do we live so our loved ones would follow
teachings.summary: With family and friends rejecting the gospel, believers should ask whether their fearless, grateful, Bible-reading, gospel-preaching lives would draw others to Christ.
teachings.text:
This is a powerful and sobering thought. Knowing your dad or mom, sister or brother, son or daughter, reject the Gospel and on the road to reprobation, or who are trapped in their zeal without knowledge, working their way to Hell by not obeying the Gospel.

We know God is perfectly just. We know in His love we are saved, undeserved, entirely by grace, because we have believed the report. But do we live in a way that these people who we care about can emulate? Would they want to? What advantage do they see in accepting salvation, in how you live?

Are you fearful? Do you stress from the news of the world, the fake and gay theater the beast system presents to keep the cattle in pens for slaughter?

Do you live in gratitude and prayer to God in Jesus name?

Do you read your Bible and go to church? Do you boldly proclaim the Gospel to every creature, giving a ready and meek answer to the lively hope you have in Christ?

teachings.title: Reasonable service and unseen rewards
teachings.summary: Says keeping the law and loving others is the bare minimum, as Luke 17:7-10 shows, and that Matthew 25:35-40 shows rewards for things done unknowingly.
teachings.text:
Side note. When we don't sin and we follow the law to the best of our human ability and we love our neighbors and our brothers and sisters in Christ, and we forgive others, we are doing the bare minimum. It's our reasonable service. 

**Luke 17:7–10**
*But which of you, having a servant plowing or feeding cattle, will say unto him by and by, when he is come from the field, Go and sit down to meat? And will not rather say unto him, Make ready wherewith I may sup, and gird thyself, and serve me, till I have eaten and drunken; and afterward thou shalt eat and drink? Doth he thank that servant because he did the things that were commanded him? I trow not. So likewise ye, when ye shall have done all those things which are commanded you, say, We are unprofitable servants: we have done that which was our duty to do.*

Of course we're going to receive rewards that have been promised to us for doing great works for Christ. 

And while I don't know exactly, I would imagine some of the things that we were commanded to do will produce rewards. Crowns in the next life. 

But the things that we're commanded to do are the bare minimum. I suppose it's the heart behind the things that we do, rather than the simple obedience that God looks at and rewards. I think God gives credit for effort, context and the spirit it was done in. 

I think Paul's warning about the wood, wood and stubble getting burnt up and suffering loss, is because there will be things that we absolutely expect to receive a reward for that ultimately were just our reasonable service. 

And we are going to receive crowns of Glory for acts that we didn't even consider were reward-worthy at the time. Things that Jesus looks at and says this was precious stones, silver or gold. Things where He will say well done my good and faithful servant, that we don't remember doing.

**Matthew 25:35–40**
*For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in: Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me. Then shall the righteous answer him, saying, Lord, when saw we thee an hungred, and fed thee? or thirsty, and gave thee drink? When saw we thee a stranger, and took thee in? or naked, and clothed thee? Or when saw we thee sick, or in prison, and came unto thee? And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me.*

While we are promised rewards, and it's often discussed the nature of them and how they are earned and what qualifies as precious stone or silver or gold, it's the little acts of love where Christ's light shines through us and others glorify God, where his mercy and his grace is magnified through the acts that we do simply because we are children of God, without any thought for ourselves. 

In fact, it's very likely that the things we expect a reward for will be burned and we will suffer loss, but it will be the times we unknowingly entertained angels, offered comfort and gave hospitality to the hopeless that will be judged worthy, on that day.

teachings.title: The mind of Christ and humility
teachings.summary: Reads Philippians 2:5-8 to urge believers to be humble as Christ humbled Himself, condescending to men of low estate that they may be saved.
teachings.text:
**Philippians 2:5–8**
*Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus: Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men: And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.*

Jesus being God and knowing he was God still condescended to become man. God humbled himself to take on mortality for the whole world. 

Let this mind be in you. Be humble. Be humble to others. Condescend to men of low estate that they may be saved.

teachings.title: Blessed when persecuted
teachings.summary: Quotes Matthew 5:10-12 and Mark 8:35 on being persecuted for righteousness and not saving one's life.
teachings.text:
**Matthew 5:10–12**
*Blessed are they which are persecuted for righteousness’ sake: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. Blessed are ye, when men shall revile you, and persecute you, and shall say all manner of evil against you falsely, for my sake. Rejoice, and be exceeding glad: for great is your reward in heaven: for so persecuted they the prophets which were before you.*

Professing Christians who express fear of the Tribulation, and persecution of the saints by the beast, saying they will flee and hide, are cowards and have little (if any) faith. 

It is wicked to be a "prepper" during the end times. Those who engage in this will be like the Jews who fled Jerusalem during the Babylonian captivity, seeking safety in Egypt. 

They were hunted down and slain. The prophet warned them;

**Jeremiah 42:19**
*The LORD hath said concerning you, O ye remnant of Judah; Go ye not into Egypt: know certainly that I have admonished you this day.*

Because they chose to rebel and hide like cowards, rather than trust God's plan, Jeremiah was instructed to prophesy that the Babylonians would invade Egypt and wipe them out, Even as the Jews forced Jeremiah and his scribe to go with them.

**Jeremiah 44:14,27**
*For none of the remnant of Judah, which are gone into the land of Egypt to sojourn there, shall escape or remain, that they should return into the land of Judah...Behold, I will watch over them for evil, and not for good: and all the men of Judah that are in the land of Egypt shall be consumed by the sword and by the famine, until there be an end of them.*

And the prophecy comes to pass. 

**Jeremiah 44:28–30**
*Yet a small number that escape the sword shall return out of the land of Egypt into the land of Judah, and all the remnant of Judah, that are gone into the land of Egypt to sojourn there, shall know whose words shall stand, mine, or theirs. And this shall be a sign unto you, saith the LORD, that I will punish you in this place, that ye may know that my words shall surely stand against you for evil: Thus saith the LORD; Behold, I will give Pharaohhophra king of Egypt into the hand of his enemies, and into the hand of them that seek his life; as I gave Zedekiah king of Judah into the hand of Nebuchadrezzar king of Babylon, his enemy, and that sought his life.*

Secular history confirms that Pharaoh Hophra (Apries) was overthrown and killed during a bitter civil war and the subsequent Babylonian invasion which targeted the regions that the Jews fled to, fulfilling the exact sign God promised to prove the doom of the Jews who fled there. Jeremiah himself and his scribe Baruch, survived to preserve this record. 

Any Christian worth his salt should know that if they seek to save their life, they will lose it. 

**Mark 8:35**
*For whosoever will save his life shall lose it; but whosoever shall lose his life for my sake and the gospel's, the same shall save it.*

teachings.title: Forgiving and praying for others' sins
teachings.summary: Teaches from 1 John 5:16-17 and John 20:23 that believers should forgive others and ask God to forgive them.
teachings.text:
The New Testament explicitly teaches that we who are saved should forgive the trespasses of others against us. That we should pray to God to forgive them. 

**1 John 5:16-17**
*If any man see his brother sin a sin which is not unto death, he shall ask, and he shall give him life for them that sin not unto death. There is a sin unto death: I do not say that he shall pray for it. All unrighteousness is sin: and there is a sin not unto death.*

**John 20:23**
*Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them; and whose soever sins ye retain, they are retained"*

This is a duty of all believers. To say "forgive them Father, for they know not what they do."

teachings.title: Supporting preaching against sin
teachings.summary: Urges believers, even when struggling, to say Amen to preaching against sin and for the assembly and the great commission.
teachings.text:
You don't have to be perfect in all your ways, but if you aren't supportive of hard preaching against sin, ESPECIALLY YOUR OWN, even if you're struggling with it, even if you aren't where you ought to be...Then you're a fool. 

Standards and rules are for God's people, that it be well with them. That they go on to perfection. They are goals we should support out of love for one another. 

Stop making excuses and start edifying one another.

Even if you smoke, say "AMEN!" when the preacher speaks against it. 

Even if you're a drunk, say "AMEN!!" when the pastor preached against drunkenness. 

If you struggle to get up Sunday morning, don't go to Sunday night and didn't even realize there's a service on Wednesday, don't you dare sit silent. Say "AMEN!" when the preacher is telling you to not forsake the assembly.
