He warns against the fool's sacrifices, his offerings and his words, not considering God's holiness and His word, uttering long prayers and excuses, a multitude of words, to make up for the lack of sincerity and humility.

Solomon compares the restless dream-filled sleep of those stressed out by their busy lives to the fool's prattling speech. Just as dreams are nonsense, so too are the fools vows;

*For in the multitude of dreams and many words there are also divers vanities: but fear thou God.*

And so, we are given another proverb against vowing vows to God that you don't mean, or are beyond your ability to keep. Fools do this, promising God a multitude of promises; turning from this sin or that, promises that for God's favor the fool will do something or give an offering for it, that is never paid.

*When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed. Better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay.*

Jesus teaches this.

**Matthew 5:34-37**
*But I say unto you, Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God's throne: Nor by the earth; for it is his footstool: neither by Jerusalem; for it is the city of the great King. Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black. But let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay: for whatsoever is more than these cometh of evil.*

James repeats the doctrine.

**James 5:12**
*But above all things, my brethren, swear not, neither by heaven, neither by the earth, neither by any other oath: but let your yea be yea; and your nay, nay; lest ye fall into condemnation.*

God takes vows seriously. He doesn't care for excuses, long public prayers, vain repetitive prayers. He wants sincere prayers and humble servants.

Better to say nothing than to be a fools.

**Proverbs 10:19**
*In the multitude of words there wanteth not sin: but he that refraineth his lips is wise*

Even a fool is considered wise if he keeps his mouth shut.

**Proverbs 17:28**
*Even a fool, when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise: and he that shutteth his lips is esteemed a man of understanding*

There are blowhards in every church in the world. Professing Christians who cannot help but make themselves known, and promote the things they do. Who make grand promises to help the church, or make this offering or that, to do works for the Lord, all to be seen by men.

It's foolishness. And vanity.

Verse 6 warns against the foolishness of talking yourself into sin, or excusing your sin as being done ignorantly. God hates this. The angel here, I believe, is the human messenger, the Levitical priest where the sacrifice is being made. But the principle remains, even now before God and His judgements.

A humble and contrite heart, this pleases God.

teachings.title: The ten commandments one by one
teachings.summary: Walks through the ten commandments to argue that they are generally easy to keep, if not perfectly.
teachings.text:
People make the 10 Commandments seem like this impossible list of things God asks for us. Sin is the transgression of the law, and these certainly are a cornerstone of the law. But they are genuinely easy to keep generally, if not perfectly.

1 - *I am the Lord thy God...*Thou* shalt have no other gods before me.*
2 - *Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image...Thou shalt not bow down to them or serve them*.
3 - *Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain...*
4 - *Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy...Six days shalt thou labor, but the seventh is the sabbath.* (We rest in Christ, Who is our Sabbath)
5 - *Honour thy father and thy mother...That thy days may be long upon the land.*
6 - *Thou shalt not kill.*
7 - *Thou shalt not commit adultery.*
8 - *Thou shalt not steal.*
9 - *Thou shalt not bear false witness against thy neighbour.*
10 - *Thou shalt not covet...Thou shalt not covet thy neighbor's house, wife, or property*. 

It is easy to not place another god in your life or to avoid idols. It's easy to not take the Lord's name in vain. Christ is our rest. Honoring your parents isn't difficult. Neither is not being a murderer, an adulterer or a liar. It's kind of easy to not covet things that aren't yours and you don't deserve. 

Jesus upped the ante by making it the spirit of these things, holding it in your heart being as bad as acting on it.

teachings.title: Stiff necks and the hated upright
teachings.summary: Those who harden their necks against reproof come to destruction without remedy, and the wicked hate the righteous because they hate Christ and the light that exposes their evil.
teachings.text:
**Proverbs 29**, the last of the sayings of Solomon transcribed by order of Hezekiah, begins with the reality of reprobation in those that stiffen their necks to reproof. The Bible often shows examples of heart hardened people, like Pharaoh and the Pharisees, coming to destruction without remedy, despite the reproof of the Lord.

**Romans 1:18-19**
*For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, who hold the truth in unrighteousness; Because that which may be known of God is manifest in them; for God hath shewed it unto them.*

Plagues, curses from Heaven, the reproof of Christ among them, all revealing the iniquity and unrighteousness of men, who refused to acknowledge the truth set before them. And their foolish hearts darkened. There became no more remedy for them, no repentance towards the truth of God. And so they are destroyed.

Vs 2 echos similar sayings, that the rule of the righteous brings joy to the people, but the wicked kings bring mourning.

Vs 3 brings another reminder to honor your father. A wise son will pay tribute to him, but the whoremongers spend what should rightfully be the family's wealth.

Verse 4-8 show some of the ways that a wicked man lays snares for kings and neighbors. With gifts and flattering words, seeking favor. Or by the transgression of an evil man, there lies a snare of sin for others. Vengeance, wrath, or even common cause for filthy lucre's sake, others can be caught up in it when the wicked sin. But the righteous song and rejoice, happily trusting God. Avoiding those pitfalls.

The righteous consider the poor, and turn away wrath. But the wicked don't care. Their scorn for the afflicted and bring others to transgression.

Vs *10 The bloodthirsty hate the upright: but the just seek his soul.*

The bloodthirsty, the violent man, the scorners and scoffers and fools, they all hate the upright man, the righteous in Christ. Their deeds are wicked, and the good man magnifies the light within him.

**John 3:20**
*For every one that doeth evil hateth the light, neither cometh to the light, lest his deeds should be reproved*.

Jesus warns us of this truth;

**John 15:18-19**
*If the world hate you, ye know that it hated me before it hated you. If ye were of the world, the world would love his own: but because ye are not of the world, but I have chosen you out of the world, therefore the world hateth you.*

They hate His children because they hate Him. They hate the light that exposes their evil. They hate reproof and become stiff necked. They hold the truth in unrighteousness.

teachings.title: Obedience modeled by the Son
teachings.summary: Christ's obedience to the Father is the example for believers, and learning to fear and honor parents is where the fear of the Lord begins.
teachings.text:
As always, Jesus is our example.

**Philippians 2:5-8**
*Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus: Who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: But made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant, and was made in the likeness of men: And being found in fashion as a man, he humbled himself, and became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross.*

Being obedient unto death, honoring the Father. The good Son.

**John 6:38**
*For I came down from heaven, not to do mine own will, but the will of him that sent me*.

**John 14:31**
*But that the world may know that I love the Father; and as the Father gave me commandment, even so I do...*

**John 15:10**
*If ye keep my commandments, ye shall abide in my love; even as I have kept my Father's commandments, and abide in his love*.

Jesus provided the example of a lifelong commitment to honoring the Father. Of doing His will. Of obeying His Commandments. A lesson in obedience that we are called to emulate.

**Hebrews 5:8**
*Though he were a Son, yet learned he obedience by the things which he suffered*.

As children of God by faith, as heirs, we owe the same honor and respect and obedience to the Lord. Even obedience unto death. Which is why martyrs are honored in heaven. Receiving greater reward and crowns.

Loving God with your whole whole and soul, having fear of the Lord, begins with fearing your parents. That is why there are so many Proverbs revolving around being a good son. Why so many call upon parents to raise their children properly.

Obedient children are a reflection of Christ and good parents are a reflection of the Lord. God, our Father. The ordered society that comes from it is a blessing. The obedience that it be well with us, that we live long upon the Earth. And to better know Him. Amen

teachings.title: He that turneth away his ear from the law
teachings.summary: Those who use liberty in grace to excuse sin and teach that God is not mad at sin have abominable prayers, while believers should affirm the law and abstain so as not to make the weak stumble.
teachings.text:
**Proverbs 28** continues.

**Verse 9**; *He that turneth away his ear from hearing the law, even his prayer shall be abomination.*

The law-haters out there, who allow the reality of grace and reconciliation in Christ to then turn their ear from the hearing of the law, should consider this saying. Their prayers are an abomination to God.

To take our liberty and use it as a cover for sin, is wicked. Rather it is a cause to cleanse ourselves, as much as possible, and to not lead those weak in the faith to stumble.

**1 Corinthians 10:23-24** 
*All things are lawful for me, but all things are not expedient: all things are lawful for me, but all things edify not. Let no man seek his own, but every man another's wealth.*

We should be a model of the law, that it convicts the unsaved, and serves to edify our brethren, weak in the faith, to do better. Not as a stumbling block or a snare, but as an example. Not being offended at the hearing of the law, but affirming it, that it may bring others to Christ. That our prayers are acceptable to the Lord.

You might not be perfect, and we all fall short, but preaching against sin, especially the sin you still do, shouldn't offend you. It should convict. It should elicit an even hardier "Amen!"

It's no wonder that **verse 10** follows;

*Whoso causeth the righteous to go astray in an evil way, he shall fall himself into his own pit: but the upright shall have good things in possession.*

**Romans 14** warns of causing a brother to sin by your liberty.

**Romans 14:14-16;21**
*I know, and am persuaded by the Lord Jesus, that there is nothing unclean of itself: but to him that esteemeth any thing to be unclean, to him it is unclean. But if thy brother be grieved with thy meat, now walkest thou not charitably. Destroy not him with thy meat, for whom Christ died. Let not then your good be evil spoken of*... *It is good neither to eat flesh, nor to drink wine, nor any thing whereby thy brother stumbleth, or is offended, or is made weak.*

If matters of conscience are left to us to determine, yet we should defer to abstain for the edification of those weak in faith, how much more so the clear things of the law which are sin?

So, those who take liberty to be libertine, and who teach that the redundant term "free grace" means "God isn't mad at your sin," to then allow fornication, drunkenness and the like, misleading others, will themselves fall victim to their sin. God will repay.

And those that deliberately bring offense, who corrupt and pervert others into sin, they will fall themselves into the pit they've dug for others. They will be snared by their own trap.

Better to have standards, to teach the whole counsel of God. To love the law and delight in it, even at liberty by grace. To put the profit of others before your own lusts and desires. To not give others cause to blaspheme the Lord. For the upright shall have good things in possession. They shall be blessed.

teachings.title: The rod, honest instruction, and wine
teachings.summary: Children need both the rod and godly instruction, honesty from parents about their own sin, and warning against drink, which God says not even to look upon.
teachings.text:
**Proverbs 23** reinforces the idea of the wise son being a blessing and a cause for rejoicing in parents. The natural need for a child to want to please their parents, to follow in their ways and to be their pride and joy, often gives way to rebellion and a need to establish themselves separately from their parents expectations.

This is why the early admonition, the scourging betimes, the willingness to both instruct your child in the way of righteousness and beat them with the rod of correction early, will help them have the foundation for fear of the Lord, and an understanding that they shall not depart from.

The two methods achieve one result. A child isn't going to die from a spanking. The purple of a bruise is a sore reminder of their foolishness and the understanding that there are consequences for their actions. The Godly instruction shows the correct path forward. All of it is given in love.

When the result is a child with a wise heart and lips speaking the right things, who harkens to the instruction of their youth, it is a cause to rejoice.

They need to hear about the ends of sin and the wages of death it brings. To see the end of the fool. To rightly judge how the latter end of the sinner is compared to the wise. They should not envy the sinners but fear the Lord.

Solomon continues the words to the wise; be no among winebibbers or gluttons. Drunks and the overindulgent come to poverty. There are examples in our own families and opportunities to show the results in our streets.

Many teach the mercy of charity and not judging to their children, without using the wisdom of example, rightly judging the situation. They end up learning a toxic empathy without seeing the fault of the fool leading to their plight.

A child raised in the fear and admonition of the Lord will seek truth and instruction over riches.

The warning against whores and strange women especially resonates, as the fairer sex was Solomon's weakness.

It is important for a young man or woman to hear the truth, even if it is your own sin that you struggle with. Objective truth should be the goal, not hiding or excusing your failings. One of the triggers of rebellion, especially in a Christian home is the dawning realization of hypocrisy from the strict parents, who don't hold themselves to the standard they are imposing. Resentment can take root.

Honesty about sin and consequences, how it has affected you personally, can help soften the blow when they reach the age where children realize Mom and Dad aren't perfect. And instruction of the gospel lets them know there is One who is perfect and holy, even if there are none righteous among men.

The final passage paints the dark reality of alcohol. It leads to sorrow and woe. Babblings and wounds without cause, from drunken stumbling. Red eyes and hangovers.

God's word says not to even look at wine as it ferments, bubbling and turning red.

So many excuse their drunkenness by using examples of the use of the word "wine" in scripture, but neglect the meaning and context. Wine often mean the fresh juice of the vine, new. Of preserved concentrate  or watered down to the point of being alcohol free. They will say that a little won't hurt...But the standard for princes is to not even look at strong wine.

The warning that alcohol causes perverse and lustful thoughts in the heart, lowering inhibitions and standards, leading to greater sin, is an undeniable truth.

The poison of a snake, the toxic nature of the drink, like the bite of an adder leads to disorientation, head spinning, unsteady feet and sickness. Hangovers. And the sad reality that those given to wine will seek it again, despite all those negatives.

Better to be sober and wise.

teachings.title: Augustine, Pelagius and the persecution of separated Christians
teachings.summary: Shows how Augustine built original sin and irresistible grace against a Pelagian strawman, and how the same false witness was used against Cathars, Waldensians, Paulicians, Lollards, Anabaptists and Baptists who lived separated lives; all that will live godly shall suffer persecution.
teachings.text:
God's gospel is simple: grace through faith in Christ's finished work, which not only saves us from Hell and gives us eternal life in Jesus, the Spirit indwelling us, quickening our spirit, sealing us unto redemption, but God also graciously empowers us to choose obedience, His paths, His commandments, allowing us to strive for maturity in Him, and live separated lives as the New Testament demands. 

But over the centuries, and even today, that simplicity has been complicated, twisted, and poisoned by human systems that shift blame from personal choice to inherited inability or divine decree, and make grace no more grace. Leading men to destruction, and to pridefully destroy those that remind them of their error. 

Augustine's doctrines of Manichaean gnostic determinism, which he championed (including his novel theory of "original sin" as inherited corruption, "prevenient/irresistible grace" as the sole cause of good, and redefining predestination as preordainment) were advanced by redefining orthodoxy against a constructed "Pelagian" strawman opposite, and attributing to Pelagius heresies which were not held by the ascetic monk in Britain.

This approach functioned as a Hegelian dialectic: Augustine pitted his views against an exaggerated opposite to legitimize them as the necessary middle ground. By securing Pelagius's condemnation through imperial and ecclesiastical pressure, Augustine's theology gained dominance in the emerging Roman Catholic Church, influenced by political patrons in the late Empire.
This pressure of being made anathema and labeled a heretic served to make others who held the Eastern, Greek traditions of New Testament Christianity and understanding fearful of being similarly labeled. The writings of Pelagius and others who held his actual beliefs were either destroyed or allowed to fall into obscurity due to this fear, and so the lack of an extensive record lends even more credibility to Augustine's false doctrines.

Regarding original sin, Augustine's formulation—where Adam's sin transmits inherited guilt and an inevitable inclination to evil from birth—was not a settled orthodox doctrine in the earlier churches.

Pre-Augustinian Christian asceticism generally viewed human nature as inclined toward goodness, if incapable of being good outside of grace entered into by faith. That man is capable of moral progress in Christ, with sin arising from personal choices, habits, or imitation of bad examples rather than a deterministic corruption inherited biologically or legally.

Despite the smears, Pelagius explicitly affirmed God's grace and the Spirit's work as essential: grace opens the heart, reveals truth, exposes snares, enlightens with heavenly gifts, and forgives sins gratuitously. In his Letter to Demetrias and other texts, he described virtue as resulting from cooperation—human consent and effort partnering with divine aid to battle sin and imitate Christ's example of holy living. This was not sinless perfection by fleshly will alone (he acknowledged ongoing weakness and the need for maturity, or perfection in Christ), nor salvation by Old Testament law-keeping (which he recognized all fall short of), but pursuit of Christ's new commandment: loving God fully, with all your heart and loving your neighbor as yourself, all enabled by grace in the regenerated life of the believer.

Pelagius wasn't claiming sinless perfection or denying God's grace and human weakness/sin, we see a view of grace-enabled free agency and moral responsibility that was orthodox into the late 4th/early 5th-century Christian theology, particularly in the ascetic context—before Augustine's influence shifted the boundaries, and changed the conversation to say men are beyond responsibility, and can only be as "good" as God predetermined they be.

In the predominantly Greek, Antioch tradition, they had grown to see the natural end result of following the New Testament was living simply, loving others, being charitable, not given to drink, gluttony, fornication, adultery, coveting, etc. To put others' profit above your own.

This contrasted with late empire libertine culture in Rome, and the gnostic influence from Alexandria, which saw excess, and to the ascetic mind, sinful living being supported by the religious leaders there.

Augustine, from North Africa with roots in Alexandrian thought, a deep Manichaean past, and limited Greek proficiency, which introduced interpretive errors and conclusions, because he lacked the ability to understand the Greek texts. So Augustine diverged from earlier traditions, and his heresies have over time become foundational for many supposed Christians.

Pelagius's outspoken criticism of Roman hedonism and clerical hypocrisy made him unpopular among those Augustine later influenced to support his theology and anathematize his critic.

This reevaluation of the false charges of "Pelagianism," isn't meant to idealize Pelagius but recognize that the traditional "heretic" label stems more from polemical and political wrangling by Augustine and others, than from his actual teachings. In that context, we should reconsider how Augustine's legacy shaped Western Christianity—often at the expense of biblical exegesis and understanding of choice, responsibility, and grace-empowered obedience. That the simplicity of the Gospel and simplicity of life we should strive for, has been complicated by systematics of men. That the separated life and sanctification believers should strive for has been abandoned by many professing Christians. And that the teachings on lack of responsibility, or "inability to respond," has allowed those influenced by Augustine to fall well short of the potential given us by grace through faith, and the example of Christ we should actually be striving for.

The pattern is clear once you see it. Groups that actually try to live the separated, simple, holy life the New Testament calls for—loving God with all the heart, loving neighbor as self, putting others first, avoiding the flesh’s excesses—have always drawn persecution from the powers that be.

Look at the Cathars (the "pure ones"): extreme ascetics who rejected Roman wealth, hierarchy, sacraments, and papal authority in favor of purity and spiritual living. Rome branded them dualist heretics with false charges and launched a full crusade to wipe them out, massacring thousands in genocidal campaigns like the siege of Béziers in 1209, where "Kill them all, God will know His own" became the motto. Their crime? Living too separated from the corruption they saw in the Church, exposing the hypocrisy just like Pelagius did.

The Waldensians ("poor men of Lyon") did the same in a more biblical way: lay preaching, poverty, charity, vernacular Scripture (KJV-like emphasis on the Word for all), no oaths or excess, and rejection of papal authority and indulgences. They wanted apostolic simplicity. Rome excommunicated them, hunted them with crusades and Inquisition, burning them at stakes, drowning families, and slaughtering villages in the Alps—murderous false witness calling them heretics for rejecting infant baptism, purgatory, and clerical pomp. Why? Because their separated life exposed clerical hypocrisy, echoing the smears Augustine used on Pelagius.

This false witness—strawmanning true believers as heretics to justify murder—didn't stop with Augustine and Rome. It continued through the Reformers: Luther labeled Anabaptists "fanatics" and supported their execution; Calvin had Servetus burned and drowned Anabaptists in Geneva for rebaptism; Zwingli oversaw the drowning of believers in Zurich rivers; Anglicans imprisoned and executed Puritans and early Baptists for nonconformity. Even "Bloody Mary" (Queen Mary I of England) burned hundreds of Protestants at the stake during her reign (1553–1558), including men, women, and children who rejected papal authority and held to Scripture alone—false witness and torture to enforce high-church conformity.

Add in the Paulicians: 7th-century ascetics rejecting icons, hierarchy, sacraments, and papal-like authority, emphasizing Scripture and simple faith—they were massacred by Byzantine emperors and labeled Manichaean heretics (ironic, given Augustine's past). The Bogomils followed, dualistic but ascetic, persecuted by Orthodox and Catholic alike with burnings and exiles. Petrobrusians and Henricians (12th century) preached against infant baptism and corruption, only to be burned alive. Arnoldists rejected clerical wealth—hunted down. And the Lollards, followers of Wycliffe, pushed Bible in English, poverty, holy living, and rejection of papal authority—branded heretics, burned at stakes under English law, their bones dug up and scattered.

Even quasi-Augustinian sects like the Puritans and Plymouth Brethren, who pursued disciplined, world-denying holiness—plain living, strict Sabbath, moral rigor—faced hostility. Puritans fled England under Anglican pressure, facing starvation and native attacks; Brethren separated from established bodies and were often mocked or marginalized, even as they carried some Calvinist errors.

Rome and high-church Protestant systems alike use political power to silence those who live too close to Christ’s example. The simple gospel—grace through faith enabling obedience, choice, and separated living—threatens any institution that has grown fat on compromise. 

When believers start striving for the real thing, the powers that profit from laxity always push back with false witness and murder. History proves it: purity draws fire, leaving a trail of blood from NT martyrs through these groups to the burnings under Bloody Mary and beyond.

Augustine’s legacy perverted the gospel and weakened responsibility which excused the excess and rationalized the evil done to separated Christians with standards; the faithful who keep trying to live Biblical lives and are persecuted for it. The pattern hasn’t changed.

The Bible says, *Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution.* Jesus warns again and again that Christians will be hated for His name. That we will suffer persecution. Paul, Peter, John and Jude all write about scoffers, mockers, persecution for the faith, and the patience of the saints who endure it. 

We count ourselves blessed that in America, today, we aren't facing any real persecution. That we are free to worship, pray, read and own the Bible, go soul-winning...all without facing the same challenges our spiritual forefathers faced. Partly because our system of government was influenced by those fleeing persecution and sectarian violence. This gave us some protection against politically connected apostates coming against us for Godly living. 

But, another reason why Bible believing Christians today, including you and I, aren't facing the same level of persecution those 1st century NT Churches faced, or the various Christians throughout the last 2,000 years have faced, is because of our own lack of separation. Because we compromise. Because we shirk standards and give in to the flesh, and aren't as perfect, or mature, as we could be. Worldly. Carnal. 

Maybe we would have the crowns of glory given martyrs if we chose to live more like Christ and followed His example, the way these earlier Christians did.

**Luke 6:22-23**
*Blessed are ye, when men shall hate you, and when they shall separate you from their company, and shall reproach you, and cast out your name as evil, for the Son of man's sake. Rejoice ye in that day, and leap for joy: for, behold, your reward is great in heaven: for in the like manner did their fathers unto the prophets.*

teachings.title: The ten commandments are not impossible
teachings.summary: Says the ten commandments are generally easy to keep, with the Sabbath fulfilled as rest in Christ.
teachings.text:
Generally speaking, and understanding that we all fall short of the glory of God, and stipulated that the Sabbath is Christ Jesus, where saved believers rest forever, but the 10 Commandments are pretty easy to keep (mostly!) 

Having no other God, not making or bowing to idols, not taking His name in vain. Resting in Christ. Honoring your parents, even as adults. 

Not killing. Not committing adultery (in practice if not in the heart). Not stealing. Not bearing false witness. Not coveting your neighbors things, or his wife, or anything he has. 

These bare minimum things are really not that difficult. Bare minimum stuff.

teachings.title: Suffering defies neat explanations
teachings.summary: Though God can use suffering to correct, Job's affliction was not for his sin, so the wise response to another's grief is humble presence and charity, not overconfident correction.
teachings.text:
Elihu's point about God speaking through dreams and visions or through pain and affliction to turn people from pride and the pit isn't entirely wrong theologically (Scripture elsewhere affirms God can use suffering redemptively **Psalm 119:67, 71; Hebrews 12:5–11).** But applying it directly to Job's case assumes the suffering is for specific sin or pride, which the book's prologue shows isn't the full story. Job's trials stem from a heavenly challenge, not personal wrongdoing. But Elihu's unable to hold enough grace and empathy to relate to Job in charity. In faith.

Young (or any) believers gain influence through quiet godliness, love, and purity, not puffed-up words that lack empathy for profound grief. Job's story shows that suffering often defies neat explanations, and the wisest response is often humble presence rather than overconfident correction.

Everyone else's misfortune isn't an opportunity to show how smart or wise or spiritual you are. No one profits from that. It leads to men despising your youth, not establishing you as more wise than they are

teachings.title: Read scripture first for how it applies to Jesus
teachings.summary: Teaches that scripture should first be read as God telling us about God and the mind of Christ, not as a text written about the reader.
teachings.text:
Speaking of natural men, and not understanding the spiritual things of God that are spiritually discerned, it is incredibly important when reading scripture to look first at how it applies to Jesus. 

A lot of people read scripture, to read themselves into the text. To make it about them. 

"God's talking to me so why isn't it about me??"

God is telling us about God. To show us the mind of Christ that we may know it. And through it the Spirit which searches all things, even the deep things of God, reveals that mind of Christ. 

**John 16:13**
*Howbeit when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth: for he shall not speak of himself; but whatsoever he shall hear, that shall he speak: and he will shew you things to come.*

The only thing self-centered about our walk with God when we read scripture, is understanding His ways and His wisdom and then we can apply the implications to ourselves. But the primary text is about the Lord. 

Almost every heresy imaginable that is drawn from the Bible, comes from people making the focus themselves. 

As John the Baptist said, I must decrease that He may increase. You're going to learn so much more of the wisdom of God keeping that fear, that reverence, first and foremost in your mind.

teachings.title: Do the hard thing, not man's compromise
teachings.summary: Ezra took the easy way of divorce, but facing the results of sin we should wait on God, accept consequences and do the hard thing he prescribes.
teachings.text:
In Nehemiah, we will see shortly that he faced a similar problem with one specific priest. And he doesn't order the priest's divorce, he removes him from office.

I think Ezra was overcome and overwhelmed by the tough choice he had to make, and when the man Shechaniah the son of Jehiel came up with the idea of putting the wives away, so that the men who transgressed could eat their cake and have it too, Ezra pounced on it because it was the easier path.

When we are faced with a hard choice because of our sins, and decisions of what to do about it will require self-sacrifice and dealing with unpleasant repercussions, we should wait on God's will. Do the hard things. Not latch on to man's compromise and easy way out.

It is hard to put someone out of church, but it is God's prescription for certain situations.

It can be hard living with a spouse who doesn't treat you right. God says stick it out.

We should patiently accept the consequences of our actions. That would show true remorse and humility before God. Not doing the easy thing and then crediting yourself for it.

teachings.title: Strange wives and the unequally yoked
teachings.summary: Ezra's crisis shows that marrying unbelievers leads men into their spouses' abominations, though God showed grace to believing outlandish women in Christ's line.
teachings.text:
Ezra, having returned to Jerusalem with the treasures to aid in the building of the walls of the city, and the establishment of God's law in the rebuilt temple, faces a crisis when he sees that the Levites among the land have taken strange and outlandish women for their wives.

He calls in prayer, recalling the words of God that Israel, upon entering Canaan would not give their daughters to the sons of the heathens, nor take their daughters in marriage.

He reasons that, given God's grace in allowing the restoration and the support of kings, and the end to captivity, this affinity with abominations cannot stand. That it would be the final straw, and God would destroy them utterly, leaving not a remnant behind. He says to God, we cannot stand before you in their trespasses.

Worse, the mixed marriages, the "holy seed of Israel" joining with these heathen nations had led to the men doing accord to the abominations of the Canaanites.

Just as the sons of God, those of the line of Seth, Enos, believers who called upon the name of God, mixing with the daughters of man, those unbelieving and from Cain, led to the wickedness and abominations that caused God to repent of creating man. Sending the flood that only Noah, perfect in his generations, and his sons and wives escaped.

Just as today, we are told not to be unequally yoked to non-believers, not just in marriage but in all spiritual enterprises.

But is the sin here the mixed marriages by ethnicity or spiritually, where the women bring the men to commit idolatry and abominations? The way that Balaam caught the Israelites at Baalpeor.

There are 4 outlandish women (Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, and Bathsheba—referred to as "the wife of Uriah") in the lineage of Christ. God showed grace to these mixed marriages, clearly. He used their offspring in the human genealogy of Christ. No greater honor could be given any woman. But these women had faith, making the difference.

That God uses our mistakes and weaknesses to His benefit and to do His will, is a lesson found throughout scripture. A sovereign Lord that doesn't simply micromanage everything, but actually allows free will, time and chance within all of His creation to determine things, and ultimately, He uses all those things for His will regardless of how they seem to us.

teachings.title: Find your place in a local church
teachings.summary: Says the best way to find your gifts and calling is serving in a Bible believing New Testament church, and that one not active in a local church is not right with God.
teachings.text:
Also! The best way to find your gifts and calling is in a Bible believing NT church. The IFB has churches all over America that need you. They need your talents and skills and energy and knowledge. They need the manpower to do God's work. 

You want to be part of something, to feel like you belong and matter, do the work of the Lord.

Stop glazing each other in chats and aura farming online. It's all vanity. Because if you're not active in a local church, you aren't right with God.

teachings.title: The very elect can be deceived
teachings.summary: Points out that Matthew 24:24 says the very elect, meaning every saved Christian, can be deceived, so believers need church and the word to stand.
teachings.text:
**Matthew 24:24**
*For there shall arise false Christs, and false prophets, and shall shew great signs and wonders; insomuch that, if it were possible, they shall deceive **the very elect**.*

You notice it doesn't say only certain Christians. People who aren't backsliding. Doesn't say people who go to church three times a week and read their Bible everyday. It says the elect. So that's every saved Christian. 

What stops a backsliding worldly, living in sin, unchurched, flesh-feeding, Grace frustrating, Spirit quenching saved Christian from believing the hype and thinking an antichrist is the Christ? 

What could possibly protect that member of the very elect? 

Because the very elect includes those people too. 

What power stops them from believing a lie?

teachings.title: Be in a local church
teachings.summary: Says a believer must be in, or actively seeking, a local called-out assembly, and answers common excuses for staying out of church.
teachings.text:
If you are not IN a local called out assembly of believers, or ACTIVELY SEEKING to join one, you aren't right with God. 

If you are helping to enable others to forsake the assembly, excusing them, encouraging them, claiming that there are "no good ones," giving them any reason to justify their being out of Church....You are not only not right with God, you are wicked.

teachings.title: Confessing faults and repenting as a believer
teachings.summary: Teaches that saved believers should admit their sin to God and stop it, and confess faults to one another according to James 5:16.
teachings.text:
There is a repentance of sin that all saved believers should strive to do, admitting your faults and iniquities to God, and then turning from those things. To be honest with yourself and God. 

He doesn't want you to be sorry, or need you to be sorrowful, the Lord just wants you to admit it's wrong and stop it. 

So do most normal, healthy people. Parents understand. People who have had relationships with family or friends with drug addiction or other similar behaviors, they understand. No one wants to hear excuses. No one wants a slobbering apology. Just admit you were wrong, to God at least, and stop doing whatever it was. Especially be willing to make amends with the brethren;

**James 5:16**
*Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much.*

You want your fervent prayer to avail much? Confess your faults and pray for each other. And forgive your brother when he does, as you would be forgiven.

teachings.title: Paul kept the faith
teachings.summary: Reads 2 Timothy 4 to show that Paul's 'kept the faith' refers to his ministry and reward, not holding on to personal belief to stay saved.
teachings.text:
2 Timothy 4:1-13
 *I charge thee therefore before God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, who shall judge the quick and the dead at his appearing and his kingdom; Preach the word; be instant in season, out of season; reprove, rebuke, exhort with all long suffering and doctrine. For the time will come when they will not endure sound doctrine; but after their own lusts shall they heap to themselves teachers, having itching ears; And they shall turn away their ears from the truth, and shall be turned unto fables. But watch thou in all things, endure afflictions, do the work of an evangelist, make full proof of thy ministry. For I am now ready to be offered, and the time of my departure is at hand. I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith: Henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness, which the Lord, the righteous judge, shall give me at that day: and not to me only, but unto all them also that love his appearing.*

Paul, in an emotionally charged farewell to Timothy, and really to the reader, says he is ready to die. He has run the race set before him, as He says in **Hebrews 12:1-3**
*Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us, Looking unto Jesus the author and finisher of our faith; who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising the shame, and is set down at the right hand of the throne of God.
*
In the King James, a keeper is a person or entity that holds, guards, maintains, or has custody of something or someone. This can refer to someone like a prison keeper, the keeper of a park or flock, or someone responsible for a sacred place. The concept extends to holding a position of oversight, like a keeper of the great seal, or having a moral responsibility for another's welfare, as seen in the question "Am I my brother's keeper?"

Paul is talking about his life of ministry, as a keeper of the faith, as the evangelist to the Gentiles. Paul kept the faith and would expect a crown of righteousness for his reward, for those works. 

This has nothing to do with holding on to personal beliefs. 

Context matters.

teachings.title: Did ye at all fast unto me?
teachings.summary: God rejected the exiles' self-made fasts because what pleases Him is true judgment, mercy and care for widows and the fatherless, not religious ritual.
teachings.text:
Here, in the return from the exile in Babylon, the people send men to Jerusalem to inquire about the fasting the Jews had begun while in captivity. They would "weep" during the 5th month, Av, commemorating the time of the desolation of Jerusalem and destruction of the temple. Fasting over their loss.

**2 Kings 25:8-9**
*And in the fifth month, on the seventh day of the month, which is the nineteenth year of king Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, came Nebuzaradan, captain of the guard, a servant of the king of Babylon, unto Jerusalem: And he burnt the house of the Lord, and the king's house, and all the houses of Jerusalem, and every great man's house burnt he with fire.*

And the Lord mentions the similar fast in the 7th month, commemorating the slaying of the Jewish governor Babylon had set over the people;

*And as for the people that remained in the land of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had left, even over them he made Gedaliah the son of Ahikam, the son of Shaphan, ruler....But it came to pass in the seventh month, that Ishmael the son of Nethaniah, the son of Elishama, of the seed royal, came, and ten men with him, and smote Gedaliah, that he died, and the Jews and the Chaldees that were with him at Mizpah.*

But the word of the Lord comes to the prophet, asking *When ye fasted and mourned in the fifth and seventh month, even those seventy years, did ye at all fast unto me, even to me?*

Their fasts were self-centered, remembering their own woes, not to God to bring them out of the situation. Neither were their feasts, when they ate and drank, it was for themselves, not to honor Him.

He references the prophets that came before the captivity, Isaiah and Jeremiah and others, who told them what to do to get right and avoid the destruction that came. To show judgment and mercy. Not grand acts of fasting and weeping.

When things were good, they ignored the prophets. As things improved with the end of captivity, they still hadn't learned the lesson in many ways.

*Thus speaketh the Lord of hosts, saying, Execute true judgment, and shew mercy and compassions every man to his brother: And oppress not the widow, nor the fatherless, the stranger, nor the poor; and let none of you imagine evil against his brother in your heart.*

This is what is pleasing to God, not the blood of bulls and goats. Not the religious acts of piety. Not fasts and rituals. To do unto others. To love thy neighbor. To care for the fatherless and widows.

**James 1:27**
*Pure religion and undefiled before God and the Father is this, To visit the fatherless and widows in their affliction, and to keep himself unspotted from the world.*

This is what God expects of His people. But they had hardened their hearts. And so God says when He cried to them, they wouldn't hear, and so when they would weep for Jerusalem and the Temple, ultimately for themselves, He would not hear them. That He made Jerusalem desolate for their failure to hear. They should be more worried about that judgment than if they should continue in fasts they invented to console themselves.

teachings.title: The way of the Lord is not equal
teachings.summary: Ezekiel 33 concerns physical judgment, not losing salvation; a backslidden believer's past works buy no pass from chastening, while a sinner who gets right is blessed.
teachings.text:
Following the parable of the watchmen, Ezekiel preaches a message to the people; repent and be saved.

The prophet preaches that if the righteous do wicked, are backslidden and not right with God, they will perish in the judgment of Judah. But if the wicked turn to God, restore their pledges and right their wrongs and walk in His statutes, they are forgiven. He shall not die during their tribulation.

*Yet the children of thy people say, The way of the Lord is not equal.* Man says it isn't fair that the wicked be saved by getting right, and their sins are no longer held against them, when their righteousness is forgotten with every sin. They say the Lord's judgment isn't fair.

*O ye house of Israel, I will judge you every one after his ways.*

God's mercy on the sinner who repents isn't fair, it is grace. We all deserve worse. That Him for His grace.

The righteous sin, and think they are better than the wicked who sinned and gets right. This hypocritical judgment is iniquity. It's one of the things God hates the most.

This portion of **Ezekiel 33** is about physical salvation, with a spiritual picture for us today. Many make the entire message spiritual, and apply this to salvation, that you can lose salvation or that we must turn from our sins to be saved. But the context is the physical destruction of Jerusalem and her people.

The spiritual and practical application for believers is that we are His people, as saved Christians. We are Israel. And so, in this life, God will withhold His wrath and chastening to those believers who, however backslidden, come back to the statutes of life; the commandments. The way of the Lord.

While God's wrath is kindled against the backslidden believer who sins, despite their past righteousness.

In practical terms; if you are now living in sin - fornicating, lying, defrauding others, violent, hypocritical, covetous, worldly...or not in prayer, not reading your Bible, not attending church or soul-winning, it does not matter what works of righteousness you were doing before. They don't buy you a pass. You can't coast on "Well, I used to go to church and I used to go soul-winning. I did it for years!"

If you've stopped, you aren't right with God.

And if a greater sinner than you ever were, who never did those things in their life, starts today, they are more right with God than you.

And if you don't think that's fair, you are committing inequity. You are no different than the people who said the way of the Lord is not equal, who were destroyed by the Babylonians.

Again, this applies to chastening of believers. We are saved by grace through faith, not of ourselves. It is a gift of God.

But the blessings of this world come when you are right with God. And He withdraws His protection when those who call themselves by His name don't walk in His ways.

*It is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God.*

If you aren't right, get right. Life is but a vapour. The time is now. Don't rest on your laurels, but press forward for the mark of a triumphant Christian life.

teachings.title: The fathers have eaten sour grapes
teachings.summary: Ezekiel 18 teaches against original sin: each man is judged for his own sin, and each generation must get right regardless of its fathers.
teachings.text:
This prophecy of Ezekiel is an often cited chapter regarding the doctrine of "original sin," which it clearly teaches against. But it is also cited by workies as to why turning from sin is part of salvation. But as always, we need to look at the context.

First, the parable among the children of Israel in Judah, that the fathers ate sour grapes, but the children's teeth are on edge, has to be understood. And it is something many of us are guilty of saying.

The judgment against the people had come, and Babylon was bringing them into captivity, and slaying many. So the younger generation was blaming the sins of the older generation for their troubles. That their fathers had eaten the sour grapes but they were the ones with the taste in their mouth. That God's judgment was unfair, and they were being punished for the sins of the father.

We often blame Boomers for ruining the country they inherited, and it is true. They set up high places and committed adultery and violence and rejected the God of their fathers. But many who complain the loudest about this are themselves living the same way, or worse.

Revival is on us, today and our present generation. As it says in verse 14, *Now, lo, if he beget a son, that seeth all his father's sins which he hath done, and considereth, and doeth not such like*...he shall surely live.

It is up to us to get right, regardless of the hole dug by our parents. This is true regardless of the age we live in. And if we haven't, there's always time for turning from our own sins, and walking in righteousness, through Christ.

The Lord has no pleasure in the deaths of the wicked, but rejoices in those who turn to Him and live.

The word of the Lord shuts down the idea of original sin condemning us. The sins and the righteousness of each generation are their own. A man isn't judged by the sins of their father or his righteousness, but by theirs. And vice versa.

We aren't condemned by Adam's sin, but by our own. We have his nature, being sons. But we all make our own way.

But the Lord challenged the people saying He is unfair, because in fact they did as their fathers.

teachings.title: Grace sufficient and disagreeing peaceably
teachings.summary: Recounts a sermon on Philippians 4:19 and Lazarus and the rich man, then shows from 2 Corinthians 12 that God's grace is sufficient and urges peaceable disagreement between brethren.
teachings.text:
A brother recently guest preaching for an ailing pastor, preached a great sermon on the promise of God from **Philippians 4:19**;

*But my God shall supply all your need according to his riches in glory by Christ Jesus.*

And while making great points on walking in the Spirit, expecting chastisement rather than blessings if you're backsliding, he made an odd choice to use the story of Lazarus and the rich man from **Luke 16** to say that Lazarus was clearly backslidden and being punished by God for his sin, but despite that he was still saved. 

His premise was that, because **Philippians 4:19** is true, that the only explanation for him being a believer, yet a filthy beggar of crumbs, covered with sores, liked by dogs, having misery in this life, was he was backslidden and unresponsive to God's chastening. 

Immediately, my mind went just a few chapters to the left, to **Luke 13:1-5**;
*There were present at that season some that told him of the Galilaeans, whose blood Pilate had mingled with their sacrifices. And Jesus answering said unto them, Suppose ye that these Galilaeans were sinners above all the Galilaeans, because they suffered such things? I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish. Or those eighteen, upon whom the tower in Siloam fell, and slew them, think ye that they were sinners above all men that dwelt in Jerusalem? I tell you, Nay: but, except ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.*

Or why Job's friends were wrong to assume he deserved what was happening to him, or **Matthew 5:45**;

*That ye may be the children of your Father which is in heaven: for he maketh his sun to rise on the evil and on the good, and sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust.*

Or **Ecclesiastes 9:11**
*I returned, and saw under the sun, that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favour to men of skill; but time and chance happeneth to them all*.

I also thought of this story from **John 9:1-7**; *And as Jesus passed by, he saw a man which was blind from his birth. And his disciples asked him, saying, Master, who did sin, this man, or his parents, that he was born blind? Jesus answered, Neither hath this man sinned, nor his parents: but that the works of God should be made manifest in him. I must work the works of him that sent me, while it is day: the night cometh, when no man can work. As long as I am in the world, I am the light of the world. When he had thus spoken, he spat on the ground, and made clay of the spittle, and he anointed the eyes of the blind man with the clay, And said unto him, Go, wash in the pool of Siloam, (which is by interpretation, Sent.) He went his way therefore, and washed, and came seeing.*

My brother's assumption that Lazarus' life contradicted the promise of God to fulfill all his needs, and so had to be rationalized into making sense, failed to take into account the glory of God being demonstrated. That when Abraham says to the rich man in Hell, *Son, remember that thou in thy lifetime receivedst thy good things, and likewise Lazarus evil things: but now he is comforted, and thou art tormented*, that the story has served as a comfort to the broken hearted and a warning to the proud, that has been used uncountable times to show the glory of God and His promises. 

What my friend saw as eternal shame for Lazarus in Heaven, every time the story is preached, I see as a wonderful blessing for a faithful man who lived under terrible conditions for a brief moment, but who is in eternity with Christ, knowing that what he suffered on earth wasn't in vain. 

And finally, that while our expectations for God's promised providence should be trusted, in the end our suffering may not be of our own cause, but for His glory. His grace should be sufficient.

**2 Corinthians 12:7-9**
*And lest I should be exalted above measure through the abundance of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me, lest I should be exalted above measure. For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me. And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.*

So, while he was correct in preaching against spiritual complacency in expectation of the promise of blessings, I vehemently disagreed with his proof text and assumptions. 

My pride wanted to immediately confront him on it. That he was drawing inferences that weren't present in the text and that he was missing the bigger picture, and that there is no inherent contradiction between the promise to provide and Lazarus' life. That His grace is all the provision we need, anything else is a blessing. And while, when we are afflicted, we should examine ourselves before complaining to God, we shouldn't assume every bad thing that happens to another is for their own sin...I wanted badly to confront him with this truth. 

But, praise God, I stopped to consider the matter first. To reflect before speaking. To make sure I was acting out of love for a brother, not my own pride. 

At the end of the day, it's a minor disagreement over an opinion. And despite being convinced I have all the facts and all the arguments and all the proof texts and everything else, I determined it is better to allow him his opinion, and talk softly about what mine is, and why, than charge at him in rebuke.

Don't let how Internet fights are conducted influence you, especially in real life. Understand that there's room for disagreement. That other people don't have to have total conformity to your opinion to be brothers. That *If it be possible, as much as lieth in you, live peaceably with all men.*

teachings.title: Do not wait for persecution to go soul winning
teachings.summary: Pairs Acts 1:8 and Acts 8:1-4 with Matthew 24 to warn that complacent Christians may be scattered by persecution, and urges going soul winning now.
teachings.text:
**Acts 1:8**
*But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth.*

**Acts 8:1-4**
*And Saul was consenting unto his death. And at that time there was a great persecution against the church which was at Jerusalem; and they were all scattered abroad throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria, except the apostles. And devout men carried Stephen to his burial, and made great lamentation over him. As for Saul, he made havock of the church, entering into every house, and haling men and women committed them to prison. Therefore they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word.*

Jesus told them to go out to the world and spread the Gospel to every creature, to the uttermost parts of the Earth. And instead they stayed in Jerusalem. 

So the Lord brought tribulation and persecution to them in Judea, scattering the saints abroad, so that they would preach everywhere. 

Are you waiting for the tribulation to go out into all the world and preach? 

**Matthew 24:9-14**
***Then shall they deliver you up to be afflicted, and shall kill you: and ye shall be hated of all nations for my name's sake.** And then shall many be offended, and shall betray one another, and shall hate one another. And many false prophets shall rise, and shall deceive many. And because iniquity shall abound, the love of many shall wax cold. But he that shall endure unto the end, the same shall be saved. **And this gospel of the kingdom shall be preached in all the world for a witness unto all nations; and then shall the end come.***

When Christians are complacent and don't go out into the highways and hedges, compelling others to come in, spreading the gospel, God will bring persecution and tribulation to get us off our pews. 

Don't wait to be persecuted for His name's sake before you get up and go soul-winning.

teachings.title: Chastening of the proud believer
teachings.summary: Like Nebuchadnezzar, a prideful backslidden believer may be chastened by God, even with mental affliction.
teachings.text:
One last point; God chastens whom He would, scourging every son. Too many Christians get comfortable in the blessings and protection God provides us. Like Nebuchadnezzar, we not only take things for granted, but begin to pridefully take credit for the things in our life that are by the grace of God.

He heard God's word and forgot all about it. He became prideful and paid for it.

I think mental illness is often from God, making us deal with the cognitive dissonance of our lies and self-deception and the truth of His word.

Don't be surprised if you continue down the road, backslidden, to have this type of punishment. I have both observed it and experienced a fraction of it. Don't let it happen to you!

teachings.title: Call the sabbath a delight
teachings.summary: The Sabbath in Isaiah 58 is spoken of as Him, Christ, and keeping it means resting in Jesus and lifting the burdens of others.
teachings.text:
*Then shalt thou call, and the Lord shall answer; thou shalt cry, and he shall say, Here I am. If thou take away from the midst of thee the yoke, the putting forth of the finger, and speaking vanity*.

The Lord promises us redemption, restoration. The reestablishment of our nation. Blessings and hope for many generations after us. He seeks mercy and righteous judgment, not the blood of bulls and goats. Not fastings and vain words.

*If thou turn away thy foot from the sabbath, from doing thy pleasure on my holy day; and call the sabbath a delight, the holy of the Lord, honourable; and shalt honour him, not doing thine own ways, nor finding thine own pleasure, nor speaking thine own words:*

Notice something here, that the word says the Sabbath is a "Him." The delight of the Holy One. Christ Jesus. Doing that which He did. Healing the sick. Tending to the broken hearted. The Lord of the Sabbath calling us to take the time, ceasing from our labors to help others. Not to be a burden, but to lift others from theirs. To rest in Jesus.

And delight ourselves in the Lord. Amen

teachings.title: Flee fornication, marry, and church discipline
teachings.summary: Teaches from 1 Corinthians 5, 6 and 7 that those living together unmarried should stop and marry, and that a brother in unrepentant fornication is to be disciplined out of the church.
teachings.text:
**1 Corinthians 6:18-20**
*Flee fornication. Every sin that a man doeth is without the body; but he that committeth fornication sinneth against his own body. What? know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you, which ye have of God, and ye are not your own? For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God in your body, and in your spirit, which are God's.*

If you are currently living with or fornicating with your boyfriend or girlfriend, you should stop and get married. 

**1 Corinthians 7:2**
*But to avoid fornication, let every man have his own wife, and let every woman have her own husband.*

**1 Corinthians 5:9-11 **
*I wrote unto you in an epistle not to company with fornicators: Yet not altogether with the fornicators of this world, or with the covetous, or extortioners, or with idolaters; for then must ye needs go out of the world. But now I have written unto you not to keep company, if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolator, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat.
*
You should be disciplined out of the church if you are living in sin or engaging in fornication, and won't abstain and get married.

teachings.title: Leaving the consequences to our children
teachings.summary: Some sins bring lasting consequences on our children, so put them above yourself and turn quickly to the Lord when you err.
teachings.text:
Yet, Hezekiah takes the wrong lesson from this warning, taking comfort that the worst will be for future generations, and not his to deal with.

How familiar this is for us today. How our fathers fell to sin and pride, squandering the blessings of God, and leaving their children to deal with the inevitable consequences? That is why, even when we backslide, even when we let our pride get the better of us, and we do that which is wrong in the sight of God, that we turn again to Him in humility, seeking forgiveness.

There are some mistakes we make, and sins we commit, that have long lasting repercussions. An act of fornication that results in a baby, or a disease. A marriage broken by adultery. A drunken night ending in death.

Hezekiah had his pride become a cause for his children to be slaves and his nation made desolate, and he took selfish solace in the fact it wouldn't affect him. What a wicked thing.

Put others, especially your children, above yourself and when you err, turn to the Lord for forgiveness least your sins rebound in future generations.

teachings.title: Holding the standard in church and life
teachings.summary: Pairs Romans 7:12 and 1 Timothy 1:8-11 with the point that a person cannot expect society to keep godly standards if the church and the believer do not.
teachings.text:
**Romans 7:12**
*Wherefore the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good.*

**1 Timothy 1:8-11**
*But we know that the law is good, if a man use it lawfully; knowing this, that the law is not made for a righteous man, but for the lawless and disobedient, for the ungodly and for sinners, for unholy and profane, for murderers of fathers and murderers of mothers, for manslayers, for whoremongers, for them that defile themselves with mankind, for menstealers, for liars, for perjured persons, and if there be any other thing that is contrary to sound doctrine; according to the glorious gospel of the blessed God, which was committed to my trust.*

How can we make society conform to Godly principles and standards if you aren't even holding them in your church or your life.

teachings.title: Trusting in Egypt is death
teachings.summary: Egypt pictures the world and our old life of bondage, and God's children must not turn back to it for help in tribulation.
teachings.text:
The prophetic warning to Judah, that when their time of tribulation came, the captivity to Babylon, not to flee to or trust in Egypt to save them, was fulfilled in Jeremiah's day.

He also warned them, referring back to the prophets, beginning with Isaiah. God, knowing what they would do, warns against it. And you know those in Jerusalem who believed the word of God did not flee, and be destroyed in the way.

The dual fulfillment here is also clear, the Holy One of Israel, the Lord Christ Jesus at His second coming and the wrath that pours out from His lips, the fire of Tophet, a name for Hell, is lit from the brimstone from His mouth, that kindles it.

Egypt is a representation of the world, our pre-Christian life of sin, under the yoke of the law, slaves to sin. As the Bible says again and again of the Israelites being led by Moses, that in their freedom they would long to return to the bondage of Egypt out of fear or inconvenience.

**Exodus 13:17**
*And it came to pass, when Pharaoh had let the people go, that God led them not through the way of the land of the Philistines, although that was near; for God said, Lest peradventure the people repent when they see war, and they return to Egypt*.

This is written for our admonition, that we who are His children don't turn again to the world and to sin when we face tribulation. That trusting in Egypt is death.

We all come out of Egypt. We all are baptized in the crossing, and sojourn in the wilderness, awaiting the promised land.

The promise of paradise on the other side is the hope of our faith. Without that hope, we fear and faint. Relying on the world to save us is folly, we should suffer gladly that the Lord delivers us.

The wicked will be punished. The Lord will fight for us, and destroy those that trouble us, and has a place prepared for them, deep and large, the pile is fire and much wood. The breath of the Lord is like a stream of brimstone. Amen

teachings.title: Following God's commandments and the law used lawfully
teachings.summary: Calls believers to keep God's commandments, tithe, attend church and win souls, and says the law is good when used lawfully.
teachings.text:
Follow the commandments of God that it be well with you. Follow the Law to show that you love Jesus. Hold others to standards that it should lead them to understand they are sinners in need of redemption. Advocate for the law because it is good, when used lawfully, to punish evildoers. 

Romans 7:12
*Wherefore the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good.*

Tithe. Go to church. Stay sober and vigilant. Win souls. Edify the brethren. Don't lie. Don't steal. Don't lust in your heart or fornicate with your members. Don't cheat each other. Look after one another and place the brethren's profit above yours. 

This shouldn't be controversial.

teachings.title: Reading the Bible for yourself
teachings.summary: Encourages reading the Bible itself through a reading plan instead of study Bibles or devotionals, and notes that Psalms and Proverbs read twice cover a year.
teachings.text:
If you want to grow closer to the Lord this year, I encourage you to find a Bible reading plan and stick with it. 

Don't use study Bibles or devotionals or a verse of the day. Make 2025 the year you take the training wheels off and read the Bible for yourself in the Spirit. 

There is no devotional or study guide better than the Bible itself. We have the whole word of God, He can talk to you every day if you let Him. What a privilege! What a blessing!

Did you know there are 150 Psalms and 31 chapters of Proverbs? That's 181 chapters. If you use them as a daily devotional in addition to regular reading, that covers a half of a year. 

If you read through Psalms and Proverbs twice, that's 362 days. (God even gives you 3 days of grace a year!)

Instead of reading other people's prayers, or verses curated and taken out of context in a devotional, why not read the prayer book and wisdom written by the Lord?

teachings.title: God desires mercy, not sacrifice
teachings.summary: Sacrifices were always for man's benefit, pointing to Christ's once-for-all offering, and God desires obedience, confession and mercy toward others.
teachings.text:
God delighting in mercy and right judgement over sacrifices is a theme of scripture.

**Psalm 51:16-17**
*For thou desirest not sacrifice; else would I give it: thou delightest not in burnt offering. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit: a broken and a contrite heart, O God, thou wilt not despise.*

**Psalm 40:6-8**
*Sacrifice and offering thou didst not desire; mine ears hast thou opened: burnt offering and sin offering hast thou not required. Then said I, Lo, I come: in the volume of the book it is written of me, I delight to do thy will, O my God: yea, thy law is within my heart.*

**Isaiah 1:11**
*To what purpose is the multitude of your sacrifices unto me? saith the Lord: I am full of the burnt offerings of rams, and the fat of fed beasts; and I delight not in the blood of bullocks, or of lambs, or of he goats.*

**Jeremiah 7:21-23**
*Thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel; Put your burnt offerings unto your sacrifices, and eat flesh. For I spake not unto your fathers, nor commanded them in the day that I brought them out of the land of Egypt, concerning burnt offerings or sacrifices: But this thing commanded I them, saying, Obey my voice, and I will be your God, and ye shall be my people: and walk ye in all the ways that I have commanded you, that it may be well unto you.*

**Hebrews 10:4-10**
*For it is not possible that the blood of bulls and of goats should take away sins. Wherefore when he cometh into the world, he saith, Sacrifice and offering thou wouldest not, but a body hast thou prepared me: In burnt offerings and sacrifices for sin thou hast had no pleasure. Then said I, Lo, I come (in the volume of the book it is written of me,) to do thy will, O God. Above when he said, Sacrifice and offering and burnt offerings and offering for sin thou wouldest not, neither hadst pleasure therein; which are offered by the law. Then said he, Lo, I come to do thy will, O God. He taketh away the first, that he may establish the second. By the which will we are sanctified through the offering of the body of Jesus Christ once for all.*

The sacrifices were always for man, not God. Even the greatest and only true sacrifice for sin, the blood of Christ Jesus, is for our benefit, not God's.

He wishes us to seek Him. To obey, and to confess to Him when we fall short. To turn to Him continually. And to show mercy and judgement and love, one to another. Forgiving and being forgiven. Being sown in righteousness by faith, and reaping the fruit, bringing in the sheaves. Others brought to the truth, calling upon the name of the Lord. Taking care of the widow. Judging the fatherless. Esteeming the profit of others more than ourselves.

The sacrifices were to show the Israelites of Christ to come, and satisfy that itch in us that there must be blood to pay for our inequities.

Upon the unrighteous, blood is required of blood. But the purpose of Jesus' sacrifice is that we have settled that debt of sin forever, washed clean in His blood, that we may go forth in mercy and His light so shine from us.

teachings.title: Lying vanities forsake mercy
teachings.summary: Warns that those who deceive themselves with vain lies about their behavior forsake their own mercy and reap what they sow.
teachings.text:
One of the things that you learn when you read the Bible regularly is that if you choose to deceive yourself, and tell yourself vain lies about your own behavior, God has no mercy for you. You will reap what you sow. 

That should terrify people. And yet...

**Jonah 2:8**
*They that observe lying vanities forsake their own mercy*.

teachings.title: Raising children in a separated home
teachings.summary: Reflects on fundamentalist families whose children turn to the world as adults, urging patience, ruling well and the Psalms as David's example of right doctrine.
teachings.text:
The fundamentalist revival we are having over the past 10 years or so, has produced more young Christian families than we have had in a long time, living separated lives. 

We have **entire congregations** raising their children as "pastor's kids." A generation of them. The first of them hitting adulthood now. Raised in the Internet age. Who near majority age and turn immediately to the world, who knows they are in sin, become resentful of their upbringing, and look to paint their parents, and forebears in the faith, as the actual wicked ones. The real workers of iniquity. 

Not them, fornicating and drinking and doing drugs, consuming worldly music and entertainment, being willful and shameful. 

They never leave their "abusive home" and go to a new church and just be on fire for the Lord, doing their own thing. 

It is tear them down so you can justify your sin. 

And now we know there are vultures who will prime the pump, reprobates who are, the Bible says;

...*filled with all unrighteousness, fornication, wickedness, covetousness, maliciousness; full of envy, murder, debate, deceit, malignity; whisperers, backbiters, haters of God, despiteful, proud, boasters, inventors of evil things, disobedient to parents, without understanding, covenantbreakers, without natural affection, implacable, unmerciful: who knowing the judgment of God, that they which commit such things are worthy of death, not only do the same, but have pleasure in them that do them.*

So we know that the world loves to snare fundamentalist Christian kids. 

Separation is commanded. 

How do you navigate this going forward, to avoid that outcome, the world leading them astray. 

*For of this sort are they which creep into houses, and lead captive silly women laden with sins, led away with divers lusts*

It's a tough one. I am glad most of my kids are grown, and I've been through this myself, and it is hard. 

I have learned a few things. Each kid has it better than the last. I can tell you read your Bible, be patient and fair. Rule well. And if the occasion comes for discipline, use your best discretion. 

That's the Biblical way to raise your children. 

Every kid is different. YMMV but start with scripture

David was a man after God's own heart. We have the example of his life, and an amazing window into his thoughts on God, his prayer life and right doctrine in the Psalms. 

What an amazing gift God has given us for what pleases God in our lives. And what we should avoid that displeases Him. And how to act when we screw up anyway.

teachings.title: Honoring parents and forgiving debts
teachings.summary: Reminds that rewards at the judgment seat are not for being a victim of one's parents, that a forgiven believer should not dwell on what others deserve, and cites the Lord's prayer on forgiving debts.
teachings.text:
People should pray that their pastor's biggest flaw is that their children say they were disciplined too much, rather than too little.

At the judgment seat of Christ, no one's going to give you rewards for how big a victim you were. You won't receive crowns because of how unfairly your parents treated you when you were a child. 

But you will be judged for how well you honored them.

You deserve death and hell. If you're a saved Christian, you've been forgiven that debt. 

Should we then start talking about what people who have wronged you deserve....? Really?

**Matthew 6: 9-13**
*After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. Thy kingdom come. Thy will be done in earth, as it is in heaven. Give us this day our daily bread. And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors. And lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil: For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. Amen.*

teachings.title: Let us walk in the Spirit
teachings.summary: Paul encourages believers to walk in the Spirit and bear its fruit, which shows the fruit is not automatic or outwardly obvious, rebuking fruit inspectors' hypocrisy.
teachings.text:
*This I say then, Walk in the Spirit, and ye shall not fulfil the lust of the flesh. For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would. But if ye be led of the Spirit, ye are not under the law.*

After upbraiding the Galatians for being misled by Judaizers, and destroying the idea that salvation requires a form of sanctification of the flesh to be had, the Apostle goes on to encourage them to walk in the Spirit, that they can manifest the fruit of the Spirit:

 *But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, longsuffering, gentleness, goodness, faith, Meekness, temperance: against such there is no law. And they that are Christ's have crucified the flesh with the affections and lusts. If we live in the Spirit, let us also walk in the Spirit. Let us not be desirous of vain glory, provoking one another, envying one another*

Let us...If we...let us... Encouraging the brethren. If such fruit were naturally come by, and obvious to outside observation, it would not need to be encouraged. It wouldn't need to be something to strive for. And the provocation and envying, the accusing hypocrisy of fruit inspectors, the leaven of the Pharisees, wouldn't be being rebuked.

teachings.title: Saved but living in the old flesh
teachings.summary: A saved person can return to the old life since good works are not automatic, so we should disciple and encourage rather than doubt their salvation or condemn them.
teachings.text:
There's also a lesson here for saved Christians. Those who are the rocky soil, who receive the truth of the word with gladness and hope, but because they have no root in themselves, with her and die without producing fruit.

It is possible to receive the gospel and believe unto salvation and yet return to the same old life. Healed, washed, clean and reborn the way the Syrian Captain was, and yet living in the old flesh doing the same old things.
